webLocationsForLocation.name: 5 Mile
webLocationsForLocation.description: Great rock with a wide variety of problems right next to the road make 5 Mile one of the most popular areas in the canyon. Ever popular moderate offwidth, 'Big Mouth' can be found within a few feet of the road, with many quality slabs and juggy faces nearby. Plenty of quality intermediates like 'Surfboard', 'Green Face', 'Baldy' are all right there. Loads of advanced and elite variations cover the 'Mr. Smiley' face on the Split Boulder. 'Butt Trumpet' is a popular advanced line, and has several elite variations. The Golden zone to the east has several great advanced lines like 'Golden' and 'Mr. T' as well as the elite highball 'Kill it in the Evening' and smaller moderates scattered through the surrounding woods. The newer Sentinels Zone is home to elite line 'Omega Man' and lots of highball moderates and intermediates and projects though the trail system is less developed.

parent_location.name: Little Cottonwood Canyon
parent_location.description:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s climbing area sits just 20 minutes southeast of downtown Salt Lake City and stands as one of North America’s most concentrated city-side climbing spots. Both local and professional traveling climbers have spent decades developing the canyon, which now boasts over 5,000 boulder problems. 

The canyon’s granite walls have drawn climbers’ attention for more than 40 years, however, the area has experienced rapid growth over the last several years—now hosting two of the hardest problems in the country, “The Grand Illusion” and “Sosa,” both (V16).

Little Cottonwood’s unique quartz monzonite walls give climbers a unique granite experience, with some small pockets of limestone throughout—particularly at the mouth of the canyon. The rock is characterized by crystal-heavy slopers and crimps lower in the canyon, tighter grained rock at higher elevations, friction dependence, and slippery, textureless holds on more popular climbs.

Season:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s best climbing happens during fall and spring. The canyon’s climbing conditions reach their sweet spot in October/November. Temperatures stay between 66°F highs and 44°F lows. Nearly all areas will be accessible during these months.The spring also offers great conditions, however climber’s will have to navigate the melting snowpack, the degree to which varies year-to-year.

History:
Mike Beck began climbing in the mid 1980s. In 1988, following a bouldering trip to the world-famous Fontainebleau, France, Mike Beck was inspired upon returning back home to Salt Lake City. At the time, there were maybe 50 problems in the canyon, maximum. That visit to France kicked off an explosion of him and his friends seeking out and developing the bouldering in LCC in a concerted effort.

He and his friends collaborated to create The Black Bible, a guidebook to Utah bouldering. Mike lead the charge on the LCC chapters and this was the primary source of recorded bouldering information for many years. In more recent years, Mike teamed up with a newer climber and data geek, Scott Stoddard. Together, using Scott’s technical and organization skills and Mike’s historical knowledge, they authored a new and extremely comprehensive guidebook for Little Cottonwood Canyon on KAYA.

Read the full article for everything you need to know when bouldering at Little Cottonwood Canyon: https://blog.kayaclimb.com/essential-lcc-climbing-guide-when-where-how-to-boulder-in-little-cottonwood/

webLocationsForLocation.name: Cabbage Patch
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Cabbage Patch is one of the most accessible roadside areas in the canyon. Jack's Boulder just feet from parking is loaded with popular moderates like 'Jack's Slab' and intermediates like 'Fat Albert Gang' and 'Fungus' and the ever popular 'Double Dyno' is just up hill. The 'Dean Problem' and its harder variations on the back of Jack's are some of the most interesting shothole climbing in the canyon, and reach into the advanced range. To the west 'Tom's Problem' is a popular intermediate, and just above it the Bagins cave houses a myriad of popular advanced and elite variations. To the west the Tiger Snake has several worthy lines and the area uphill around the Monolith also has many good lines including the new 'Luke's Dyno'.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Crescent Crack boulders are mostly new blocks up by the cliffs from a recent rockslide. There are two ways to get there. Either park at the Park n' Ride and walk through Secret Garden and take the left turn up the Alpine Loop Trail, or reach the same turn coming from Cabbage Patch. Follow the trail up hill and you'll reach the Crescent Crack area as you approach the cliffs.

webLocationsForLocation.name: East Gate
webLocationsForLocation.description: Though just yards away from The Gate, The East Gate wasn't developed until decades later in the 90's. It is packed with great problems on quality rock, but it is a little harder to navigate and less busy than it's more popular neighbor. 'Round Room' is really unique and one of the most popular intermediates in the canyon. Other popular intermediates include 'Anonymous Arete', 'Coffee Girl', 'Red Stain' and 'Hidden Arete'. There are plenty of good moderate slabs scattered around the area, along with more on the Icarus boulder, the Between Boulders, and 'Potty Mouth' crack is great. Selection gets thinner in the advanced range, but 'M&M Roof' is a popular line and the newer 'Sunrise Arete' high in the talus and 'Jameson Breakfast' out east in The Farm zone are both worth a visit. Elite potential can be found on undone projects including some near the parking lot and many more up in the newer areas.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Everything
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Everything area above The Parking Lot and Secret Garden is a bit of a hike, but explorers will be rewarded with some excellent problems and plenty of project potential. There are several unknown blocks with project potential on the way up the east side of Bong Eater. Chad's Cave, just northeast of Bong Eater houses loads of fun intermediate and advanced lines on steep and blocky Big Cottonwood style features. Continue up the gully to a nice new elite line 'Elevated Squeezing' and project potential on the nearby Samurai Slabs. At the top of the area is the Everything Boulder with several high quality Advanced and Elite problems on a tall slightly overhanging face with Big Cottonwood style rock. A few large boulders hide potential projects higher on the hill.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Green A. Gully
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Green Adjective Gully is a newer area up the hill to the east of The Gate. The huge boulders high in the talus are densely packed with excellent problems and lots of projects waiting to be done with expansive views of the canyon. The West Gate zone off the left side of the trail has great problems across the grades from silly moderate 'Far Away Horse' to new intermediate classic 'Knockin' Boots' and the more advanced 'Body Shop' and 'Enter the Brine'. Further up is the daring high ball 'Last First Crack' surrounded by more great problems and potential projects. High on the hill in the talus to the right elite lines can be found like 'Hour of Power', 'Mr. Peanut' and 'The Settlement' as well as loads of excellent intermediates like 'The Fin' and 'The Shield' along with advanced problems like 'Karate Chop Kid', 'Halcyon' and 'Naughty Neighbor'.

webLocationsForLocation.description_bouldering: The Green Adjective Gully is a newer area up the hill to the east of The Gate. The huge boulders high in the talus are densely packed with excellent problems and lots of projects waiting to be done with expansive views of the canyon. The West Gate zone off the left side of the trail has great problems across the grades from silly moderate 'Far Away Horse' to new intermediate classic 'Knockin' Boots' and the more advanced 'Body Shop' and 'Enter the Brine'. Further up is the daring high ball 'Last First Crack' surrounded by more great problems and potential projects. High on the hill in the talus to the right elite lines can be found like 'Hour of Power', 'Mr. Peanut' and 'The Settlement' as well as loads of excellent intermediates like 'The Fin' and 'The Shield' along with advanced problems like 'Karate Chop Kid', 'Halcyon' and 'Naughty Neighbor'.
webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Park at the Gate then head north west past the Standard Overhand and the Tower to reach a large talus field. West Gate is to the left, University is to the right. Continue on up the trail to reach the main Green A Boulders.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Grit Mill
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Grit Mill (Sometimes mistakenly called the Grist Mill) is a few boulders around the Grit Mill parking lot below the LDS church vault. All the boulders in the guide are on public land, but going above the higher road behind Golden plates is private property. The Vault Roof cluster visible from the parking lot holds a variety of fun moderates, intermediates and one advanced problem: 'The Vault Roof'. 'Lava tag' is a unique intermediate on the back side. The rest are fun moderates with a few getting pretty tall on the south side. the huge 'Golden Plates' boulder straight up from the parking lot has several highball slabs and a few intermediate problems around the back. Just above it to the northwest is an interesting cave called Davey Jone's Locker that houses a few problems and lots of potential variations. The 'Holy' boulder has two fun intermediates 'Holy' and 'Full Authority'. There is some project potential down by 'Beach Town' and up the gully above 'Gripsalot'.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Hidden Forest
webLocationsForLocation.description: Hidden forest is a beautiful secluded area with an excellent handfull of classic boulders. Great rock quality is spread across a broad range of grades including the advanced sloper testpiece 'Duct Tape', great introductions to intermediate LCC with 'Dale's Arete' and 'Steve's Problem' and lovely moderates like 'Kate Moss'.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Highborn
webLocationsForLocation.description: Developed by Landon Schoenmann, the Highborn boulder is a medium sized block resting high on the sloping cliffs to the south of the Parking Lot and Temple Quarry. There are only two lines on the block, but they are good quality and the view is phenomenal.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Hitch Hiker
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Hitch Hiker area includes some great boulders to the west along the creek along with a string of smaller blocks to the east. Older favorites like the moderate Hitch Hiker slabs are joined by popular newcomers like 'Air Jordan' and 'Gone 'Til November'. Boulders in the creek bed are best climbed later in the Fall when the creek is low.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Jimbo Boulders
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Jimbo Boulders, found by Jim, are in a secluded forest area to the east of the foot bridge with a few good blocks including the advanced testpiece slab 'Neurosis' V8 and several fun lines on the Ms. Smiley Boulder along with some potential for more lines on other small blocks in the talus above.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Junkie Boulders
webLocationsForLocation.description: Junkie Boulders have been around since the 90's, and while the area enjoys cooler temps and all day shade, it is lesser known and tends to be less crowded. With good moderate slabs, and well liked intermediates like 'Junkie Arete', and several notable intermediate and advanced lines on the Batman Boulder, along with elite new lines like 'Pain and Ankle' in the talus, it's worthy area to spend some time. There is still plenty of project potential in the talus as well as a few undone lines on the 'Trail of Fears' Boulder by the trail.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Outer Canyon
webLocationsForLocation.description: An expansive boulder covered hillside north west of the canyon entrance, Outer Canyon gets year round sun, so it's a good place for Winter climbing, and gets quite hot in the summer. Some of the rock can be rather chossy, but a few gems are worth the hike including the massive Golden Egg, crystal covered Gemstone, and the Feature covered Dice Cube. There are also several excellent kid friendly boulders like The Shard, and The Birth Mark. Ever wish you could bring pooch to LCC? You're in luck! Outer Canyon is also the only boulder area in Little Cottonwood where dogs are allowed. Some boulders are on private property, but Salt Lake City is OK with bouldering as long as people stay away from the clearly marked water tanks, control startion, and service road in the Shark Tooth and Pioneer sub areas.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: About a mile north west of the Little Cottonwood Park n' Ride, there is a dirt pullout on the east side of the road. Park here and head east up the trail at the south corner of the pullout to access the main boulders. The trail will head uphill for about an 8th of a mile to reach the Pioneer Boulders off to the left of the trail. Then the trail curves around to the south past the Golden Egg and onto The Shard and The Gemstone. To access The Dice Cube it is easier to hike along the dirt road heading south from the pullout until you reach the Meat Balls boulders, and head up the switchbacks from there.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Parking Lot
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Parking Lot has a handful of fun boulders within seconds of your car. The cluster around the Shothole Boulder near the entrance has a number of good moderate and intermediate lines as well as the new elite problem 'Criminology' and a handfull of potential projects. Another cluster can be found along the beginning of the trail up to Secret Garden including solid intermediate slab 'No Parking' and a handfull of advanced lines around 'Holy Hell' that deserve more traffic. The Bush boulder has several quality moderates along with some newer advanced variations.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Riverside
webLocationsForLocation.description: Just across the road from 5 Mile, Riverside is home to a wide variety of classic problems on both sides of the creek including the picturesque 'Blue Steel'. Many quality problems across the grade range can be found right by the road on the Syringe boulder with many fun moedrates and intermediates on the way down the trail and to the west. The Riverside boulder proper is home to classic advanced line 'Shivers' and intermediates 'Jim' and the classic LCC slab 'Feck'. Across the bridge behind 'Blue Steel' are the advanced classic 'The Buzz' and it's elite variations as well as "Alzheimer's' in the Buzz zone. Further west on teh Far Side boulder popular intermediate 'Seems Easy' can be found along with several good moderte face problems on the back, and nearby the advanced arete 'Surprise' and it's elite variations are well liked. Newer boulders up in the Expadition zone are mostly in the moderate and intermediate grades, but a hand full of harder problems like 'The Sorting Hat' and 'JRich' have been established. West world has a few good lines and several smaller blocks awaiting development.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Park on the south side of the road just past a guard rail and work your way down the hill near the guard rail to reach the quarry trail below. Find a good place to cross the creek and there are some trails through a clearing on the other side leading into the woods where Shadows can be found in a gully.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Snowbird North
webLocationsForLocation.description: Snowbird North includes two fantastic boulders with great rock quality near the road. The first is the Inception boulder with loads of moderate slab problems on the north east side, some popular intermediates on the south side like 'Jansen's Problem', and loads of harder lines with variation in the cave on the west side like 'Inception' and 'Super Chunk'. Further up the trail is the Sam Trap Boulder with popular 'Dick Van Dyke' traverse, 'Ping' great slabs on the west side and the elite traverse 'Wheel of Snowbird'.

Detox is a rounded bulge hidden near the road, while Swamp Thing is a slightly overhanging face down in the reeds by the creek.

parent_location.name: Little Cottonwood Canyon
parent_location.description:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s climbing area sits just 20 minutes southeast of downtown Salt Lake City and stands as one of North America’s most concentrated city-side climbing spots. Both local and professional traveling climbers have spent decades developing the canyon, which now boasts over 5,000 boulder problems. 

The canyon’s granite walls have drawn climbers’ attention for more than 40 years, however, the area has experienced rapid growth over the last several years—now hosting two of the hardest problems in the country, “The Grand Illusion” and “Sosa,” both (V16).

Little Cottonwood’s unique quartz monzonite walls give climbers a unique granite experience, with some small pockets of limestone throughout—particularly at the mouth of the canyon. The rock is characterized by crystal-heavy slopers and crimps lower in the canyon, tighter grained rock at higher elevations, friction dependence, and slippery, textureless holds on more popular climbs.

Season:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s best climbing happens during fall and spring. The canyon’s climbing conditions reach their sweet spot in October/November. Temperatures stay between 66°F highs and 44°F lows. Nearly all areas will be accessible during these months.The spring also offers great conditions, however climber’s will have to navigate the melting snowpack, the degree to which varies year-to-year.

History:
Mike Beck began climbing in the mid 1980s. In 1988, following a bouldering trip to the world-famous Fontainebleau, France, Mike Beck was inspired upon returning back home to Salt Lake City. At the time, there were maybe 50 problems in the canyon, maximum. That visit to France kicked off an explosion of him and his friends seeking out and developing the bouldering in LCC in a concerted effort.

He and his friends collaborated to create The Black Bible, a guidebook to Utah bouldering. Mike lead the charge on the LCC chapters and this was the primary source of recorded bouldering information for many years. In more recent years, Mike teamed up with a newer climber and data geek, Scott Stoddard. Together, using Scott’s technical and organization skills and Mike’s historical knowledge, they authored a new and extremely comprehensive guidebook for Little Cottonwood Canyon on KAYA.

Read the full article for everything you need to know when bouldering at Little Cottonwood Canyon: https://blog.kayaclimb.com/essential-lcc-climbing-guide-when-where-how-to-boulder-in-little-cottonwood/

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From the parking walk up the road until you see an old dirt road heading down to the right. Follow the road east until you are parallel with Swamp Thing, then do a little light bushwhacking into the woods on swampy soild to find it near the creek.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Temple Quarry
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Temple Quarry is a great place for kids and beginners with it's easy trails, good landings, and friendly boulders like the Dragon Egg right next to the parking lot. There are historical markers along the trail with some history about the Mormon Pioneers that quarried here for the Salt Lake Temple. While most of hte lines are in the moderate and intermediate range, there are a few good harder problems up on the Overlook Boulder up on teh south hill and the elite 'Sizzle Grips' just across the creek.

webLocationsForLocation.name: The 3rd Planet
webLocationsForLocation.description: The 3rd Planet is a small cluster of boulders developed by Nikki Smith. Most of the established lines are moderate and intermediate, but a few harder projects are still waiting for FAs.

webLocationsForLocation.name: The Gate
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Gate area is one of where bouldering began in Little Cottonwood back in the 1960's. The 'Standard Overhang' is one of the most popular intermediates in the canyon along with several other nearby favorites like 'Surprise Ending', 'E.B.P.', 'Left Side Direct' and the goof 'Party Trick'. Some of the best moderates in the canyon can also be found here with the well known slabs on the west side of the Gate Boulder and Greasy variations on the neighboring Spinal Twist boulder as well as fun aretes and faces on the Tower Boulder. Advanced problems include 'Crystal Pinch', 'Superfly' and 'Barfly' on the Standard Overhang boulder. 'Spinal Twist' is an older elite problem put up by Chris Sharma, and there are loads of other elite variations on the Standard Overhang Boulder. The Banjo zone is less trafficed but has several great problems and a newer zone including several undone projects for the adventurer.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From the parking head up a short trail in the north west corner of the parking lot

webLocationsForLocation.name: The Gullies
webLocationsForLocation.description: Situated between the Riverside Buzz zone, and The Swamp, the Gullies is a lesser known area with a handful of worthy lines developed and documented by Niki Smith, Jay Keener and Victor Copeland. Great moderates like 'Rough Cut' and 'Darth Moss' can be found higher up the gully along with potential intermediate classic 'Blood Diamond'. Nearby 'Brute Fracis' is a well liked advanced line, and a few more elite lines and projects can be found down lower on the Remainder and Funner boulders.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Park the same as the Swamp, cross the creek by the Moon Rock, then head uphill on a trail that veers right to the west. After coming to the Funner Boulder, continue on up the hill to reach The Gullies.

webLocationsForLocation.name: The Hill
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Hill is a steep area of densely packed boulders with a few outlying areas on the edges. It is known for elite lines like 'Triple Threat', 'Sean John', and 'Dominatrix' but is also home to loads of easier high quality problems. There are excellent tall slabs and moderate lines throughout the area starting with some good problems on the Obelisk and Stick boulders right near the road. Several popular intermediate lines can be found on Tom's Wall along with many others spread around The Hill. 'Wormography' and 'H King' are two excellent advanced problems along with the harder 'Jumper', 'Loggerhead' to the east and the very exciting 'Holy Moly' high up on the cliff band. Due to its faint trails and steep complex layout The Hill is less traveled, and still holds many projects across the grades for those willing to venture...

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From the parking head across the street and east toward the Stick Boulder. There is a path into The Hill just before reaching the Stick Boulder.

webLocationsForLocation.name: The Swamp
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Swamp is a good collection of large boulders across the road south from The Gate that can be found along the quarry trail. Classic intermediates like 'The Big Guy', 'Don't Fall' and 'Pride' are joined by a long list of popular Elites like 'Confluence', 'Tiny', 'Alchemy', 'Dunks on Deck', 'Eclipse' and 'Transience'. Loads of tall moderate slabs are peppered through the area along with a great collection of advanced problems like 'Maisch Slab', 'Extreme Hammocking', 'Smells Like Font' and newer lines up in the Talus like 'Redheaded Ramblings' and 'Sticks and Stones' in the new East Swamp area. There are plenty of projects remaining to be done.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From the parking head down to the creek. There are good place to cross the creek near the Moonrock, or further upstream by the Japanese Garden. In the Spring when the creek is too high, The Swamp can be reached by crossing the bridge in Riverside, and hiking east for a few minutes.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Trench Warfare
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Trench Warfare area is a densely packed cluster of enormous boulders high on the south side of the canyon across from Cabbage Patch and west of Wasatch Resort. This newer area has a few well known lines including the popular elite 'Red Letter Day' and several other good problems spanning the grades on the surrounding boulders. 'Blueberry' is an excellent advanced problem to try out, and 'Papa Bell's Arete' is a fun intermediate at the bottom of the zone. With loads of newer problems and plenty of project potential this beautiful area is worth getting to know.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Valhalla
webLocationsForLocation.description: Valhalla is a large area high above White Pine North. There are only a handful of established problems including the elite highball 'Legends Only' and the majestic intermediate arete 'Terminus'. There are dozens of other boulders scatted up the hill with lots of potential if you're willing to make the hike.

webLocationsForLocation.description_bouldering: Valhalla is a large area high above White Pine North. There are only a handful of established problems including the elite highball 'Legends Only' and the majestic intermediate arete 'Terminus'. There are dozens of other boulders scatted up the hill with lots of potential if you're willing to make the hike.
webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Park in the White Pine parking on the north side of the road, then climb up the trail near the south end of the pullout. After reaching the Sky Boulder zone in the talus either head straight up to reach Terminus, or head up behind Mullet Master to get to One of the Ones. Head directly west over the ridge behind Mullet Master to reach Brown Sugar.

webLocationsForLocation.name: Wasatch Resort
webLocationsForLocation.description: The Wasatch Resort is an the most expansive area in the canyon with twice as many problems as most other areas. The beautiful tree covered south hill is heavily shaded and home to a huge collection of fantastic boulders. The main access point is just west of the last home in the Wasatch Resort neighborhood. The home owner at the west end of the neighborhood is friendly to climbers, but be respectful and don't enter their property. The boulders right next to their backyard are fine to climb on, just be respectful and don't make a lot of noise. The massive Wasatch Resort area can be divided up into three main vertical sections with the Water Tower areas on the east, Dean, Paul Bunyon, and Upper Wasatch areas in the middle and the Cube, Yukon and Battle Star areas to the west. The Water Tower areas are a bit of a hike, but many excellent problems make the trek worthwhile including classic intermediate 'Classic' and quality advanced lines like 'Beck Face'. A handful of elite problems like 'Muenster Cheese Squeeze' and 'The English Patient' are nearby. Higher on the hill and further east potential projects abound! Up the center areas there are lots of moderate problems with good landings near the bottom of the area with plenty of popular intermediates like 'Sad Face Clown', and 'Der Undergriff'. Higher on the hill 'Will's Face' is well liked as well as high balls 'Babe' and 'Prime Rib' high up by the cliffs. Elite lines and variations are all over including 'Muffler' and 'Rodeo Sloth'. On the west end of the Wasatch Resort the Cube boulder is home to some great slabs and a few harder problems. Further west is the very popular advanced line 'First Down' with more popular advanced high balls up hill in the Yukon zone like 'Ready to Die' and 'Big Baby Jesus' and the short but well liked 'Toolshed' and 'Mini-Maisch'. Throughout the west zones elite high ball lines can be found from top to bottom with quite a few new problems going up in recent years like 'Wind Waker', 'Belly Grip', 'Klondike' and 'High Horse'. Potential projects abound, especially up toward Battlestar. With so many great problems in such a beautiful area, Wasatch Resort is worth exploring!

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Park at the Grit Mill parking lot, then cross the road to the south. Find a trail next to the entry road for Wasatch Resort and follow it down toward the creek. Cross just west of the last house and head up the trails into Wasatch Resort Boulders. May not be crossable in the Spring. It is possible to cross the bridge in Riverside, and bushwhack in from the east, by the Surprise Boulder.

webLocationsForLocation.name: White Pine Chutes North
webLocationsForLocation.description: The north White Pine Chutes is a medium sized talus field with loads of tightly packed problems including several well liked lines from the lower east 'Rainbow Cave' up to popular intermediates 'Fat Lip' and 'Red Headed Stepchild' high in the talus, and several advanced lines on 'Chocolate Starfish' in the brush to the east.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Park in the long pull out on the south side of the road then find a trail near the east end of the pull out and follow it downhill to the south to find the boulders in the woods.

webLocationsForLocation.name: White Pine North
webLocationsForLocation.description: White Pine North has a great collection of beloved lines on excellent covered rock spanning a huge talus field that extends high into the Valhalla Area above. From popular moderate lines on the Ping Pong boulder and the intermediate 'Fortune Cookie' near the road, to more advanced favorites on the Head On Boulder in the central area and committing high balls at the top of the talus, White Pine North has something for everyone. Check out the newly documented Tingy Town area to the east developed years back by Sam Tingy which includes lots of nice moderate lines along with a few undone projects in hidden pits and caves.

webLocationsForLocation.name: White Pine South
webLocationsForLocation.description: White Pine South is a sprawling talus high in the canyon with hundreds of great problems on quality patina'd rock including the beautiful moderate slabs on the Moose Boulder, and popular intermediate highball 'Mom' as well as the epic V16 cave 'Grand Illusion'. Other favorites include intermediates like 'Tequila Sunset', 'Blunder' and 'Ring Toss', Advanced lines like 'Stephan's Dihedral', 'Prowler', 'Matt's Roof' and 'Nest Egg' and loads of other elite lines like 'Euro Roof', 'Grand Illusion',  'Mangalyaan' and 'The Good Listener'. Along with all these favorites are plenty of potential problems scattered throughout the vast talus fields, just waiting to be climbed.

webLocationsForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Park on either side of the road and head south across the creek. There is usually a log or two for crossing the creek at various points toward the middle of the parking area. Crossing the creek can be difficult in the spring. A longer safer spring route can be taken by parking at the White Pine Trailhead to the east and crossing that bridge then bush whacking across the meadow into the Moose Boulder area.

webLocationsForLocation.name: White Pine Trailhead
webLocationsForLocation.description: White Pine Trailhead covers a wide swath of aspen forest scattered with a wide variety of boulders. The most popular are the L' Heritage (AKA Great Divide) and the Wire Trail (AKA Crimpin' Connies) with lots of great problems at all levels. Lesser known newer areas to the west include great lines like the intermediate 'Solar Power' as well as advanced problems like 'Finders Keepers' and 'Fern Gully Roof' with a few harder problems like 'Super Serious'. There is a fair bit of new problem potential up in the Ferngully area, though recent avalanches have left some debris that may need to be cleared.

webSearchForLocation.name: Squamish
webSearchForLocation.description:
Over time the monolithic granite fell from The Chief's high walls creating a huge labyrinth of boulders. The forest and moss hid these boulders until 1996 when the modern Squamish bouldering boom took off. Since then Squamish has become a world class bouldering destination with thousands of quality boulders scattered across the Sea to Sky.


— LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT —
We respectfully and humbly acknowledge that rock climbing in Squamish and the Sea to Sky takes place on the unceded traditional territories of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish), xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam), and səlilwətaɬ (Tsleil-Waututh) Nations. With this acknowledgement we share our gratitude and offer our support to be stewards of the land.


—WEATHER —
The climbing season extends from about April to October with the best conditions on rare dry winter days. The driest (albeit warmest) weather is during the summer months July through September. The forest canopy keeps the boulders shaded and significantly cooler on warmer days.


— CAMPING —
There is a BC Parks pay campground below The Chief with walk-in and vehicle sites. There are numerous options around town as well: https://squamish.ca/discover-squamish/camping/


— GEAR —

webSearchForLocation.name: Red Rock
webSearchForLocation.description:
Red Rock Canyon, one of North America's premiere climbing destinations, has a rich history alongside other well-known crags such as Hueco Tanks, Yosemite, Bishop and Joshua Tree, dating back to the mid-1970s. It has been extensively explored and documented through numerous legends over the decades and Tom Moulin's comprehensive paper guidebook for Red Rock and the other Southern Nevada crags is one of the best bouldering guidebooks in the world. There have been many iterations over the 2000s with the latest being available here: https://www.snellpress.com/snb3.

Located just 10 minutes away from Summerlin and 25 minutes away from the Las Vegas Strip and Harry Reid International Airport, it is easily accessible to Las Vegas locals, domestic and international travelers alike. With over 2500 currently eastablished boulder problems across all grades (yes even V17), and such ease of access, it is one of the most traveled rock climbing destinations in the world. Containing world-class classics at every grade and of every climbing-style imaginable, spread across over 15 different canyons with varying levels of popularity, Red Rock provides something for everyone. You can choose to climb classics with a long legacy and short approaches in areas like Kraft and Red Spring, or go off-the-beaten path in remote canyons like Mud Springs and Mustang. Whichever you choose, remember to follow leave-no-trace and general respectful best practices:

- Stay on designated trails. Red Rock Canyon is a National Conservation Area managed by the Bureau of Land Management with over 3 million visitors a year. BLM, Park Rangers, SNCC and locals spend time building designated trails to preserve and restore wildlife habitat, natural resources, and prevent unnecessary erosion.

- The vast majority of rock type in all of Red Rock Canyon is the type of Aztec Sandstone which is prone to breaking after rain. Depending on how much rain has accumulated, do not climb for anywhere from 24-72 hours. The Southeastern side of Las Vegas does have some climbing alternatives after rain, such as Big Sandy or Keyhole Canyon, although of considerably less quality than Red Rock. Gyms in town such as Red Rock Climbing Center and The Refuge are also options.

- Be mindful of all other visitors enjoying and admiring what Red Rock has to offer. Depending on where you choose to climb, you will likely run in to many climbers and non-climbers alike enjoying the beauty that Red Rock has to offer. This includes monitoring pets especially in crowded areas like Kraft, Red Spring, First Pullout and Willow Springs.

Located within the desert the weather and climbing season of Red Rock favors the Winter months. The most prime days ranging from November-March, with shoulder-season climbing possible in September/October and April/May if you're willing to chase shade. It is common to have stretches of rainy days and weeks even during the prime months, where climbing becomes no longer possible until the sandstone dries.

- Pay attention to designated boulders that have been marked off limits and closed for various reasons. This includes, but is not limited to, the Birthing Boulder in Kraft with the old-school classic Caliman V7, any climbs near the Red Spring Boardwalk, including the modern testpiece Tourist Trap V9, another old school classic Desert Rain V10 in First Pullout, as well as Ambacamba V10 near the Fish Head in Windy Canyon. All generally closed due to proximity to Native American Rock Art, protected under the Archaelogical Resources Protection Act.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Red Rock Canyon bouldering is generally categorized into four areas:

1. The zones within the Calico Basin are the first you approach from Charleston Blvd as it transitions into SR159. You turn right onto Calico Basin Rd to access either the Red Spring, Calico Basin, Kraft or Gateway Canyon boulders via designated parking spots. These areas are free of charge to access, the most popular and densely crowded. Kraft, Calico and Red Spring generally have short approaches with some outliers, and Gateway is farther in. Park only in designated spots, and be prepared to find alternative locations if parking is full, especially during the prime months of the season.

2. The majority of Canyons are within the 13-mile Red Rock Canyon Scenic Loop which is more restrictive to climb at. A timed reservation booked through recreation.gov is required from October 1st to May 31st and the entry gate is only open from 8am-5pm. There is a $2 fee for every reservation, and either a $20 per-day entry fee or an annual pass such as America the Beautiful or Red Rock. Reservations tend to get full during prime-time slots. The zones accessed through this loop are First Pullout, Second Pullout, Sandstone Quarry, White Rock Springs, Willow Springs, Ice Box Canyon, Pine Creek Canyon, Juniper Canyon, and Oak Creek Canyon. First Pullout can be accessed from outside the loop via Red Spring with more hiking, and Oak Creek Canyon can be accessed from outside the loop via Middle/South Oak Creek Trailhed with more hiking. The 13-mile loop is one-way, thus once you go past a particular zone, you cannot go back to it without a new reservation and re-entering the loop. Do not stay past dusk.

3. South Oak Creek Canyon near Mount Wilson and First Creek Canyon are accessed via designed parking lots past the exit of the Red Rock Canyon Scenic Loop on SR159. They are free of charge and you do not need to drive through the loop.

4. Southern Outcrops, Windy Canyon, Mud Springs Canyon, Black Velvet Canyon and Mustang Canyon are all accessed via SR160 south of SR159. Most easily accessible through different road forks off of the Late Night Trailhead, each with their own designated parking spots, these generally require cars with good ground clearance, but the flattened level of the dirt roads can change from season to season. There is no charge for climbing in these canyons.

webSearchForLocation.name: Bishop
webSearchForLocation.description:
Small town with a big backyard. Bishop’s tagline captures the literal and emotional spirit of this special place. It’s no secret to climbers that the sleepy little town of Bishop is the base camp for some of the most outstanding recreation in North America. Historic testpiece climbs dot the landscape at every grade level. Legendary climbers have been drawn to the area’s boulders, cliffs, and mountains over generations, and the thousands of ascents spell out the evolution of modern bouldering. From Robinson’s Rubber Tester, to Iron Man, to the Swarm, Bishop is about connecting to the story of modern climbing in a breathtaking location amidst friends and perfect weather.

This guide covers the Buttermilks (areas accessed from Buttermilk Road) and the Tablelands (areas accessed from Chalk Bluff Road). More sub-areas will be added over time. Please reach out with additions and revisions, tread lightly, and enjoy the boulders!

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Bishop could also carry another tagline: Small Town with a Ton of Visiting Climbers. Bishop Bouldering is a world-class destination experience, and with that hallowed status comes added responsibility for visitors. Climbers are by and large a great user group, and by doing a little research and exercising some decent judgment, Bishop’s iconic climbing will be enjoyed for generations to come.

Travel: Bishop’s remote yet accessible location is part of what makes it such a special place. 250 miles north of Los Angeles and 350 miles west of the Bay Area, Bishop straddles Highway 395 in the Eastern Sierra region of California within “long-weekend” driving distance of 20 million people. In 2021 Bishop began commercial flights to its regional airport, BIH. United is the only airline that flies there, with service to SFO and DEN currently.

Camping: Camp in existing, designated sites, and stay up to date on fire regulations. Best yet, stay at the Pleasant Valley Pit Campground ($5/night bathrooms and trash) or in town at the Tri-County Fairgrounds ($15/night with showers and electricity!) Absolutely don’t park on vegetation or create new fire pits.

Roads: Drive slow (25mph) on dirt roads. This goes a long way to improve climber-town relations and keeps the roads from getting (more) hammered than they already are. Buttermilks road is in pretty bad shape and no plans are currently in the works to grade or repair it. See area descriptions for specific road concerns.

Trails: Bishop Climbing Rangers and volunteer groups have done a great job designating most trails in popular areas. The result has been an amazing rebound of local vegetation. The same goes for your pup. Dogs off leash are capable of harming the area as much or more than humans. In the Happy’s, Sad’s and Buttermilks, there is rarely a need to go off trail.

Toilets and trash: Pack it in, pack it out. Obviously don’t litter, and maybe even pick up some trash you see! Build up some karma for that time you will inevitably forget your used finger tape somewhere.

webSearchForLocation.name: Joshua Tree
webSearchForLocation.description:
Joshua Tree National Park is an other-wordly climbing area in the Southern California encompassing parts of the Mojave and Sonoran deserts. Complete with over 10,000 roped climbs and over 2,000 boulder problems, you'll stay busy here. It's a Winter paradise, with fair weather and lots of sun during the cold months. The prime season runs from October to April, and even May, with a month or so on either end being a bit warm.

Being in a National Park, these climbs are monitored well. Stay on established trails, keep boulder pads off vegetation, pack out all trash, and respect wildlife/others so as to help keep access to these areas open for all of us and future generations of climbers.

Purchase the paper guide by Robert Miramontes here: https://www.wolverinepublishing.com/shop-all-guidebooks/p/joshua-tree-bouldering

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Joshua Tree is located in the high desert of Southern California, about 2.5 hours East of Los Angeles // 5 hours Southeast of Bishop // 4 hours Southwest of Las Vegas.

As with all major National Parks, day passes and yearly passes are sold at any park entrance. Fees are $30 per vehicle or $55 for an Annual Pass.

Camping at the park is available at Hidden Valley, Ryan, Sheep's Pass, Jumbo Rocks, and Belle campgrounds. Reservations can be made at Recreation.gov or by clicking here: https://www.recreation.gov/gateways/2782

webSearchForLocation.name: Hueco Tanks
webSearchForLocation.description:
Hueco Tanks is the mecca of American bouldering. This state park is home to incredible indigenous history, archeology, nature, and some of the most iconic boulders in the world. The uniqueness of the movement and rock features have solidified Hueco as a boulderer's paradise. Please respect park rules, archeological sites, and nature as access is very fragile and climbing is a privilege.

Do not walk or stand in huecos, stay on trails, and don't slide pads around in the dirt in order to prevent erosion.

PARK HOURS
October to April:
8 a.m. – 6 p.m.

May to September:
Friday to Sunday: 7 a.m. – 7 p.m.
Monday to Thursday: 8 a.m. – 6 p.m.

ENTRANCE FEES
Adult : $7 Daily
Child 12 Years and Under: Free

For more information, visit the Texas State Parks website: https://tpwd.texas.gov/state-parks/hueco-tanks

Purchase the North Mountain paper guidebook at the Hueco Tanks office or online here: https://sagetosummit.com/products/hueco-tanks-vol-1-north-mountain

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Hueco Tanks is located about 45 minutes East of El Paso International Airport.

RESERVATION INFORMATION

North Mountain access requires reservations and is self-guided. 70 total visitors are allowed into the park at any given time, and 60 of those spaces are able to be reserved in advance. The remaining 10 are left open for walk-ins, so if you DO NOT have a reservation but still want to climb on North Mountain, it's best to arrive at the gate at least an hour early in the busy season, but you may need to arrive even earlier and wait for the gate to open at 8am.

In order to make a reservation in advance, you must call this number: (512) 389-8911 - No online reservations are possible.

East, East Spur, and West Mountains are NOT accessible without a guide. Guided tours can be arranged by calling (915) 857-1135 and can be arranged a minimum of a week in advance.

webSearchForLocation.name: Joe's Valley
webSearchForLocation.description:
Joe's Valley has been a world class bouldering destination for decades. Given the beautiful sandstone, seemingly endless problems in a variety of grades and, in many cases, literally roadside approaches, this comes as no surprise. High desert elevations provide long seasons of good climbing conditions. Take your pick between easy camping on public lands, designated BLM/USFS campsites or a multitude of lodging options in the nearby towns. Prime seasons are spring and fall, but it is possible to climb at any time of year. Summers can get quite hot but provide a good playground for vacation style climbing. In the winter you may have to wait out snow or other bad weather, but the temps can also be super sendy.

IMPORTANT: Don't climb on wet rock and allow it to dry fully after a storm - usually at least 24 hours (check weather conditions at https://www.joesvalleyfest.com/weather )

New Joe's will typically be your warmest option and has a great concentration of a variety of grades. The Wash, across Highway 57 from New Joe's, has a slightly longer approach than most Joe's climbing, but this can make for a great way to get away from the crowds. Left Fork and Right Fork are great options during the prime season as you can chase shade or sun all day, as you desire. Dairy Canyon is slightly higher in elevation so can also be a good way to beat the heat. The Wash is another slightly long approach by Joe's standards, but it is well worth the hike to sample the offerings there. Nothing is too far away in Joe's Valley, so it is easy to sample several subareas in a given day and still make it back into town to grab a send donut at the Food Ranch or a celebratory milkshake from Fatty's.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
The majority of Joe's Valley bouldering is located on public land operated by the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management. The Joe's Valley Coalition, the area's Local Climbing Organization, partners closely with these organizations as well as the local community to maintain access to and assist in stewardship of the lands. Interested in giving back? Follow @joesvalley to learn about monthly trail building volunteer projects. Or consider becoming a Joe's Valley Coalition member at joesvalleycoalition.raklet.com/apply.

Be a good steward while you are in Joe's. Don't climb on wet rock and allow it to dry fully after a storm - usually at least 24 hours (check weather conditions at https://www.joesvalleyfest.com/weather ). Clean your tick marks. Pick up trash. Stay on the established trails. No wire brushes. No chipping holds. Treat people with respect. And have fun! 

About grades. We have aimed to make grades as consistent as possible across Joe's. And have taken into account that height differences can impact grades. In the cases where a given climb is particularly height sensitive, you'll see a slash grade in the climb description.

webSearchForLocation.name: Victoria
webSearchForLocation.description: Though bouldering development in Victoria goes back at least to the early 90's, even local climbers in the mid 2010's could have been fooled into thinking there was little here of note. In the last decade the popularity of Victoria bouldering has exploded, spurred on by the new gyms, the overall increase in climbing’s popularity and the publication of the first bouldering guides since 1999, areas which used to be the playgrounds of small groups of dedicated boulderers have finally gained the attention they deserve. Though none of the areas in Victoria are especially large, or dense when compared to places like Squamish, or even the Duncan Boulders, the great diversity of rock types, and locales makes it a great year round bouldering spot, since there is always a different zone in season.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Territorial Acknowledgement:  We acknowledge that the bouldering areas on the southern tip of the island are found on the traditional territories of the Coast Salish people including the Lekwungen Speaking Peoples of the Songhees and Esquimalt Nations as well as the Territories of the SENĆOŦEN language speakers of the T'Sou-kwe and W̱SÁNEĆ Nations; including: Tsartlip Nation, Tsawout Nation, Tseycum First Nation,  Pauquachin Nation. Our bouldering also encroaches on the territories of the Malahat Nation who is a member of Naut'sa mawt Tribal Council.

Check out the individual areas, subareas and boulders for approach information.

webSearchForLocation.name: Clear Creek Canyon
webSearchForLocation.description:
Clear Creek Canyon is one of the finest destinations on the Front Range. This 14 mile-long gorge offers over four hundred problems and more than a thousand routes; it's no surprise that the area remains extremely popular year-round. The sheer variety of gneiss and schist granite is part of what makes Clear Creek such an enjoyable place to climb, especially for boulderers. There is not another place in Colorado where it is possible to climb on bullet, water polished features and square-cut, blocky horizontal roofs just beside one another, let alone almost every other style of granite imaginable.

Bouldering in Clear Creek requires very low commitment. The heavily trafficked US-6 provides easy access to every problem in the canyon, despite the constant yammer of trucks engine-braking down the entire length of the road. There isn't a single problem here which requires an approach longer than thirty minutes (although most are under ten), making it a premier after-work destination or quick hit during a time constraint. Additionally, three different gyms are located within fifteen minutes from the entrance of the canyon, which climbers often utilize for warming up, or bailing in the case of inclement weather.

One aspect of the canyon that isn't seen much elsewhere on the Front Range is the area's weirdly urbanized atmosphere. Some rocks have suffered from graffiti, while others are just close to the highway and the road noise is obnoxious. Although the most accessible, trafficked boulders certainly don't have a pristine feel, Clear Creek can still be wild and remote. I encourage people to take interest in those problems that are slightly further from the car; they can provide a nice and quiet change of scenery from the usual popular zones.

SEASON:
Bouldering in Clear Creek is possible through every season. Spring is likely the best time to boulder here, because temperatures are slightly warmer than during the dead of winter, but ice bridges still grace the river. Summers are hot, with eighty-ninety degree days on the regular. By chasing shade or climbing at night, a few still make it happen. The fall season is similar to spring in terms of temperatures, although creek-crossers will have to wade until early December usually. The shady aspects of the canyon are difficult in the months of December-February, but many hillsides receive sun all day and are the first blocks to dry on the Front Range. Alternatively, the Nomad Cave attracts swarms of climbers when every other boulder in the state is wet.

TRAVEL INFO:
Clear Creek Canyon is a part of Jeffco Open Space, meaning the land is an outdoor recreation park and private property isn't ever an issue. Overnight parking/camping is not allowed in the canyon (not that it would be enjoyable), but Golden and Idaho Springs both have several amenities for those staying in the area for an extended period of time.
webSearchForLocation.description_bouldering:
Clear Creek Canyon is one of the finest destinations on the Front Range. This 14 mile-long gorge offers over four hundred problems and more than a thousand routes; it's no surprise that the area remains extremely popular year-round. The sheer variety of gneiss and schist granite is part of what makes Clear Creek such an enjoyable place to climb, especially for boulderers. There is not another place in Colorado where it is possible to climb on bullet, water polished features and square-cut, blocky horizontal roofs just beside one another, let alone almost every other style of granite imaginable.

Bouldering in Clear Creek requires very low commitment. The heavily trafficked US-6 provides easy access to every problem in the canyon, despite the constant yammer of trucks engine-braking down the entire length of the road. There isn't a single problem here which requires an approach longer than thirty minutes (although most are under ten), making it a premier after-work destination or quick hit during a time constraint. Additionally, three different gyms are located within fifteen minutes from the entrance of the canyon, which climbers often utilize for warming up, or bailing in the case of inclement weather.

One aspect of the canyon that isn't seen much elsewhere on the Front Range is the area's weirdly urbanized atmosphere. Some rocks have suffered from graffiti, while others are just close to the highway and the road noise is obnoxious. Although the most accessible, trafficked boulders certainly don't have a pristine feel, Clear Creek can still be wild and remote. I encourage people to take interest in those problems that are slightly further from the car; they can provide a nice and quiet change of scenery from the usual popular zones.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Clear Creek Canyon is east-west running and access is incredibly easy from either side. From downtown Golden, take State Highway 58 west to the intersection between SH-58 and SH-93/US-6. Head straight (west) into Clear Creek. From Boulder, it will be a right turn onto US-6, and from Denver a left. To enter the canyon from the west (upper) side, head along I-70 East from Idaho Springs. Take exit 244, which is a left exit, onto US-6 and follow it into the canyon, passing the huge Albert Frei & Sons Mine.

webSearchForLocation.name: Ogden
webSearchForLocation.description: Nearly all of Ogden Bouldering is comprised of super clean white tintic Qurtzite. This 300 million year old glass like stone has been well cemented and stained with patina containing striking reds, oranges, yellows. The quartzite is well featured and often times very steep, this makes for virtually every decent sized boulder a great candidate. The highly featured rock makes for all kinds crazy link-ups, thus creating a great training ground for fitness.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: How to get to the Ogden Boulder Field, if coming from the North or the South, I-15 is the most direct way, take either the Ogden 12th st. exit or the 21st. exit. Head East to the East bench until reaching Harrison Blvd. From Harrison Blvd go East on either 22nd st or 27th st. One can either Park at the Indian trail head at the top of 22nd st, or one may park at the top of 27th st. The boulders can be accessed by either parking area, the 22nd st Parking has much more room if 27th st is full.

webSearchForLocation.name: Lincoln Lake
webSearchForLocation.description:
The bouldering at Lincoln Lake is, in a word: adventure.

Visiting Lincoln Lake, or any true alpine zone, demands a certain level of outdoor expertise. While the approach is fairly short, it is incredibly steep, and more than one climber has vomited from the brutal hike out. The trail is poorly formed, very rocky, and not maintained. The talus blocks, which have drawn the climbers, are massive, and there are extremely deep and dangerous pits throughout the field. Additionally, the sun and wind are often intense. Every climber should wear SPF 50 sunscreen, have extra warm clothes, sunglasses, and be prepared for snow or intense thunderstorms any time of day, any day of the year.

Temperatures can drop very quickly due to the thin air. Even on nice days, once the sun sinks behind the cliff, the temperature can plummet 20 or 30 degrees. A gorgeous 60-degree day can be transformed by blowing wind and snow in a matter of a few minutes. Warm clothes and a rain jacket are imperative. Conversely, it can feel downright hot in the direct sun. The important thing to remember is that Lincoln Lake is a place of extremes.

The landings at Lincoln Lake are generally bad. It is imperative that you have at least two crash pads. If this introduction seems pedantic, that’s because the author cannot emphasize this point enough: the bouldering at Lincoln Lake is the most extreme in America. Don’t be fooled by the easy drive and relatively short approach. Be prepared for the worst, expect an adventure, and take responsibility for your actions.

CELL SERVICE:
Usually available at the parking, cell service can be very spotty/non-existent at the boulders so plan on not having it.

SEASON:
The gate to the road to Lincoln Lake typically opens around Memorial Day and closes sometime around the first of October, although the specific dates vary depending on the snow level. Lincoln provides the coldest conditions of any area in the guidebook. Climbers are free to hike in from Echo Lake anytime of year, but only the most hardy of souls have taken up this endeavor.

PARKING:
One of the biggest concerns climbers raise in regards to Lincoln Lake is the parking situation.

For someone fit enough to boulder at Lincoln Lake, and who is willing to drop down that massive hillside, tacking on an additional 20 minutes of easy walking along the road shouldn’t be a problem. Taking this into consideration, I counted 136 available parking spaces. For the intrepid climber willing to walk 3 miles, there is unlimited parking.

For the less motivated, for which even a one mile walk along the road seems too daunting or difficult, let’s look at the available parking spaces within a half mile of the generally used spots: I conservatively counted 98 available spaces. This amounts to about 7 times the number of cars that are parked at Lincoln on very busy days, freely available for anyone willing to add an extra ten minutes of walking down a flat road.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
From Denver, head west on Interstate 70 for 39 miles to the town of Idaho Springs. Take Exit 240. Turn left onto CO 103, following signs to Mt. Evans for 14 miles to Echo Lake Park. Turn right onto the Mt. Evans Scenic Hwy. After 0.1 mile, drive through the entrance ranger station where you will be forced to stop and talk to a ranger. While there are various fees for cars wishing to drive to Summit Lake or to the final parking lot just below the summit, there is no fee for parking on the side of the road to access Lincoln Lake. Tell the ranger at the station you are bouldering at Lincoln Lake, and they will send you through, free of charge. If you do wish to drive to Summit Lake or the Mt. Evans summit, remember to pay for the pass.

From the entrance station continue driving 4.5 miles. The scenery here is dramatic, and the road makes a hard bend to the left. There is a large pull-out here on the left, which is never filled, and for the next 3.5 miles, sporadic roadside parking is available. At 5.6 miles, the road makes a sweeping turn to the right. Parking is available here at the apex of the bend on the left, and just beyond the bend on the right, in a small pull-off beyond a cliff. This is the best place to park if you wish to access the bouldering nearest the lake. This is the East Parking Area.

For the next 1.1 miles, there are a number of parking areas along the road. Parking along the road here is rarely necessary, and does requires a short and easy walk to reach the East and West drop-in points.

At 6.7 miles from the entrance station, the road bends back to the right. This is the West Parking Area for the west trailhead. The main trail down to the boulders at Lincoln Lake begins here. There are enough spaces on the left side of the road for about 10 cars. Please park in the direction of traffic.
webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering: The road accessing Lincoln Lake will be closed through Spring 2026. Lincoln Lake can still be accessed via Echo Lake campground, but the approach trail is quite long and intense. For more info: https://highways.dot.gov/federal-lands/projects/co/mount-blue-sky-highway

webSearchForLocation.name: Guanella Pass
webSearchForLocation.description:
Guanella Pass has slowly come into its own as one of the best and most popular bouldering areas in Colorado. While the bouldering here is referred to as Guanella Pass, all of the described climbing is well below the actual summit of the pass, which is several miles beyond the established bouldering. While climbers have been putting up classic lines in this verdant valley for years, it is only recently that Guanella has caught on as serious destination, with many classic problems of all grades. Driving up to the actual pass to watch the sunset on Mt. Bierstadt (14,060 ft) is an incredible way to finish a day at the boulders. The rock is beautifully polished gneiss, with rounded slopers and square cut edges and the access is some of the easiest in the state. Short approaches and generally flat landings makes this a not-to-be-missed experience. The scenery here is outstanding, particularly in the fall, when the aspens inject veins of gold between stately fir trees.

SEASON:
Guanella Pass is best during the fall, when the aspen put on a dramatic display. The bouldering typically stays snow-free until the end of October. Climbers can also catch good conditions in the spring, sometimes as early as March, but more regularly into mid-April and May. The occasional cool day can be found in June. July and August are typically too warm for a serious boulderer looking for good conditions, but the pass is certainly climbable at this time of year. Mosquitoes become an issue in late June and remain so until the end of August.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From Denver, head west on I-70 for 45 miles. Get off the freeway at Exit 228. Turn left, driving underneath the overpass, and continue to a traffic circle. The gas stations at this intersection are the last place to fuel up and find cheap food. At the traffic circle, turn right onto Argentine St. In 0.5 mile the road forks. Take the left fork (continuing straight). Drive for 0.01 mile and turn left onto 6th St. Take 6th St. for 0.1 miles, and turn right onto Rose St. Take Rose for 0.02 miles, and turn left. This marks the beginning of the Guanella Pass Rd. All of the bouldering described in this guide under the Guanella Pass section is off this road.

webSearchForLocation.name: Lake Tahoe
webSearchForLocation.description:
Get the paper guide at https://www.laketahoebouldering.com or your local climbing store.

OVERVIEW:
With the recent discovery of thousands of new problems, Lake Tahoe is now a world-class bouldering area. These guides include every pebble that has ever been wrestled in and around Tahoe, with full color photos, topos, GPS, and everything else needed to get you to the boulders. Tahoe has 10,000+ problems which range from novice to expert on many different rock types. It is one of the few places on Earth where you can boulder year round in a beautiful mountain setting. Come and experience the magic for yourself.

SEASON:
The bouldering season in Tahoe is generally from May through the end of October. Sometimes, when climbers are lucky enough, winter holds off for a while and the season extends all the way through November and into early December in a dry year. Once winter hits, it’s over for the high elevation areas, but you can typically still get some climbing in at areas like Bliss and the Pie Shop until the first big lake level snowfall.

When things get rolling in the spring varies from season to season. Normally, the lower areas are good by May and even the highest elevation spots are dry by mid-June.

We all know conditions are everything in bouldering, and it goes without saying that fall is the best in Tahoe, as it is for most of the country. Spring is a combo of cool days mixed with the dreaded heat of summer. Once summer is in full swing the only option is shade and/or higher elevations. That’s when places like Castle Peak and Sugar Pine offer some escape and better conditions. The only downfall at this point is the bugs. Sometime in early July a ruthless bug hatch happens and the mosquitoes and biting flies can get downright unruly. By the end of August the bugs start to die off and the epic fall conditions are just around the corner.

There are many good options for wintertime recreation in Tahoe, especially if you ski or snowboard. But if you’re hellbent on bouldering there are some options. During long dry spells places like the Pie Shop, South Bliss, Woodfords Canyon, and Jobs Peak Boulder are a few of the places that stay dry. The entire East Shore, known as the banana belt, melts fast and stays warm on sunny days. But the best spot hands down, aside from making a trip to the Eastside, is Doyle. Doyle is 1 hour from Reno and 2 hours from Tahoe. If you’re willing to make the drive you will find out why Doyle is the Buttermilks of the Tahoe Area. In summary, even though Tahoe gets snow in the winter, you can climb in and around Tahoe year round as long as it’s not storming.

ETHICS:
Unlike route climbing, bouldering is pretty casual regarding ethics, but there are a few things to think about. Chipping holds is not practiced in Lake Tahoe. Dogs can be a major nuisance and are not allowed in state parks such as Bliss. If you bring dogs, please consider other climbers and how your dogs are behaving. Dogs running all over the pads and getting underneath climbers is not cool.

I know everyone loved the movie Rampage and some climbers like to yell words of encouragement and beta. Maybe think twice about this practice. Silence is golden. Unless someone asks for beta or is about to take a huge fall because they are missing an obvious hold, I suggest just letting the climber concentrate. Bottle caps, tape and cigarette butts are trash. It’s out of hand how much of this stuff is found at the boulders. And finally, If you need to take a dump at the boulders use common sense.

LODGING:
Tahoe is filled with many hotels to fit any climber’s budget. There are also many campgrounds around the lake that can be crowded in the middle of summer, so reservations may be needed. A good web site that lists many campsites in Tahoe is: https://www.explorer1.com/tahoe/camping.htm

You can also call the U.S. Forest Service Campgrounds at (800) 280-2267 or California State Parks at (800) 444-7275 for info and reservations. There is also a lot of Forest Service land where dispersed camping is permitted. Phantom Spires, The Secrets, Upper Sugar Pine, Blackwood Canyon, White Rock Lake, Doyle, and select spots at the Sierra Buttes, are a few examples of spots where you can camp just about anywhere.

During the driest years, fires may be prohibited. If they are permitted, fire permits are required at many spots, so be sure to get one. For a list of ranger stations from which to get a fire permit visit: https://www.fs.fed.us/r5/tahoe/

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Tahoe is massive. North and South Lake could easily make for entirely separate climbing trips, so make sure you develop your tick list accordingly! Most of the North Lake bouldering is adjacent to I-80, while South Lake climbing is accessible via CA-89 and US Route 50. Reno-Tahoe International Airport is the closest major airport to North Lake Tahoe at just 45 minutes away.  Sacramento International Airport is a 2 hour drive, while San Francisco Airport is 3.5 hours away.

webSearchForLocation.name: Little Cottonwood Canyon
webSearchForLocation.description:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s climbing area sits just 20 minutes southeast of downtown Salt Lake City and stands as one of North America’s most concentrated city-side climbing spots. Both local and professional traveling climbers have spent decades developing the canyon, which now boasts over 5,000 boulder problems. 

The canyon’s granite walls have drawn climbers’ attention for more than 40 years, however, the area has experienced rapid growth over the last several years—now hosting two of the hardest problems in the country, “The Grand Illusion” and “Sosa,” both (V16).

Little Cottonwood’s unique quartz monzonite walls give climbers a unique granite experience, with some small pockets of limestone throughout—particularly at the mouth of the canyon. The rock is characterized by crystal-heavy slopers and crimps lower in the canyon, tighter grained rock at higher elevations, friction dependence, and slippery, textureless holds on more popular climbs.

Season:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s best climbing happens during fall and spring. The canyon’s climbing conditions reach their sweet spot in October/November. Temperatures stay between 66°F highs and 44°F lows. Nearly all areas will be accessible during these months.The spring also offers great conditions, however climber’s will have to navigate the melting snowpack, the degree to which varies year-to-year.

History:
Mike Beck began climbing in the mid 1980s. In 1988, following a bouldering trip to the world-famous Fontainebleau, France, Mike Beck was inspired upon returning back home to Salt Lake City. At the time, there were maybe 50 problems in the canyon, maximum. That visit to France kicked off an explosion of him and his friends seeking out and developing the bouldering in LCC in a concerted effort.

He and his friends collaborated to create The Black Bible, a guidebook to Utah bouldering. Mike lead the charge on the LCC chapters and this was the primary source of recorded bouldering information for many years. In more recent years, Mike teamed up with a newer climber and data geek, Scott Stoddard. Together, using Scott’s technical and organization skills and Mike’s historical knowledge, they authored a new and extremely comprehensive guidebook for Little Cottonwood Canyon on KAYA.

Read the full article for everything you need to know when bouldering at Little Cottonwood Canyon: https://blog.kayaclimb.com/essential-lcc-climbing-guide-when-where-how-to-boulder-in-little-cottonwood/

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Take the 6200 South exit from I-215 and follow the ski resort signs. The canyon road (Route 210) guides you straight to the climbing spots, and you'll park along the road to reach most areas. Use KAYA to navigate the approaches directly to your climb of choice.

Due to the city-side nature of the canyon, you are never more than 20 minutes from snacks, gas, food, and water. There are numerous great places to eat in Salt Lake City, but climber favorites include Central 9th Market, Pretty Bird Hot Chicken, and Spitz.

webSearchForLocation.name: New River Gorge
webSearchForLocation.description:
The New River Gorge is world renowned for it's perfect single-pitch climbing, but that bullet hard Nuttall sandstone extends beyond the cliffs. The New, Meadow, and Gauley River Gorges have thousands of high quality sandstone boulders lurking in the vast forests, just waiting to be climbed on. Most of the climbing areas here are small with quick approaches. The overall concentration of rock in and around the New River Gorge is particularly high: nearly every tributary of the three rivers contains boulders. It has been posited that there is more rock in a 30 minute radius of Fayetteville than anywhere else of similar size, east of the Mississippi.

If there is anything that the New lacks, it’s a high concentration area such as Stonefort or Rocktown, although Hawks Nest, Pirates Cove and Meadow Top are not far off. The distribution of boulders allows for hundreds of climbers to be in the region without any one area seeming crowded.

You can boulder year round at the New River Gorge, but some seasons are definitely better than others… Visitors swarm to the New in the summer, and even though it isn’t prime bouldering conditions and you probably won’t send your hardest, you’re still climbing great boulders in a beautiful place. It’s hard to plan a climbing trip for the winter, because the weather is all over the place. It is, however, when you can find the best friction, so those looking for an edge on their projects will want to come in winter.

October and November are beautiful months here. Highs are usually in the 50s and 60s, lows from the high 20s to 40s. October is the driest month of the year on average, and November’s not far behind and offers better temps. Spring is identical to fall, except a bit rainier and more humid. Still, if you watch the weather, you can get prime bouldering conditions through April.

Bouldering at the New River Gorge is just now coming into the spotlight, so help make sure that all of the attention we get is positive attention. Here’s some pointers to follow:

Leave No Trace. Follow all park rules. Some examples: keep all pets leashed at all times. Don’t trespass on private property. Park in designated parking only. Use existing trails only.

Don’t be a jerk. Remember that everyone has an equal right to be out there in the boulder field.

Walking on railroad tracks is illegal. If you walk near tracks, you are doing so at your own risk. Never walk ON the tracks.

This topo builds on the excellent efforts of previous guidebooks, in particular “New River Gorge Bouldering” by Micah Klinger and Stella Mascari published in 2015. Stella Mascari and Aaron Schneider are the primary authors for the New River Gorge region topos. For any questions, concerns or suggestions, please use the Report Content feature in the app and your comments will be sent directly to the authors.

Accomadations:
There are numerous places to stay as a climber visiting the New. Here are some popular options:

The Arete Hotel – Climber owner and operated, this beautiful hostel includes a training facility for rainy stretches.
The AAC Campground – A mainstay for those looking for a cheap n’ dirty camping option. Bonus, there are boulders IN the campground.
ACE Adventure Resort – Offers cabins and grub close to town.
