webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
The New River Gorge is located in south central West Virginia, just outside of the town of Fayetteville.

There are several major freeways connecting cities around Fayetteville, so directions are different depending on where you're coming from.

From the Northeast (PA, NY, etc.): Take I-79S until exit 57, where you merge onto US-19S. It's about 50mi to the town of Fayetteville from there.

From the east (DC, VA, etc.): Take I-64W to exit 156 where you turn onto US-60W. After 35mi, merge onto U-19S. It's about 6mi to the town of Fayetteville.

From the South (NC, TN, etc.): Take I-77N to exit 48,where you merge onto US-19N. It's about 15mi to the town of Fayetteville.

From the West (KY, MO, etc.): Take I-64E to exit 85, where you turn onto US-60E. After 30mi, turn straight/left onto WV-16S. From there it's almost 10mi to US-19 and the town of Fayetteville.

From the Northwest (OH, MI, etc.): Take I-77S to exit 85, where you turn onto US-60E. After 30mi, turn straight/left onto WV-16S. From there it's almost 10mi to US-19 and the town of Fayetteville.

webSearchForLocation.name: Coopers Rock
webSearchForLocation.description:
I always considered myself a big wall climber, so bouldering had always taken a back seat. I was always of the opinion that bouldering was “practice climbing”, but I didn’t think Practice Climbs of the Cheat Canyon would sell too well, so here we are. Though it wasn’t my first choice, there’s a lot of boulders around, and it certainly has been the best form of training, given that I haven’t had a gym for most of my time here.

My first experiences were at Coopers Rock, getting the beatdown on the standard sandbags, luring me in with their low grades, and subsequently shredding my fingers to bloody stumps. I quickly concluded that the area was fun for the occasional local outing, but didn’t have much worth serious effort. It was frustrating to climb V8 in the gym and get shut down on V3s on the gritstone, but that’s how it goes around here. Thus, I resorted to exploring and developing new climbs in Snake Hill, which was a safe haven from sandbaggers, and really any people at all. I found all sorts of chossy little lines (some good ones, too), and had convinced myself they were all excellent, really because I had no expectations to ruin my experience; it was just climbing for the sake of climbing. No names, no grades, no people.

In fact, this aspect of the Cheat Canyon climbing scene has always been the thing cherished the most by locals, so much so, that the concept of a guidebook was quite provocative at first. I never thought “adventure bouldering” was a thing. It’s a bit of an oxymoron, but this was the thing that locals wished to preserve for years. While I do acknowledge that writing a guidebook does eliminate some of the exploration, the abundance of rock leaves no shortage of exploratory outings to be had. This guidebook doesn’t even come close to documenting all of the bouldering in the area, and I’m certain there’s still some incredible lines no eye has seen.

CLIMBING ETHICS:
Many newer climbers are not aware of the subtleties of bouldering and climbing ethics, which results in some silly things at Tilted Tree, where one of the highest concentrations of moderates can be found. So, I want to make you all aware of some ethical quandaries that I often find.

Chalk: Use climbing chalk/gym chalk (magnesium carbonate). This is harmless and washes off easily. DO NOT use rosin, sidewalk chalk, or any other substance to dry your hands, as it can damage the rock for future climbers.

Brushing: Please brush tick marks off of climbs when you are finished, and avoid slapping excess amounts of chalk onto holds. If the chalk has filled in the gaps between the sand grains, you have decreased the friction of the hold. Brush off any excess chalk when you are finished, so that the next climber doesn’t have to.

Wet Rock: Due to the large sand grains that make up the gritstone, holds often seep. DO NOT smack a bunch of chalk on wet holds and climb on them. Not only does this polish the holds in the long run, it isn’t very successful in drying the rock, as the chalk absorbs moisture (that’s why we use it on our hands, duh). In addition, the rock quality can vary here from being bullet-hard to soft and featured. Avoid climbing on soft, sandy, or heavily-featured rock in wet conditions, as this increases the likelihood of holds breaking and permanently altering the climb for future climbers. However, our rock is generally harder than many western sandstones, and the more solid, less-featured rock is often ok to climb when it’s a little damp, as long as you avoid climbing on flakes. If you are not sure, just wait and climb it another time. If you need to dry the rock, use a towel, a fan, or (pro tip) be clever and stuff a piece of aluminum foil in the hold and climb on that. DO NOT torch holds to dry them. This was popular in the ‘90s, and the effects can be seen with many black holds on popular classics in Tilted Tree like Pocket Prow V7 (subsequently, a crystal broke from inside one of the pockets, making the line much harder than its original V6 version).

Dirt and Grime: Goodness, this one annoys me more than anything. DO NOT step in the dirt and immediately onto the rock. This smears dirt on the footholds, and eventually polishes them, permanently altering the climb and changing its difficulty. In addition, DO NOT grope the holds of a difficult climb without chalky hands, especially while somebody is projecting it. The oils from your hands also polish the hold. Your greasy little paws on the crux holds of somebody’s V10 project will ruin the next several tries for them.

GEOLOGY:
The rock in the Cheat Canyon and the surrounding area is predominately made up of Upper Connoquenessing Sandstone of the Pottsville group, more easily referred to as “gritstone”. It is a quartzose sandstone and conglomerate, most similar to the world-famous Millstone Grit found in the U.K.

PAPER GUIDEBOOK:
For more stories, longer essays, and a deep dive into the history of Cooper’s Rock, buy the paper guidebook here: https://cheatcanyonrockclimbs.com/cheat-canyon-bouldering

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Parking: Don’t block the road or park in an inconsiderate or illegal manner. That will get areas shut down really quickly. If an area is really busy (Tilted Tree is in view here), just go somewhere else. I bet there’s lots of climbs here you haven’t sent yet.

Respecting Nature: There are endangered and threatened species to consider when climbing here, including the American Chestnut, Eastern Hemlock, Green Salamander, and the Flat-Spired Three-Toothed Land Snail, found only in the Cheat Canyon. Many southwestern Pennsylvania areas have been shut down due to Green Salamander conservation, and despite local lore, the snail is a real thing. It is part of the reason for the Coopers Overlook closure. If you see one, respect its space. Avoid excessive cleaning of landings, routes, or topouts. Oh, and keep your eyes peeled for snakes; Timber rattlers can be life threatening. If you see one, record your coordinates and be sure to report it to Frank Jernejcic by calling 304-612-7725 or emailing fjernejcic@comcast.net.

Hunting Season: Wear orange during hunting seasons if you will be outside of the designated no-hunting zone.

Camping: There really isn’t much in the way of dirtbag camping around here unfortunately. While expensive, camping at Coopers Rock is generally the nicest option, offering both the McCollum and Rhododendron campgrounds for a total of 50 sites. The McCollum Campground has more space, and can host RVs, while the Rhododendron Campground is slightly more primitive, and is great for car camping or tent/hammock camping. As a climber, camping at Rhododendron campground will keep you within walking distance of a lot more climbing options, including fantastic bouldering caves behind sites #1 and #10. Alternatively, one can a camp at Chestnut Ridge Campground or Sand Springs Campground, which are both minutes from Coopers Rock and Darnell Hollow. If you’re willing to drive a little further, camping at Teter’s Campground near Albright is cheaper, and provides you with quick access to some fun bouldering by the Cheat River, though it is about 25 minutes from Coopers Rock proper. Please keep in mind that camping in the University Forest and in wildlife management areas is prohibited.

webSearchForLocation.name: Smith Rock
webSearchForLocation.description: Shadowed by the world renowned sport climbing, Smith bouldering is usually overlooked. With variety in all grades, its worthy to put the rope and harness away for a day to explore. There are problems on both the Tuff and Basalt. The Tuff tends to be sharper and more crumbly, while the Basalt is more "laser cut" and slippery.

webSearchForLocation.name: Black Mountain
webSearchForLocation.description:
Located in the San Bernardino National Forest in the San Jacinto Mountains is one of the best bouldering areas in Southern California, Black Mountain. There is a long history of climbing here from the Stonemasters, to locals coming from some of the first climbing gyms, to Chris Sharma in Rampage and beyond. Unfortunately, most of this history has gone unrecorded and will not be a priority in this guide. The priority is to document and share as much information as possible so that it is not lost and can be passed down for as long as possible. That being said, I am only one person and my goal is for this to be a living, breathing document of Black Mountain. I encourage everybody to contribute to the names, grades and any known history to any of the documented or undocumented climbs so that we, as a community, can pass this information down to future generations.

Below is a list of all other pertinent information:

The Paper Book:
Purchase the paper guidebook by Kimbrough Moore and Ian McIntosh here: https://www.blackmountainbouldering.com/

The Season:
Black Mountain is best in the Fall and Spring. It can be absolutely great in the Winter if it isn’t too snowy, however the road most likely will be closed (more info in “The Road” section). The summer can be pretty hot and isn’t ideal for climbing at your max but it is one of the few areas in Southern California at elevation, so it is often better than nothing.

The Road:
The majority of the climbing in Black Mountain is accessed off Forest Road 4s01 which is a dirt road that is only occasionally maintained, which means the road can be quite rough. The road is most likely to be maintained just before Memorial Day weekend, so it is good to assume that the further away from Memorial Day, the worse the conditions of the road might be. 4WD/AWD is strongly recommended, however the vast majority of the time, most cars can make it up the road to the majority of the areas (The Chappies and Ragger’s Point being the main exception).

The Gates:
About 2 miles up the dirt road is a gate that is open seasonally. It is most often closed at the first snow of the season and opened when the forest service deems it safe to drive back up (sometime in Spring). If the road is closed, it is only closed to vehicles, which means hiking up the road is still an option and often leads to very few people and amazing weather, just be ready for a .45 - 1.5 hour hike.

The other major gate is just before Boulder Basin Campground. The gate is generally open from Memorial Day weekend to Oct/Nov. There is plenty of parking below the gate and the hike to the campground is quite short so it isn’t too much of a hindrance.

The Camping:
The easiest camping is in Boulder Basin Campground which is $10/night and an additional $5/vehicle. The majority of the camping is first come, first served, however there are some sites in the campground that can be reserved ahead of time. The sites do not have running water, but do have pit toilets, picnic tables and fire pits.

Besides Boulder Basin Campground, there are some Yellow Post Sites which are free for camping. These sites have fire pits and picnic tables but do not have water or toilets. They also fill up extremely quickly so don’t rely on getting one.

Please be up to date on fire restrictions. Just because there is a fire pit does not mean access to the fire pit is allowed. Not obeying fire restrictions can lead to severe fires in the area and hefty fines.

The Grades:
So much of the climbing at Black Mountain has little to no consensus. While I did the best that I could to get as accurate of a grade for every climb documented in this guide, this is just the start. Grades are a consensus of the community and often the grades represented here are from just one person in this community. Please do your part and contribute to the consensus by not just taking the grade that the climb is given but to give your own well thought out opinion. Climbs are a different experience for everybody so there is no reason to feel judged on your opinion or to be rude to another person’s opinion.

The Names:
As alluded to in the introduction, much of the history of Black Mountain is unknown or lost to time. Many of the names given to the problems in this guide have been given a very generalized name and as a result, may be inaccurate. This is again where I ask you to do your part and contribute to the history. If you are aware of any inaccuracies, please just reach out so they can be adjusted.

The Amenities:
-Cell service is spotty and highly dependent on area, but it is best to assume that your cell phone will not work.
-There is a water spigot located between OK Corral and Boulder Basin, however its accessibility is seasonal and unreliable so it is best to not count on it.
-The closest gas station is in Pine Cove and tends to be surprisingly cheap.
-The closest restaurants and grocery stores are in Idyllwild, which can take 30-45 minutes to get to, depending on where in Black Mountain you are.

-LA/Orange County:
Head east to Banning. From Banning take the 243 for 16.6 miles and turn left on Forest Route 4s01. Find directions for individual areas in their specific area description.

-San Bernardino County:
Head south to Banning. From Banning take the 243 for 16.6 miles and turn left on Forest Route 4s01. Find directions for individual areas in their specific area description.

-San Diego County:
Head to Temecula and take the 79 S for 17.9 miles, turn left onto the 371 E for 20.7 miles, turn onto the 74 W for 12.4 miles, continue onto the 243 N for 12.5 miles and finally turn right onto Forest Route 4s01. Find directions for individual areas in their specific area description.

webSearchForLocation.name: Leavenworth
webSearchForLocation.description:
The small tourist village of Leavenworth is nestled at the edge of the granitic Wenatchee Mountains, on the eastern edge of Wenatchee National Forest. Bizarre festival weekends, a cornucopia of kitschy gift shops, and an abundance of overpriced hotels make this faux Bavarian village in the middle of the state Washington’s second-biggest tourist destination. Visitors to Leavenworth who don’t appear horribly out of shape are probably there to sample many of the outdoor recreational activities available in and around the town.

Each weekend brings groups of helmet-heads to Leavenworth to climb moderate trad climbs in the Icicle and Tumwater Canyons, and in recent years, hordes of boulderers eager to sample the area’s bounty. Leavenworth’s bouldering had been locally well-known but underappreciated for many years until the early 2000s, with most people seeming to equate it to much of the area’s roped climbing: off-vertical, sandy, and not especially exciting. Even John Sherman wrote in Stone Crusade that “Swiftwater Picnic Area is one of the few spots with enough problems to constitute a circuit, and even then one must hunt around in the woods for some of the boulders.” The venerable Verm must have donned an awfully thick pair of beer-goggles for his visit, as Leavenworth’s canyons are literally lined with a diverse array of pristine bouldering areas!

In addition to Little Bavaria’s well-traveled classics, the area is home to many newer problems that are steep, high, or hard – or all three. For a good sampling of the bouldering here in Leavenworth, make an attempt to check out all three major areas in this guide: Icicle Canyon, Tumwater Canyon, and Mountain Home Road. Each individual area within this guide sports a unique blend of stone, a pleasant setting, and at least one problem guaranteed to make your day. So go and explore for yourself – who knows what you might find?

FROM THE WEST

Southern Route

From I-5, take Exit 164A for I-90 east. Follow I-90 over Snoqualmie Pass and take Exit 85 for WA-970 N near the town of Cle Elum. Stay on Route 970 for 10 miles until it becomes US-97 N. Follow Route 97 for roughly 35 miles up and over Blewett Pass until it intersects US-2. Turn west onto Highway 2 and follow it four miles to the eastern edge of Leavenworth. This route is best when coming from downtown Seattle, Sea-Tac, Olympia, and other places along Puget Sound.

Northern Route

From I-5, take either Exit 171 for Lake City Way / WA-522 or Exit 175 for NE 145th St. / WA-523. Follow either until they join Route 522 at the northern end of Lake City, following 522 east through Bothell and a few other suburbs until it crosses under I-405 and becomes a two-lane road. Reach the town of Monroe roughly 22 miles from Lake City. Follow the exit for Highway 2 east and follow it 85 miles over Stevens Pass to Leavenworth. On the way, you’ll pass climbing/bouldering destinations in Gold Bar, Index, Skykomish, Stevens Pass, Smithbrook, and Nason Ridge. This route is best when coming from points north or east of Seattle (see below).

Bellevue etc.: When coming from the east side of Lake Washington, this route is best accessed via I-405 N. Take Exit 23 onto Route 522 and proceed as above.

Bellingham/Canada: When coming from Bellingham or the Canadian border, it’s best to take Highway 2 directly from I-5 in the city of Everett. Take Exit 194 off I-5 (about 25 miles north of Seattle) and follow Highway 2 100 miles through Monroe and over the pass to Leavenworth.

FROM THE EAST

Southern Route

The easiest way to get to Leavenworth from the east is to take I-90 west to Exit 106 in Ellensburg for US-97 N. Follow Route 97 north for 51 miles over Blewett Pass to the intersection with Highway 2, turn left, and follow it four miles west to Leavenworth.

Northern Route

When coming from Spokane and other points directly east of Leavenworth, it’s sometimes nice to take Exit 277 off I-90 and follow Highway 2 west.

webSearchForLocation.name: Kelowna
webSearchForLocation.description:
Join the Okanagan Bouldering Society for a discount on this and all other KAYA guides! See:

https://www.okanaganboulderingsociety.org/join-donate-obs

Kelowna, British Columbia is a prime base for climbers, centrally located in the heart of the Okanagan Valley. Known for its diverse climbing opportunities, Kelowna is surrounded by crags and boulders that offer climbs for all skill levels. The city's warm climate and long seasons make it ideal for outdoor pursuits, with Okanagan Lake providing a scenic backdrop for rest days filled with swimming, paddling, or hiking. After a day on the rock, climbers can explore Kelowna's vibrant downtown, enjoy local craft breweries, or visit the nearby wineries that make this area famous. With its blend of urban amenities and easy access to some of British Columbia’s best climbing spots, Kelowna is a must-visit destination for any climbing enthusiast.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: You can reach Kelowna by either air or road. If traveling by road, the drive from Vancouver takes about 4.5 hours, following Highways #1, #5, and #97C. From Calgary, the journey is approximately 7 hours, following Highways #1, #97A, and #97. For those coming from the US, you can either travel to Vancouver or Calgary and continue from there, or cross into British Columbia from Washington at the Oroville-Osoyoos border and head north on Highway #97 for about 2 hours. For air travel, direct flights to Kelowna are available from major cities such as Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto, Montreal, and Seattle. The airport, located at the north end of Kelowna, is about a 30-minute drive from downtown.

webSearchForLocation.name: Hatcher Pass
webSearchForLocation.description:
Hatcher Pass is the heart of the rock climbing scene in Southcentral Alaska, with some of the only granitic rock accessible from the road system. This includes roped climbing, which is quickly growing as new routes are developed. From a bouldering perspective, the potential is endless. Huge talus fields stream down the mountain slopes, occasionally casting rocks into the meadows beyond. At the height of summer, sunlight bakes the Diamond all morning until Toto Buttress shades it in late afternoon. Near sunset the soft light streaming through Fairangel Valley is a truly glorious sight. This pocket of granite on the edge of the Talkeetna Mountains, just a short drive from Anchorage, is paradise for those willing to explore. But there are some things you should expect as you adjust to paradise. Coming here for the first time can be confusing and overwhelming. There is so much rock, it takes time to adjust your perspective and learn to navigate through the talus. You should expect to hike, a relatively novel concept for many boulderers, since short approaches here are around 10 minutes.

Approaches through the talus field can be confusing, difficult, and dangerous. Many of these areas are not suitable for small children or dogs. Although some landings are perfect, many of the boulders in the talus have complicated landings requiring more pad coverage than most other climbing destinations. Do not expect to climb the same grade as you do in the gym; it just won’t work until you learn how to climb here.

Hatcher’s sharp crystals reward thick skin and devour baby-soft finger pads, so your first few days will be short but great. It all takes time to adjust, but the work is what makes it so rewarding. If you’re lucky, you will get a great day of climbing on Hatcher granite in the sun. It’s not impossible, we’ve seen it before, even if some years you are more likely to sit under a tarp than let your shoes dry out under the sun. Either way, a trip to Hatcher Pass is worth the work.

WHEN TO COME TO HATCHER PASS:

WINTER: October - March
Winter is a long season in Hatcher Pass. Days are short, dark, and snowy so rather than trying to boulder outside you should do something else: ski, go the gym, train, ice climb (if you must). Not convinced that there are better ways to spend your time? OK. During the winter the Mat-Su Ski Club (MSSC) grooms ski trails at Independence Mine and Archangel Road up to the gate. Few boulders will be climbable or dry, but you can try. Snow machines can also access Archangel Valley from Gold Mint Trailhead, which would make the endeavor of winter bouldering noisier but so much easier. 

SPRING: April - May
While snow starts melting at sea level, the boulders in Hatcher usually remain blanketed and difficult to access until Archangel Road opens. However, long days and bright sunshine make it possible to climb if you pick the right problem and have the right gear. Bike or ski up Lower Archangel Road for Aldershade. Marmot Meadows and several boulders in the Lost World and the Diamond can be good in the early season too, although the approaches are longer. Chugach National Avalanche Center maintains a webcam and a snow stake at Hatcher Pass Lodge which is useful for judging the snow levels on Archangel Road. 

The Road Run Sector is also a popular early season objective, with its steep, short approach. Also, ski touring up Independence Mine can be a fun way to mix sports and access boulders.

EARLY SUMMER: Late May - Mid June
Warm weather and sunny days mean the itch to go climbing is going to be strong, but the gates at Archangel Road and Independence Mine will likely remain stubbornly closed. A boulderer with an average bike and a strong pair of legs can use this time to extend the start of the season. Lower Archangel is reliable, but Lower Reed Valley and Marmot Meadows can be roasting too. If you can make it further up the road you will likely find lingering snow fields scattered from the Lost World to the Diamond. The Monolith might be okay around this time. Fairangel and Independence Mine are probably not the best places to go.

In the early summer, runoff from the snowpack will make crossing Archangel Creek very difficult until most of the snow has melted. On warm days the creek rises and by the afternoon crossing back to the road can be very difficult. 

SUMMER & FALL: Mid June - Early October
Archangel Road reliably opens around the second or third week of June. This date is subjective and based on avalanche debris on the road and the discretion of State park rangers. The long days of June tend to be the driest part of the year and parking at the Diamond can get busy as climbers flock up on weekends. 

July and August are when the mosquitos come out, ranging from generally absent to pretty bad, so bring bug spray. The weather is less reliable, potentially rainy, so check the weather stations and the webcams: the Marmot weather station, webcam at the snow stake, the Independence Mine webcam, and DOT webcam pointing towards Archangel Road. Sometimes the best way to check the weather is to go and see for yourself. 

The climbing season easily extends into September when the temperature and humidity usually drop. Anything in the shade (Fairangel southern areas) stays damp unless the rock is super clean. No (or less) mosquitos, but bring a puffy jacket, especially if camping. As the termination dust (first snow of the season) starts creeping down the mountain sides you’ll realize the season is almost over. The road typically stays open until the second or third week of October, when snowfall on the road causes the State Park to close the gate.

ETHICS:
Like most other climbers we tend to think of Hatcher Pass, its cliffs, crags and talus, as our special place. This sense of entitlement comes from the time spent in the valley and an intimate connection climbers have with the landscape on which we recreate. However, it is important to remember that we have no ownership nor do we hold any special rights above other user groups in Hatcher Pass. We only own our actions and, to that end, we have a responsibility to minimize our impacts to other climbers and users.

TRASH: Don’t leave any. This includes the boulders, trails, parking areas and campsites. I once climbed with someone who said he could leave his used tape behind because he had cleaned up spill sites somewhere else. I never climbed with him again.

HUMAN WASTE: Plan ahead and make a stop at the gas station on the way or at the outhouse at the parking lot at Gold Mint Trailhead. Remember that the outhouse at the Diamond is not a trash can. If doing your duty while among the boulders (it happens) find a hole in an obscure part of the talus or bury it. No one wants to step in that. 

NOISE: Be mindful of other users, hikers, and climbers. They may not want to hear your terrible choice of music.
Pad stashing: In recent years, pad stashing has become more regular in Hatcher due to long approaches and bad landings. We’re not opposed to it, but any stashed pads should be invisible from hikers and other users. From a climbing perspective, no one should have to move your pads to climb a boulder. Remember that in other parts of the country, people take/remove pads that are unattended; while I don’t condone this I am also opposed to visual eyesores.

DEVELOPMENT: Most people probably won’t develop new problems, but if you are compelled to do so, here are some considerations. There are anywhere between 100-300 problems which have not been included in this guidebook. There will likely be 100 more within a year of this guidebook’s release. Don’t assume you did an FA without some serious work. If you barely have to brush something, it is probably not new. So you climbed something first. Big whoop. Did you truly clean it enough that the second person can enjoy the climb? That’s the difference between doing a first ascent and developing a new problem. First ascents are fun, but don’t expect any “thank yous”. I love flat landings, so if I find a perfect patio of rocks under a new climb I would be psyched. Plus it’s a good workout. It should go without saying, but I’ll risk being explicit. Chipping, manufacturing, or creating holds in Hatcher Pass is NOT COOL. There are many boulders with blank faces and that can be a bummer, but leave them that way. There are plenty of climbs to find and clean. Just go look around and explore. A lobotomy is a better use for your chisel.

ACCESS ISSUES: The majority of bouldering in Hatcher Pass does not have access issues and is either on public land or mining land with few difficulties of access. The exception is Independence Mine, where it can range from agressive landowners to tour companies that have tasked themselves with policing the random signes dictating boundaries. It is important to try and respect the boundaries when possible.

HISTORY: When I started climbing in Hatcher Pass around 2009 there was no information available unless you were climbing with Todd Helgeson. Todd had been part of the first round of bouldering development in the pass along with Dan Kryger, Chris Terry, Jeff Claeson, and a few others. From 1996-2008 these guys cleaned a little, climbed a lot, and explored most of the valleys up Archangel Road putting up 700-800 problems. Everywhere we went in Hatcher it felt like Todd knew of established climbs on the best looking rocks. Will and Drew Crowther had made that mistake before, cleaning and naming an excellent problem (Top Gun) only to find out later it was called Humpty Dumpty. Despite the massive number of boulders in Hatcher, my initial impression was that most of the best boulder problems had already been climbed. I could not have been more wrong. By the time the first edition of the Alaska Bouldering Guide was released in 2013, my perspective on the development potential of Hatcher Pass had shifted. I knew the location of most of the established problems in Hatcher and realized I had been walking past potentially excellent problems for years. I made it my mission to redevelop the Diamond, adding density by cleaning the long ignored problems which had escaped the eyes of uber strong climbers. There was a lot of psych in these days, undimmed by the unexpected closure of the eroding bridge over Archangel Creek in 2014, which made the approaches from Reed Lakes Trailhead much longer. The bridge closure opened up new possibilities too, including the development of the Snowbird Talus in Lower Reed, exploration of Sydney Creek Bowl, and a marathon effort to climb Vertical Life in Snowbird Valley. All of Archangel Road was closed for the 2015 season while they repaired the bridge and turned the pot-holed, alder tunnel into a wide-open gravel pad; so we biked the road to get to the Diamond. Climbers were the only ones in Archangel Valley that year.

BUY THE BOOK:
https://www.climbak.com/product-page/hatcher-pass-bouldering-guide

webSearchForLocation.description_short_bouldering: The highest concentration of quality boulders in Alaska. Situated in an alpine setting within the Talkeetna Mountains.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Hatcher Pass is located 50 miles from Anchorage at the edge of the Talkeetna Mountains. From Anchorage, drive north along the Glenn Highway about 36 miles to the exit for Trunk Road. Take Trunk Road north for about 6 miles until it runs into Palmer Fishhook Road. Turn left and follow Palmer Fishhook Road into Hatcher Pass; Archangel Road is about 12 miles from the turnoff of Trunk Road; Palmer Fishhook Rd. ends at Independence Mine about 16 miles up. The drive from Anchorage takes about 1 hour and 10 minutes. From Wasilla or Palmer it’s about 25 minutes.

Archangel Road: Archangel Road covers the majority of this book. The areas of Lower Archangel, Sydney Creek Bowl, Reed Valley, Archangel Valley, Fairangel Valley, and Lane Valley are all found off this one dirt road. The road is blocked by a gate that usually opens sometime in June. It can really depend on snowpack and if the park service forgets about it. The road is still accessible when the gate is closed, but you are required to walk or bike. The first 2 miles are generally good, where most vehicles will have no problems. This changes dramatically when you get to the small bridge over Archangel Creek. From this point on, it gets dicey. If you are driving a low clearance vehicle of any type, you should consider stopping before the bridge. There is a large parking lot for Reed Lakes Trail, although you do have to pay the $5 daily parking fee. This parking area can fill up quickly on a sunny weekend and cars may be parked down the road. This can be a common problem when trying to get by, as people often block large sections of the road with their vehicles. Don’t be a jerk, and pull far off the road. Bring loppers to cut back the alders if necessary, or if you just need to burn some energy.
 Once you pass the bridge we don’t take any responsibility for what happens to your oil pan. If you’re worried about your vehicle just hop out and walk, it’s only an extra 15-20 minutes to the end. 

Independence Mine: Continuing past Archangel Road on the main paved road, you’ll round the mountain and come to a large parking lot leading up to an old mine. This is a very obvious area with lots of signage, and during the summer should have plenty of tourists around. During the early season it is similar to Archangel Valley as there is a gate blocking the upper parking. This can add a mile of paved road into your approach. Once the gate is open daily, it usually closes much too early. It is important to look for signs for when the gate will close. They usually close it a little early (7pm in recent years) so make sure to be gone before it’s locked. If not, you may end up knocking on doors or spending the night in the parking lot. A $5 fee is required for parking.

webSearchForLocation.name: Devil's Lake
webSearchForLocation.description:
Devil’s Lake State Park is located at the heart of the Baraboo Hills in southern Wisconsin. It is one of the most popular state parks in the area and is mostly known for its beautiful crystal clear lake and numerous hiking trails that scale the bluffs on either side. There is also a long and storied history of rock climbing in the park. Documentation of climbing on the quartzite cliffs surrounding the lake started in the 1920s. Bouldering itself became popular when John Gill visited the park in ~1958. He established “The Little Flatiron,” which stands as a standard test-piece V4 to this day. The generations that followed John Gill have each contributed a unique vision to the park. From establishing trailside classics, such as “The Zipper” and “Big Bud” to exploring the far reaches of the South Bluff, then to eventually discovering the massive potential of the talus fields. Today, there is still extensive development occurring. Some of the best and hardest ascents in the park have gone up within the last decade, and there appears to be no end in sight. Overall, Devil’s Lake is a great place to visit as a new climber looking to enjoy a beautiful and unique setting or as an experienced climber looking to try hard. 

The rock at Devil’s Lake, Baraboo Quartzite, is metamorphic and thought to be approximately 1.6 billion years old. During the Precambrian Era, the area that now makes up the Baraboo Range existed as a shallow sea near the equator. The sand that was deposited there was eventually subjected to intense pressure and heat, forming the dense quartzite we see today. The unique purple color comes from the presence of iron and other impurities. 

Many find climbing here to be a frustrating experience that takes time to master. The style is generally technical and unforgiving, due to the glassy nature of the rock. This, and it being an old-school area, can make grades feel sandbagged at first.  Conditions also seem to be a more influential factor here than other places. Crisp days in the shoulder seasons are the best times to try hard, though many enjoy climbing year round.

Local Ethics:

Quartzite is far more resistant than other rocks and normally dries within a few hours after rain in exposed areas of talus. Be mindful of brushing tick marks. Please clean up after yourself (and pick up other’s trash if you can!). No fires. No dispersed camping.

Purchase the paper book(s):

Devil's Lake Bouldering: https://kdanielspublishing.com/cart/index.php/guide-books/devils-lake-bouldering.html

MN & WI Bouldering: https://escapeclimbing.com/products/ecxbo02

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Devil’s Lake is centrally located in the state and normally accessed via US HWY-12. It’s about an hour from Madison, two hours from Milwaukee, two and a half hours from Green Bay, and three hours from Chicago (depending on traffic). Camping is only allowed in designated campsites (which need to be reserved through the park website or by calling) or in one of the many private campsites in the nearby area. The park is open from 6 AM to 11 PM year round. Summer months can be busy with other tourists, so arriving before 11am is recommended to secure a parking spot. Day passes or annual passes are required to enter the park and can be purchased at the main gates on either the North Shore or the South Shore. 

Access Issues:

Many boulders at the park require some form of bushwhacking or talus scrambling to get to. Proper hiking shoes and a pair of long pants should be part of a boulderer’s kit. There are a few areas where the boulders are near private property. The guide normally addresses this when relevant, but please be aware of where you are hiking. Some of the adjacent landowners are known to be litigious.

webSearchForLocation.name: Poudre Canyon
webSearchForLocation.description:
Cache La Poudre Canyon runs for about 50 miles starting near Bellvue, Colorado and all the way up to Cameron Pass. Initially settled by the Ute Indian Nation, its name comes from French settlers using the canyon to “stash their gun powder.” It is one of the few rivers in the country with a Wild and Scenic designation from the BLM. Most of the canyon falls within the Canyon Lakes Ranger District of the Roosevelt National Forest, with some areas also managed by the Dept. of Wildlife.

Camping options are plentiful in the warmer months, with many Forest Service pay sites listed on Recreation.gov, generally costing $6–12. Privately-owned options exist as well, with Archers Resort being one of the best (poudreriverresort.com). Free camping is increasingly rare, though Pingree Park Road, Red Feather Lakes, and Laramie River Road remain potential options. Car camping is officially illegal, but maintaining a low profile is key.

Many areas require river crossings ranging from ankle-deep to hazardous, and assessing conditions is a learned skill. No tyroleans are used due to the boating community and short crossable season. Waders, sandals, or old shoes are recommended. Winter crossings often involve frozen river travel, which also requires careful judgment of ice quality.

The High Park Fire (2012) burned over 87,000 acres and affected portions of the Narrows and Lower Canyon. While no climbing damage has been documented, access and hillside stability remain concerns—be cautious of burnt trees, rockfall, and unstable slopes.

Waste disposal is essential. Dig cat-holes or use Wag Bags and avoid going within 100 yards of water or parking. Many bathrooms exist throughout the canyon.

Dogs are welcome but require awareness of other users, highway proximity, cactus, and river safety. On DOW land, dogs must remain under voice control.

Wildlife is abundant—bighorn sheep, mountain goats, and moose are common near the highway. Moose require distance and respect. Rattlesnakes can be present in the Lower Canyon in summer. Bears, lions, and lynx are present but rarely encountered.

New route development is ongoing. Most hardware is stainless steel (3/8” or 1/2” wedge bolts, or SS 5-piece). Report any damaged bolts to the NCCC (nococlimbers@gmail.com
). Many sport routes now use fixed carabiners for lowering; inspect before use, lower directly through them, and donate replacements if they are worn. Use your own gear for top-roping.

Fort Collins is the nearest major town, offering a vibrant arts scene, breweries, outdoor access, and a mild climate.

Home to historic Ute Nation land and later French trappers who “stashed their gunpowder” here, the canyon is now a Wild and Scenic river corridor with abundant climbing, camping, and year-round outdoor access.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Most of the canyon sits within the Canyon Lakes Ranger District of the Roosevelt National Forest, with some portions managed by Colorado Department of Wildlife.

Camping:

Numerous Forest Service pay sites ($6–12), many reservable through Recreation.gov.

Private options exist, including Archers Resort.

Free camping is limited; possible zones include Pingree Park Road, Red Feather Lakes, and Laramie River Road.

Car camping is officially illegal but sometimes tolerated if low-key.

River Crossings:

Many climbing areas require a river crossing.

Conditions vary from easy to dangerous—evaluate carefully.

No tyroleans used due to river traffic and short crossable season.

Waders or water shoes recommended; in winter, evaluate ice thickness before crossing.

Post-Fire Zones:

High Park Fire burn areas remain unstable with falling tree and rockfall hazards.

Waste Disposal:

Use cat-holes or Wag Bags; stay 100 yards from water sources and parking.

Dogs:

Allowed on Forest Service land; must be under voice control on DOW lands.

Watch for cactus, river hazards, and traffic near the highway.

Wildlife:

Expect moose, bighorn sheep, mountain goats, rattlesnakes, and occasional large predators.

Yield to wildlife and keep distance, especially from moose.

Bolting & Hardware:

Routes use SS 3/8”, 1/2” wedge bolts or SS 5-piece bolts.

Report damaged bolts to NCCC (nococlimbers@gmail.com
).

Fixed carabiners at anchors are used for lowering—inspect first, replace if worn, and use personal draws for TR.

Nearest Town:

Fort Collins—major services, supplies, culture, breweries, and amenities.

webSearchForLocation.name: Vedauwoo
webSearchForLocation.description:
"John ­ there is more to life than Vedauwoo"" - Kyle O. (he's never climbed here)

Vedauwoo is known for a lot of things, good bouldering should be one of them. The most unique thing about the area is the amount of high quality crack bouldering climbs. The area is home to one of the hardest crack boulder problems in the world (Cry Me a River ­ V13: See Spaghetti Wall area). But it is also home to many great problems for practicing crack technique and fitness, as well as crimping strength, the strength of your ankles, and testing how bold are you really? People have been bouldering at Vedauwoo forever. Hull's Boulder (V0), at Turtle Rock, was done prior to 1966. John Gill has some great problems here. There is a rich history that I can't do justice. Just know that people have been bouldering here for quite some time, well before mega crash pads were a thing.

Vedauwoo can be split into two main areas, which are separated by Happy Jack Rd. (210): North of Happy Jack, and Vedauwoo Proper. Vedauwoo proper does have the vast majority of the problems, but a more secluded experience can be found North of Happy Jack. Some people are into that sort of thing.

Vedauwoo is unique in there is vast amount of public land that is all connected and access to many problems is trivial. Additionally, the sheer amount of high quality crack problems, as well as face and slab problems, is extremely unique. That's why you meet people from Slovakia at the Nautilus on a Tuesday. Use by all outdoor enthusiasts has increased drastically in the past 10 years. Please prioritize being a good steward of the area. If you are unsure of what this means, educate yourself. The SE Wyoming Climbers Coalition (SEWYCC) is the best resource to get started. Please donate if you can! 

FIRST ASCENTS

My FA is missing!!! We tried really hard to contact people and get all relevant information. We can't get it all. Please contact us to update. 

Lack of FA information: There are a lot of problems. FA information is hard to get for all problems. In the spirit of the second edition, we decided to drop FA information for most problems. 

ETHICS

Clean your tick marks. Ticking is helpful, but an eyesore. ­Do not chip holds or glue holds. Do not dry tool problems. ­Do not drive off of forest service roads. Even if you have 4WD. Even if you see someone else do it. When in doubt walk farther. ­Dogs: I don't mind dogs but I clean up after my dog and generally have him off leash if no one else is around. But, I carry a leash with me. If your dog doesn't have good recall (or you don't know what that means), or any sort of issue with other dogs or wildlife, then leash it. In some areas expect cattle and/or horses, so plan accordingly. ­Restroom: Try and find an established restroom. Otherwise, wagbag. Do not dig a hole at your campsite to take a dump in. ­Speakers: The music you play if you have these is bad. Be respectful of others. Just because you arrived first doesn't mean it is 'your space'.

CAMPING

Vedauwoo is one of the easiest places to camp at. There are designated sites in Vedauwoo proper, as well as paid camping spots. The designated sites, as of 2023, are first come first serve along Vedauwoo Rd. North of Happy Jack Rd. and the Blair area has less designated camping, for now, but you should only be camping at established areas. That means places where people typically camp. So not driving 300 ft. off the road wherever you want. When to come: I don't know why people climb so much here in the summer. The best months for bouldering here are September to December, then April to early June. If you are local, then great days can be had in January. But otherwise it's not worth the drive. Trust me ­ I have driven here more than you.

That means you are driving to a spot you've been psyched on and it looks ful! Oh well ­ I'll just drive on some of that sagebrush nearby and make a comfy spot for me. This is what you shouldn't be doing. Every approach here is trivial ­ walk the extra 30 seconds instead of expanding parking spaces by driving off established roads.

webSearchForLocation.name: Lake Ramona
webSearchForLocation.description:
Lake Ramona is quite an amazing area for San Diego climbing. Those seeking out a more “modern” style of climbing than the nearby Mount Woodson will love it here. The boulders have holds. And while it’s still a very technical style of climbing, it tends to be quite different from the rest of San Diego County: quality face climbs on amazing, unique rock, athletic movement, and of course some amazing splitter cracks. When you first get a glimpse of the hillside, the number of boulders is staggering. Nearly all of them have (or will have) climbs. I’ve spent a lot of time exploring the hills of San Diego looking for boulders, this is by far the most concentrated in quality that I have come across. It is just a big playground!

Access Issues

The parking lot opens at sunrise and closes at sunset. There is private property surrounding the hillside, but all of the climbing listed here is public. Please keep off of the rocks that surround the dam when hiking up!

Local Ethic

Since this place doesn’t have much history, it is up to us to establish the ethics. Due to its proximity and similar style to Mt. Woodson, it’s best kept similar. Toprope bolts are generally OK if there is no opportunity for gear anchors, and if the height warrants it. Sport climbs don’t really exist here, mostly because the boulders aren’t big enough. Stick to the established trails and game trails as much as possible. The brush here is very resilient but the soil will have a harder time recovering. Brush off excess chalk/tick marks, and wipe any dirt off your shoes off before getting on the rock. Of course, no chipping, manufacturing, or gluing holds! Holds break. It may be a bummer but it’s not worth gunking this place up. Pick up any trash left or found, and just be respectful of the area. This place has a such a cool vibe to it, let’s keep it that way.

History

People have been climbing here off and on since the late 70’s. We recently learned that one of the first persons to climb up there was John Sherman. He established the Summit Crack (5.7), Summit Lieback (5.8), and Slacker Cracker (V4/5.12-), and likely several more. He also had tried what is now Lifeblood (5.13+) on a few different days.

In 2016, Andrew (AJ) Burch made the first modern mission to the hillside, putting up the difficult tips crack, Izabella (5.12a), and several moderates. Almost exactly a year later, Ben May paid a visit and began putting up difficult face climbs, which sparked my interest, and development of the area has been pretty steady since then.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
It takes just about an hour to reach the best concentration of climbs. The hike is not too strenuous, but it’s long enough that you’ll want to make a full day of it. Park in the Blue Sky Ecological Reserve lot (NOTE: parking lot opens at sunrise and closes at sunset. Make sure to plan your day accordingly.) Begin the 2.5 mile hike up to the Lake Ramona Dam, following obvious signs along the road. The first part of the hike is very pleasant and flat (20 min), before hoofing it up the road to the dam (20-30 min). This section is mostly a gradual uphill with a few
steep sections, though no steeper than the Mount Woodson trail. Once at the top of the dam you’ll see the boulders on the hillside north of the lake. Continue along the road to the hillside. There are multiple spots you can head up the hill depending on what area you’re headed to. Hiking up the left side of the hill (before the road makes a hard right turn) is the best way to access most of the hillside, not including the Approach Hills, Base Areas, and Lakeside Boulders. For the Main Summit Trail, hike up the short steep hill to the left, scrambling up the “granite staircase”. From there, follow the obvious, steep trail trending up and right to reach the exposed ridge. Walk along the ridge, keeping an eye out for the obvious Lighthouse Boulder. The trail heads straight to this landmark boulder. The trails to most other areas branch off of the main Summit Trail at some point and are marked in the topos. For the Base and Lakeside Areas, hike directly to the boulders from the road above the dam. The brush is low in most spots making the hillside easily navigable, but be ready for a bit of bushwhacking if you trek out to any boulders away from the main paths. Don’t worry about getting into poison oak, there is none to be found here!

webSearchForLocation.name: Rocky Mountain National Park
webSearchForLocation.description:
For many climbers, bouldering Rocky Mountain National Park represents a near-perfect experience. The towering peaks, unpredictable weather, rocky landings, difficult problems, long days, and breathtaking scenery all combine for a unique adventure found nowhere else in the world.

SEASON: Typically June through October, depending on the altitude of the zone you’re visiting. In mid-summer, the Bear Lake Parking lot can be full by 7am, so get there early!

Mid-to-late-Summer thunderstorms are common and can be dangerous - especially in Chaos Canyon, where climbers have been known to be struck by lightning. Pay attention to the weather throughout the day, as storms can build up quickly. Hypothermia and the effects of altitude are also risks in the alpine, so prepare accordingly.

ETHICS: Bouldering in RMNP is a privilege and we should do everything we can to preserve and protect the resource and our opportunity to climb there. While in the park, remember, you are in an area regulated by the federal government, and breaking the law is a federal offense. Climbers have often worked with park rangers to establish a sustainable bouldering area.

- Do not stash gear.
- Pulverized rosin (POF) should never be used.
- Chipping and gluing are absolutely not permitted.
- Stay on marked trails and social trails described in the text or rock surfaces whenever possible. Avoid trampling vegetation.
- Fires are strictly prohibited at all areas in the guidebook.
- Playing music is unacceptable. This goes against the rules of wilderness and the Leave No Trace ethic.
- No deck style landings or cutting down trees. This is one of the most significant issues facing bouldering in RMNP. Please do not cut down trees to make a landing for your sick new project.
- Be considerate of other visitors.
​​- Drone flight is prohibited in all wilderness areas as designated by the National Wilderness Preservation System.
- No dogs are allowed on trails in RMNP.
- It is the local ethic to clean the chalk off the problem as best you can when finished, and to gently brush the holds between attempts.

Buy the paper book: https://stores.sharpendbooks.com/rocky-mountain-national-park-bouldering/

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
GETTING THERE
Climbers visiting internationally should use Denver International Airport (DEN). RMNP is 71 miles from downtown Denver, and the closest town to RMNP is Estes Park - about an hour and a half drive.

ACCOMMODATIONS
Estes Park is the jumping point for most everyone entering the park from the east. There are many hotels in Estes Park, and visitors should expect to have reservations in the summer months and to pay over $200 a night.

CAMPING
For many climbers on a limited budget, hotels are simply not an option. For the climber looking to camp, there are private pay-campgrounds in Estes Park. Rates vary from $20 to $60 a night, depending on your vehicle, the season, and your desired level of comfort.

For climbers looking to camp within RMNP (closer to the boulders than Estes Park) there are five pay-campgrounds, with a total of 586 campsites. This is the cheapest option for those looking to stay in the area. The maximum stay allowed is seven nights from June 1–Sept 30  and 14 nights from Oct 1–May 31. The campgrounds closest to the bouldering are Aspenglen, Glacier Basin, and Moraine Park. Campsites are $20 a night.

Visit recreation.gov to make a reservation. Reservations can be made up to six months in advance. There is extensive information about the camping in RMNP on recreation.gov and the park service website.

For those who don’t mind making the hour or so drive (depending on the tourist traffic) every climbing day, the best option is to find a friend in Boulder or Fort Collins and crash on their couch. There is no free camping in Estes Park or Boulder.

TIMED-ENTRY SYSTEM 
As of September, 2022, there is a timed-entry system into the Park between Memorial Day and mid to late October. The permits can be obtained at recreation.gov and each permit will cover one vehicle and everyone carpooling. Each vehicle needs a permit to enter the park. NOTE: If you are attempting to climb along Bear Lake Rd, you will need a timed entry permit for RMNP + Bear Lake Rd corridor.

webSearchForLocation.name: Tramway
webSearchForLocation.description:
Alpine bouldering in the desert?!!! That doesn’t seem possible, unless you are at the Palm Springs Aerial Tramway. For over fifty years the tram has brought tourists back and forth from the steamy desert floor to the cool alpine heights. Since 2001, it has introduced the largest of only three rotating tramcars in the world! Now climbers can enjoy the same amazing juxtaposition into a wonderland of towering conifers and ancient granite boulders! 

The website www.pstramway.com offers all the information about prices to ride the tram, as well as current weather, closures, and even two tram cams for real time viewing. As of this writing a roundtrip ticket is $30.95 a day with Annual Passes $165 and Summer Passes $85 also available (April-July). The mountain station is at 8,516 feet in elevation, so the Tramway has a reputation of being a summer spot, but as a local, I can testify to climbing there year round. In fact, the best friction for the harder problems seem to be when there is still some snow on the ground. 

Since the only access is up and down the trams, keep in mind to pack only the gear you need. The space in the tram is limited so if you are traveling with others or in a group, limit the amount of crashpads you bring. The Tramway employees are aware of this issue and would appreciate it for the other guests riding. Once at the Mountain Station, a small path leads you down to Long Valley. Continue straight to the Ranger Station. 

The Tramway bouldering is within the San Jacinto State Park. The area is a fragile ecosystem often referred to as an “island in the sky”. Many animals and plants thrive there and nowhere else. For these reasons, the rangers are becoming a little weary of the new influx of climbers, (especially on the weekend), but are working along with the locals to help educate the new climbers to the State Park rules. Everyone needs to stop at the Ranger Station to fill out a free permit (one per group), and carry the carbon copy of it, and later deposit it in the lower mailbox when exiting. The rules are posted on every permit, please follow them, as well as maintain your climbing ethics by not moving rocks at the bases to prevent erosion, cleaning up the ground and tick marks on the rocks before moving on, and staying on the trails whenever possible. 
Thank you, and enjoy your time in this unique desert forest, spot each other and send hard!

With 52 square miles of hiking trails, this guide is not the entire Tramway Bouldering. It includes the most popular spots that are North (right side) of the stream that cuts through Long Valley.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
With a population of over 45,000 people, and an elevation of 479 feet, the City of Palm Springs, California has proudly hosted the Palm Springs Aerial Tramway since 1963. Located at 1 Tramway Road, the entrance is just outside of the town off Highway 111. Anyone entering the town from the West will note the iconic Modernist, Albert Frey building at the entrance which is now a tourist center. The Tramway Mountain Station is about three miles up the steep road. Be prepared to pay a $15.00 parking fee upon entering. (Summer and Annual pass holders, and Coachella Valley residents are waived.) I know it's expensive, but unlike any other alpine climbing area, there is no mountain driving to deal with.

There is primitive camping available in Round Valley and Tamarack Valley two miles higher than the bouldering in this guide. The cost is $5.00 per person with a 2 week camping limit. Information and additional permits are available at the Ranger Station or by calling (951) 659-2607. Though most climbers on an extended trip to the Tramway take advantage of the numerous hotels and lodging options located within Palm Springs.

Palm Springs needs no introduction. As the gateway city to the Coachella Valley and with its exclusive desert dining and shopping, it has been a Hollywood retreat through the ages.

From Los Angeles, (107 miles), take the 10 or 60 Freeways due East, exit at Highway 111, Tramway road is another 8 miles, turn right at the third stoplight. From San Diego (139 miles), take the 15 Fwy North to join the 215 Fwy Northeast, then East on the 60 Fwy, before connecting to the 10 Fwy East. From Phoenix, Az, (271 miles) take the 10 Fwy West getting off in Palm Springs.

Palm Springs has its own International Airport, PSP. The closest other airports are Ontario, CA ONT(67 miles), or Los Angeles International Airport, LAX (122 miles) for the cheapest flights.

webSearchForLocation.name: Ibex
webSearchForLocation.description:
Ibex is a remote climbing area in Utah’s west desert that hosts some of the best rock in the entire state, but climbers must venture into remote territory in order to experience it. The massive quartzite blocks that house world class boulder problems surrounded by soaring peaks in the Great Basin desert environment provide a unique wilderness climbing experience. This is truly a special place, and we must treat the land accordingly.

— SEASON — 

Bouldering season usually starts in late fall and can last until mid spring (November through April). The temps you’re looking for are between 32-65 degrees Fahrenheit as a high. If it’s cold, you’ll really need it to be sunny. The warmer it gets, the more you’ll need a breeze. The colder it is, that breeze will freeze your fingers off and crush your soul. And this is Ibex - some kind of breeze is usually present. Sunny winter climbing can be idyllic or miserable depending on wind speed and cloud coverage. Check the forecast, especially the fine details. 


—WILDERNESS REMINDER —

This is a remote area included in, and bordering, King Top and Wah Wah Wilderness Study Areas. That means that cell service is extremely spotty, if not nonexistent, and help is far away. You will need to be self sufficient when coming out here. Bring all of the extra food, water, gas, and spare tires that you’ll need. I recommend filling up on gas whenever possible, preferably in Delta, UT or Baker, NV, and keep an eye on how much gas you’re using when driving around. It’s 45 minutes to Delta, and a tow costs around $500, but only if you can get service. Be confident that you can get yourself out if you take a bad fall. The boulders out here are tall.

The roads out here are all dirt, and can be deceivingly rocky. Tires can be punctured by the sharp limestone rocks. Bring a spare, and know how to change a flat on an uneven surface. Or, better yet, get some good, knobby tires (KO2's, Wildpeak A/T4's, etc.). Road tires are risking it!

Leave no trace. Don’t be messy, reckless, or loud. Clean up after yourselves - that includes climbing tape! It may feel like you can do whatever you want out here, but that is not the case. More on that below. 

—ETHICS—

CRYPTO ALERT:

At first glance, Ibex can be viewed as a wasteland. Look a little closer, and you’ll see that it is quite the opposite. Many plants and animals make their lives here, and as such, its fragility can’t be overstated. Like the desert of the Colorado plateau, the Great Basin desert’s good health relies on cryptobiotic soil crust (crypto for short). Created and composed of living organisms like cyanobacteria and algae along with inorganic soil matter, this crust is a living organism that is able to photosynthesize, fixes nitrogen in the soil, retains moisture, prevents erosion, and is therefore vital for plants and animals to thrive in this harsh environment. Unlike the Colorado plateau, though, this crypto does not grow to be inches thick. It’s very subtle, growing between the limestone rocks at your feet when hiking around. It’s usually thicker in shady washes, but outside of the Red Monster area, it’s literally everywhere, so please watch your step. It can be avoided by being mindful, and all trails to bouldering areas do avoid it. But please, again, watch your step and minimize your impact on this fragile desert environment. It’s worth it.


PLANTS:

Don’t destroy or cut down any plants. They didn’t do anything to you. They’re just trying to survive, man. 

ANIMALS: 

There are many animals that call this area home, including wild cats, eagles, owls, rabbits, rodents, and reptiles. Don’t disturb any of these guys if you see them. If you happen to see a Great Basin rattlesnake who is pissed off and rattling, leave the area and climb somewhere else. This stresses them out immensely, and could put their survival at stake.

CARS: 

Drive on existing roads and pullouts so you don’t kill plants and crypto. Don’t do donuts on the hardpan/dry lake bed. I know it’s super sick, but you can always do that in your mom’s driveway when it snows. Let’s be better than the hooligans that come out here.

FIRES: 

Refrain from making fires. I know, I know, fires are an essential part of camping, but when campfires get misplaced they can explode entire boulder problems, like what happened with Ju. Let’s not give others the idea that if they can make fires, they can make them anywhere. Don’t gather firewood from nearby pinyon or juniper trees. The desert needs the dead, decaying wood to replenish nutrients in the soil, even though it takes forever to break down. All a part of the cycle. Also, this part of the state has some of the darkest skies and most vibrant stars. Why not spend the night looking at the Milky Way and pondering the universe?

WET ROCK: 

Due to the quartzite’s outstanding harness, climbing after it rains is usually not an issue. 

BRUSHES:

Don’t use wire brushes. Even though the quartzite is bomber, wire brushes will damage it. Softies only.

ROCK ART:

Pictographs can be found on many boulders around Ibex. The boulders that do are noted in this guide. Do not destroy or damage these. Look, don’t touch, just like you’re in a museum. Don’t climb on the faces that have these on them, either. Just go climb on another face. I guarantee you there’s another banger around the corner.

— CAMPING —

This land is managed by the BLM, and you can pretty much camp anywhere, but please try and camp in established, cleared areas. There are nice spots along the base of the Ibex Crags. However, please refrain from camping directly under the boulders at the Red Monster Area.


— HISTORY AND OTHER COOL NERDY THINGS —

The Ibex Crags are an unmistakable geologic feature when seen from the east; massive white quartzite cliffs soar up grandly from the valley floor. This quartzite is actually the purest quartzite in the world - more than 99% quartz! It was deposited in a near-shore environment either in shallow sea water, and/or as dunes on the beach around 450 million years ago. The quartzite is sandwiched by dolomite and limestone above and below, denoting fluctuating sea levels. It’s really cool to envision this area being a tropical, beach environment, and at one time being at the bottom of the ocean. Fossils can be found everywhere in the limestone and dolomite. In fact, the Upper Pogonip Group layer is one of the most significant layers from the Ordovician that holds an abundance of fossils. 

The geology of the Great Basin’s ‘basin and range’ topography is extremely complex and fascinating. The hot, underlying mantle is doming upwards, causing the crust to be thinned and stretched apart. As a result, the crust is collapsing under its own weight, creating valleys as the mountains are rising.  

The Desert Archaic people occupied this area dating back to 10,000 BC. Both the land and climate were drastically different than today. Glaciers high in the mountains fed into the massive Lake Bonneville, which in turn, sustained incredible amounts of life: giant sloths, vultures with 18 foot wingspans, sabertooth tigers, bears, etc. Their skeletons can be found in caves scattered across the Great Basin. You can also find pictographs, arrowheads, pottery, remnants of fires, and knappings all over this area that date back to that age. Within the last 2,000 years, the Goshute, Paiute, and Shoshone people learned to thrive as the land dried out.

In the early 20th century, a brave young sheep herder named Jack Watson came out here to built a homestead. Life was rough, and he eventually left after years of struggle. Bouldering development started in the 90’s, first by the legendary John Sherman, and then by the usual SLC suspects: Boone Speed, Mike Call, Jonathan Knight, Ian Glas, Brian Mecham, Matt Lund, Mike West, Jeff Baldwin, John Cronin. You’ll recognize those names in LCC’s development. Ok, enough nerdy stuff - go climbing.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
FROM THE NORTH: Take I-15 south to exit 228. Take a right off the exit, drive through Nephi, and turn right on 100 N towards Delta (fill up gas here!). Once at Delta, make a right onto Highway 6/US-50. Drive 50.1 miles and make a left onto the main dirt road that accesses all of Ibex.

FROM THE SOUTH: Take I-15 north to exit 62 for UT-130 towards Enoch/Minersville/Cedar City. Once you hit Minersville, take a left onto UT-21 that leads to Milford. Once you hit Milford, the highway turns into UT-257. Follow this until you hit Highway 6/US-50 at Hinckley, UT and turn left. Follow this for 44.6 miles and make a left onto the main dirt road that accesses all of Ibex. (Alternatively, you could hop onto Iron Mine Pass Road by taking a left onto center street at Milford, then a right onto Iron Mine Pass Road, take a left onto Crystal Peak Rd, then a right onto Tule Valley Rd)

FROM THE WEST: Find your way to Highway 6/US-50, the loneliest highway in America. The main dirt road into Ibex is 103 miles from Ely, NV.

FROM THE EAST: Take I-70 to Salina, UT. Hop on Highway 6/US-50 until you reach Scipio. Take I-15 south and get off on exit 178 for Delta/Holden. Follow this to Delta (fill up gas here!), then drive 50.1 miles and make a left onto the mai dirt road that accesses all of Ibex.

webSearchForLocation.name: Vancouver
webSearchForLocation.description:
Welcome to Vancouver!

Nestled between the vibrant city of Vancouver and the majestic North Shore mountains, the bouldering scene here offers a unique blend of stunning landscapes and diverse climbing opportunities. From Horseshoe Bay to Deep Cove, the granite boulders, cloaked in lush moss and surrounded by ancient forests, create a picturesque playground for climbers of all levels.

The rock formations in this area are primarily composed of the same rugged granite found in Squamish, though the boulders here are often more compact and offer their own charm and character. The natural beauty of the region is truly captivating, with lush greenery, trickling streams, and the distant sounds of nature enhancing your climbing experience. The boulders were largely overlooked until the mid-2000s, when dedicated climbers began to explore and establish routes, leading to a burgeoning community of enthusiasts. Today, climbers of all backgrounds come together to enjoy the thrill of bouldering while appreciating the rich history and natural beauty of the North Shore.

Weather
The climbing season generally runs from April to October, with summer months offering the driest conditions. Thanks to the forest canopy, climbers can enjoy cooler temperatures even on warmer days. However, be prepared for the occasional rain, as the region is known for its moisture, especially in the winter.

One of the greatest advantages of bouldering in the North Shore area is its proximity to Vancouver. Just a short drive from the bustling urban center, you can escape into the serene wilderness in no time. This accessibility makes it a popular spot for both locals and visitors looking for a quick outdoor adventure.

Stewardship
As you enjoy the bouldering areas, we encourage you to practice Leave No Trace principles. Respect the environment by staying on established trails, packing out what you pack in, and keeping the areas clean for future climbers.  Moss grows back quickly here, often obscuring excellent climbs. We recommend bringing a wire brush to keep the boulders clean and ensure these routes don’t fade into the greenery.

webSearchForLocation.name: Stone Fort
webSearchForLocation.description:
Stone Fort (also known as Little Rock City) has world class sandstone and unparalleled approach. This boulderfield is just 20 miles from downtown Chattanooga making it one of the most accessible climbing areas in the country. The high season is from October through March. 
Grades ranging from V0-V13, there is something for nearly every climber. Great for families and groups.
Stone Fort is privately owned, day passes are $10 on the weekdays, and $12 on the weekends. Restrooms and small snacks are located at the clubhouse. 
Please be respectful and allow the rocks to dry 24 hours after rain. No plastic brushes are allowed.
For more information, please see: https://www.stoneforttn.com/climbing

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
From downtown Chattanooga:

- Take US-27 North toward Soddy-Daisy.
- Continue on US-27 for about 10–12 miles.
- Take the exit for TN-153 North toward Dayton Pike.
- After merging, immediately take State Route 319 / Hixson Pike toward Mowbray Mountain.
- Follow SR-319 / Hixson Pike as it winds uphill. After several miles, it becomes Montlake Road.

At the top of the mountain, look for signs for the Montlake Golf Club.
The Stone Fort climbing check-in is inside the clubhouse.

Total drive time is usually 25–30 minutes from downtown Chattanooga.

webSearchForLocation.name: Mount Woodson
webSearchForLocation.description:
The number of boulders covering Mount Woodson is staggering. To the modern boulderers dismay, you will find that many of these smooth granite eggs offer hardly any face features. The type of rock here makes for lots and lots of thin edging and friction slabs, stellar crack boulder problems, and hard mantles. If that’s not your cup of tea, there are plenty of modern style classics scattered all over the hill. Classic, and stout, testpieces exist in just about every style imaginable. But don’t completely turn your nose down at the sight of a bald granite blob. There are many learning experiences to be had here, and you’ll become a better climber for it.

ETHICS:
Clean up after yourself. Wipe off your shoes before pulling onto the rock. Don't chip or enhance holds. Brush your tick marks. Consider bringing a pair of small loppers and help keep the climbers trails in shape.
