webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Parking is along the west side of Highway 67. You'll see the cars. The trail starts down in a ravine and heads south on a dirt path until meeting up with the paved road. This is where most areas are accessed form.

webSearchForLocation.name: Red Feather Lakes
webSearchForLocation.description:
Get the paper guide at: https://www.fixedpin.com/products/red-feather-lakes-climbing-guide or your local climbing shop.

OVERVIEW
The climbing in Red Feather Lakes is scattered around an area of nearly 90 square miles in Northern Colorado. From the Poudre Canyon in the south all the way north to the Cherokee Park Rd (CR 80C), Red Feather is a massive landscape of granite domes, boulders and cliffs. The area has been a place for fisherman, backpackers and mountain bikers. Only now is the story being told about all the climbing here. Most of the land lies on Arapahoe & Roosevelt National Forest (Canyon Lakes Ranger District) but there are also State Wildlife Land (DOW) areas and a lot of private property as well. The following information is just about everything you need to know to climb in glorious Red Feather Lakes.

ETHICS
Red Feather Lakes is only about 50% developed as a climbing area. Hundreds of routes and boulder problems remain unclimbed, and every crag in this book still holds untapped potential. Beyond these, there are countless sectors not even included here, making the overall quantity mind-blowing.

One of the most exciting aspects of Red Feather is the unknown—you can wander into the forest and find new climbs of every style. It’s a place for creativity and exploration that could keep climbers busy for decades.

- Boulder Development -
Brushes: Wire brushes and hand brooms are essential; use plastic or toothbrush-style brushes for delicate cleaning.

Vegetation: It’s fine to prune small bushes or deadfall, but avoid cutting living trees.

Lichen: Some is very tough—try “rock rubbing” if brushes fail.

Trails & Cairns: Keep trails minimal. Avoid excessive cairns—they’re unnecessary and an eyesore.

Loose Rock: Be cautious with prybars or screwdrivers—using tools scars the rock and damages reputation. When in doubt, climb it first or consult the NCCC (nococlimbing.org) before removal.

- Documentation -
To keep track of new development, submit new problems and routes on KAYA with as much information as you can include.

- Campfires & Wildfires -
The Cameron Peak Fire (2020) burned over 208,000 acres, though only a small part of Red Feather was affected.Red Feather has been lucky so far thanks to fire mitigation by the Forest Service and locals. Key takeaway: Do not start campfires. Even in campgrounds or snow, the risk of wildfire in Colorado’s dry climate outweighs the reward.

- Waste Disposal -
Carry a trowel for cat-holes or use Wag Bags to pack waste out. Stay at least 100 yards away from water sources and parking areas. Public bathrooms are available in Red Feather Lakes—use them when possible.

- Dogs & Pets -
Dogs are welcome on Forest Service land. On DOW land, they must be under voice control. If your dog chases wildlife or horses, keep them leashed or tied up. Red Feather is great for dogs—bring them, but keep it responsible.

HISTORY
The climbing history of Red Feather Lakes is fragmented and partially lost to time. Climbers have been active here for over 50 years, but much of the early activity went undocumented.

1970s–1980s:
The first documented climbing took place in the mid-1970s at the Ben Delatour Boy Scout Ranch (BDSR), where Andy Hibl and Bill Nelson started a mountaineering program. Hibl placed massive 10–12"" eye bolts to protect scout top-ropes—likely the first fixed hardware in Red Feather.

Through the mid-80s, climbers such as Mark Guzman, Bill Alexander, Mike Lawson, Pat McInearney, and others established the first technical lines around BDSR and nearby Swallow Crags.

By the late 80s, climbers like Craig Luebben, Rob Kelman, Malcolm Daly, Bryan Parsons, and Jim Brink were developing Creedmore Crag, after Brink stumbled upon it during a fishing trip. Brink later wrote the first mini-guide to the area.

1990s:
Development continued but documentation is hazy. Craig Luebben was likely still active, but much history was lost after his passing.

Andrew Mason and Matt Fanning developed routes at the Dowdy Domes into the early 2000s.

The late 90s marked a new Golden Era of bouldering, led by Geoff Sluyter, Pat Goodman, Francis Sanzaro, Mike Auldridge, and others. Areas such as the Ceremonies and numerous zones west toward Disappointment Falls were explored.

2000–2010:
The early 2000s saw a surge of development at areas like the Ceremonies, Meadow Boulders, Lady Moon, Parvin Lake, and the Capitols. Key players included Jeremy Bisher, Dave Ludders, Chuck Fryberger, Jamie Emerson, Tom Blackford, Ryan Anglemeyer, Doug McKee, Jason Tarry, and the author.

From 2006–2010, drought years brought mild winters, enabling locals to establish hundreds of boulder problems. Areas such as the Swoosh, East Dowdy Lake, Pit and the Pā, West Elkhorn Creek, and the Iron Fist Zone were developed. Climbers like Cam Cross, Collin Kopitzke, Jason Nadeau, Jamie Emerson, Jacob Ojile, Jason Tarry, and Ryan Nelson were central to this effort.

2010–Present:
Development has continued with both longtime locals and new climbers. Rope climbing has expanded at the Grazing Allotment, Swallow Crags, Pot of Gold Wall, Dowdy Domes, and new areas like Dome with a View. Contributors include Jeff Snyder, Josh Cook, Tucker Schultz, Ryan Nelson, Jason Tarry, Ken Duncan, and the author.

Bouldering has also thrived, with active climbers such as Ryan Nelson, Matt Robbin, Matt Poiesz, Brett Hoffman, Nick Perl, Ben Jurenka, Isaac Trujillo, Pete Zagorski, Drew Zweifel, and John Lombardi.

The pace of development has only increased in recent years and shows no signs of slowing.

GEOLOGY
Granite is the main rock of the outcrops in Cherokee Park and Red Feather Lakes. Fine-grained rock cooled quickly. Larger-grained rock cooled slowly, so crystals had time to form. One mineral in granite is feldspar, usually pink or white. Greyrock Mountain is a part of the granitic Log Cabin Batholith. It intruded surrounding older rock 1.4 billion years ago. The granite intrudes into other layers. As the layers erode, the load lightens and the granite cracks. Weathering is done by chemicals, water, wind and ice which enter the cracks. Weathering happens fastest at edges. Slabs of rock peel off like an onion skin in a process called exfoliation.

How do the "patina holds" in Red Feather naturally form? Patina is a term often used in reference to metals. In a general sense it is an altered layer on the outer surface of the material. This alteration is usually chemical in metals. In reference to granite, patina is an erosion feature... mostly. In eons past the erosion setting of a particular boulder or cliff may have been much different from today. Different settings may have polished the outer layer with water; water can also deposit their own thin patina layers on top or surrounding this polish. As centuries pass, the climate and erosion setting of that area may change to wind and freeze-thaw cycles rather than a water-dominant setting. These changes will cause the outer layer to slowly disappear, but not all at once. The plates we see are then created by wind, water, and other erosion processes attacking the stone and breaking down the more friable areas leaving the patina (outer layer) sticking out for climbers to enjoy. –written and compiled by Collin Kopitzke

PRIVATE PROPERTY
Red Feather Lakes is a huge residential area with hundreds and hundreds of private homes scattered around it. Along with those homes comes a lot of private property. Luckily, almost all of the climbing described in this guide is on public land. But there are also a lot of problems listed that are located on private property and are included for historical purposes only.

DISCLAIMER: The author and his cohorts are obviously complete and total hypocrites when it comes to climbing on private land. During the last 24 years of bouldering development there were hardly any climbers to speak of, and the area has changed a lot over that time span. Boulders that were once public have become private, old landowners who were ok with climber activity have sold the property to less tolerant folks, etc. Basically, the risk of getting caught trespassing used to be very, very low.

MOVING FORWARD: Please do not trespass for climbing. The non-climbing community in Red Feather Lakes has really no idea that climbing is even a thing. This book is most likely going to bring a lot more traffic to the area than these folks have seen ever before. We as a community need to give ourselves a good reputation right off the bat. Lead by example—DO NOT TRESPASS ON PRIVATE LAND WITHOUT THE LANDOWNER'S PERMISSION!

See individual Areas, Subareas, and Boulders for driving and approach info. Happy climbing.

webSearchForLocation.name: Big Cottonwood Canyon
webSearchForLocation.description:
While the bouldering in Big Cottonwood Canyon is largely overshadowed by the nearby Little Cottonwood, there is a huge variety in climbing here and a little something for everyone. Lower in the canyon, the rock is high quality quartzite and makes for lots of interesting features and good, steep climbing. Drive to the top of the canyon and you will be climbing on the lovely granite around Brighton, surrounded by aspen trees and alpine lakes. Keep driving up and over Guardsman Pass and make the hike to the Gman Boulders for a serene bouldering experience on highly unique rock. While LCC may have BCC beat for roadside classics, Big is perfect for those who love to explore and get away from the crowds.

ETHICS
No gluing, chipping, or manufacturing any holds. Generally just respect the places you get to climb at. Clean up after yourself, pick up any trash you find, brush your ticks and excess chalk off the holds, clean your climbing shoes before pulling on the wall. Stick to established trails the best you can. Respect the watershed protections, there is no swimming allowed in Lower Big Cottonwood and Brighton.

HISTORY
Big Cottonwood has a long history of sport/trad climbing, but the first recorded bouldering was likely done in the 80's and 90's. The canyon is covered in A Bouldering Guide to Utah by Baldwin, Beck, and Russo, and features many of the quartzite boulders lower in the canyon, as well as mention of the Milly Boulder in Brighton and a few surrounding lines. The rest of Brighton and Guardsman areas were a bit more recently explored, largely developed by Jay Keener, Victor Copeland, Tommy Rigby, Alec and Larson Quick, and others. The lower canyon has recently seen a surge of development, with boulders like Nightman, Forged in Fire, and the Ramp Wall being put up in the last few years. There is a lot of rock up here, and there is still plenty of development to be done, especially if you're willing to hike.

webSearchForLocation.description_short_bouldering: Big Cottonwood Canyon offers a wide variety of climbing on a wide variety of rock types. There is everything from steep, featured quartzite caves just off the road, to high quality, techy granite in an alpine setting. This is a great place to get off the beaten path!
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From I-215, take the 6200 S exit and head east, following signs to Big Cottonwood/Brighton. Once in the canyon follow directions on KAYA for parking to different areas. Guardsman Pass is also easily accessed from Park City.

webSearchForLocation.name: Flagstaff Mountain, CO
webSearchForLocation.description:
OVERVIEW
Simply put, Flagstaff Mountain is the premiere bouldering destination around Colorado’s Front Range. Hundreds of maroon sandstone boulders litter an area of less than two miles, creating the highest concentration of pebble wrestling in the state, excluding perhaps Lincoln Lake or RMNP. Many of the oldest, most historical problems anywhere belong on the walls of Flagstaff, and the area has maintained a very steady stream of popularity since the 1960’s. 

Although the rock quality and size of the boulders change vastly, Flag is not much known for its variety of style. The stone here can be famously uncomfortable, with heinous, gritty crimps, polished pebbles that don’t fit every finger, and equally bad pockets left when said pebbles explode. I wouldn’t wish a session in July here even on my worst enemy! It is not an uncommon experience (for both newbies and locals alike) to wreck the skin and crimping power on warmup problems, get completely smacked by the projects, and go home, vowing not to return until next season. Once the skin grows back however, we all realize the beauty of Flag: it’s close and it’s easy to have fun at. So come with tape, friends, and cool weather, and I guarantee you’ll have a blast at Boulder’s outdoor gym. 

HISTORY
Flagstaff is blessed to have the richest bouldering history in the state of Colorado, and numerous books and articles dive deeply into a decade-by-decade account of how Flagstaff became what it is. To keep things brief, adventure seekers have played around on the most obvious formations of Flag since the 1940’s. By the 1960’s, Colorado’s first true bouldering generation had arrived at the blocks above Boulder. Guys like Pat Ament, John Gill, Bob Williams, Bob Poling, Richard Smith, and several more established the first real problems on the area’s larger and higher quality boulders. The 1970’s brought Jim Holloway, Christian Griffith, Rob Candelaria, and other ahead-of-their-time crushers to Flagstaff. Most noteworthy from this generation is surely Holloway’s ascent of Trice- the world’s first V12 and a famous testpiece even to this day. By the 80’s and 90’s, development of the classics had slowed. Colin Lantz, Skip Guerin, David Breashears, and more continued to fill in the gaps. Y2K marked the end of Flagstaff’s booming first ascents, but Chip Phillips, Peter Beal, and more Boulder locals were ever-persistent and found new lines between the seams.

SEASON
Flagstaff is a fall, winter, and spring paradise. The sharp rock and polished stone demands friction more than most types of rock. 

ACCESS
Flagstaff is maintained and protected by the City of Boulder. Access is as easy as it gets, and there is no private land to worry about (except for the Flagstaff House Restaurant, which no boulders exist around). With that said, do stick to the trails and clean up after yourself! I’m tired of seeing tape, chalk, wrappers, and obnoxious tick marks.  If you can’t treat the outdoors with respect, go back to Movement.


A $5 parking fee is required for any vehicle parked along Flagstaff Road within the Open Space park. This fee is mandatory throughout the year, 24 hours a day. No reservation needs to be made online to acquire a pass.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Flagstaff is accessed by driving west up Baseline Road. After passing Chataqua Park and the Flatirons on the left, Baseline will become Flagstaff Road at a hard right turn as it begins to wind up the mountain. Parking and bouldering are all right off Flagstaff Road at various mileages.

webSearchForLocation.name: Rumbling Bald
webSearchForLocation.description:
Rumbling Bald is a true gem of the southeast.  The Bald has it all from crispy technical climbing to powerful overhangs. 

Rumbling Bald is managed by Chimney Rock State Park in NC and has a few rules:
1) Climbing and bouldering requires filling out a free permit at the kiosk near the trail entrance
2) Dogs are allowed but must be kept on leash - please pick up their poop and deposit at the trash cans in the parking lot
3) Stay on existing trails.  Building new trails or new landings must be approved by Chimney Rock State Park
4) Anything past the Washing Machine / Patio Roof Area off the main trail is on Private Property - please do not climb any boulders in the "Hanging Chain" area
5) Don't park outside of designated spaces or you will be towed - if the lot is full then try to catch a ride from Chimney Rock Village
6) The Park closes around sundown every day so plan to be done by then.  Hours are:
8AM-6PM Nov-Feb
8AM-8PM Mar-Apr & Nov-Oct
8AM-9PM May-Aug
**Additionally the park is closed on Christmas Day**

This guidebook contains all of the best problems and newest FA's including climbs you won't find elsewhere.

The Bald has its own microclimate which keeps temps ~10 degrees warmer than Asheville.  The Bald is climbable any time except for Summer, but prime conditions are from November through March.  

The field is broken into 3 main areas, the West Side, East Side, and Central.  All areas are accessed from the main parking lot using the loop trail. The West Side is the most popular with easy trails, a high concentration of classics, and good landings.  The East Side is a bit more rugged but boasts some of the best problems at the Bald.    The Central area has the longest approach and is the least climbed so it can be good for those seeking more solitude.

***If you have the print guidebook note that the Hanging Chain Boulders (basically anything past the Washing Machine / Patio Roof on the West Side) are on private property and CLOSED to bouldering***

If you like climbing at the bald please consider supporting the Carolina Climbers Coalition as they built the parking lot, own the West Side Boulders, and are the biggest advocate for keeping the Bald accessible to everyone.  
https://carolinaclimbers.org/donate

**
74-A and routes through Bat Cave NC are currently closed due to Hurricane Helene.  Plan to use routes through Lake Lure to access Rumbling Bald until  roads can be restored.
**


***All climbers must fill out a free permit at the kiosk in front of the trail. *** 

If the parking lot is full, try to find a spot in the village and hitchhike up.  Don't park outside of designated spots or you will get a ticket.

webSearchForLocation.name: Fraser Valley
webSearchForLocation.description:
The Fraser Valley bouldering is wild and adventurous. With overgrown trails, moss-covered boulders and the threat of running into cougars and bears, this place sure has its charm. Only two hours from Squamish it is a great alternative for those who seek to get away from the crowds and experience a raw and untamed wilderness. The rock itself is plentiful; there are well over 1000 established lines and new areas still being discovered; with the charmingly chossy talus field of Elbow Lake, the dense granite-filled forest of Hunter Creek and the raw beauty of the Fraser Canyon, there is something here for everyone.

This guide would not be possible without the people who worked to develop the boulders, preserve the areas and record the information. Marco Lefebvre, Nate Woods, Trevor Edwards, Brett Kruselnicki and Alex Stewart to name a few. 

-WEATHER-

The climbing season is typically from April to October, while the best conditions are on the dry days during the shoulder seasons. However, these shoulder seasons are cursed with heavy rainfall. Some areas do better than others at certain times of the year. This will be highlighted in their descriptions.

-ETHICS-

The Fraser Valley climbers are blessed with pristine wilderness. We have all seen the impact climbers can have on their surroundings. To minimize your impact, please respect these guidelines with climbing:
-Stay on the trail. (If you can find it)
-Pack in it? Pack it out!
-Brush your tick marks. (Let the next person have the same adventure you had)
-Be kind to all. (Especially the non-climbers and wildlife)
-If you have to leave a #2, bury it and pack out your TP.
-For bonus points: leave it better than you found it by scrubbing a boulder or moving a log off the path, etc.

-ACCESS ISSUES-
The majority of the Fraser Valley bouldering is on private or Indigenous land. While efforts have been made to secure land access, it is a privilege, not a right, to climb here. For this reason, the Valley has remained a poorly kept secret for years. Please treat these climbing areas with respect, so people can continue to climb here for years to come. 
Doing so means: 
-No loud music. 
-Keep a smaller group size.
-Keep the impact on wildlife and vegetation to a minimum.

Specifics about each area can be found in their descriptions.

webSearchForLocation.name: Reimer's Ranch
webSearchForLocation.description:
The data and descriptions for this bouldering guide are generously provided by Jeff Jackson, former editor of Climbing Magazine, the author of Texas Limestone Bouldering, and one of the original developers of Texas bouldering.

35% of the revenue from this guide supports the Texas Climbers Coalition.
https://www.texasclimberscoalition.org/ Situated right off the Pedernales River, Reimer's is Austin's popular and much-loved sport klettergarten. The stone cleans up beautifully and holds are abundant. Bolts are abundant, too, and a couple of generations of tweakers have left their mark with some mighty desperate sport climbs. The bouldering at Reimer's is also excellent, although it tends to lend itself to more moder-ate lines. My guess is that some altruist will one day soon take on the task of cleaning up the many problems along the Downstream Band. When that task is complete, Reimer's will house the densest collection of easy/moderate problems in the area.

Special Thanks to Evan "Action" Jackson, Tommy Blackwell, Luke Bowman, Karl Guthrie, and Eric "EP" Patrick for depeloping the new areas such as The Dugout, Beyond the Hand Beyond, and End of the World. All of the informa-tion contained in this guide for those areas was donated by Evan Jackson.

webSearchForLocation.description_routes: Reimer’s Ranch, located along the Pedernales River just outside Austin, Texas, is one of the state’s premier sport climbing destinations. The limestone cliffs here offer hundreds of well-bolted routes ranging from steep, pocketed faces to technical vertical walls, catering to a wide range of abilities. The rock’s sharp texture and abundance of features make for powerful, dynamic climbing, especially in the shady canyons that stay cool even as Texas heats up. The prime season typically runs from late fall through early spring, when mild temperatures and low humidity create ideal conditions for sending.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From Town Lake follow Mopac South to Southwest Parkway. Turn right. When Southwest Parkway dead ends into 71, turn right. Turn left onto Ranch Road 3238 (Hamilton's Pool Road) and continue for 13 or 14 miles. Turn right at a sign that reads "Milton Reimer's Fishing Ranch." Follow the dirt road, staying left at the first fork, to a house. Continue on, staying left at the forks and park at the parking area.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_routes: Reimer’s Ranch is about a 40-minute drive west of downtown Austin, making it an easy day trip for climbers. To get there, head west on Highway 71 toward Bee Cave, then turn left onto FM 3238, also known as Hamilton Pool Road. Follow this scenic Hill Country route for roughly 12 miles until you see the park entrance on your right at 23610 Hamilton Pool Road in Dripping Springs. The main road into the park is paved, and signs will guide you to the climbing area parking lots near the North Shore. The drive winds through classic Texas limestone hills, and though the roads narrow near the park, access is straightforward year-round.

webSearchForLocation.name: Horseshoe Canyon Ranch
webSearchForLocation.description:
Horseshoe Canyon Ranch is the most popular bouldering and climbing area in Arkansas. With convenient access and trail systems HCR is one of the best places to go if you are trying to dive into climbing outdoors for the first time. HCR also hosts some of the best hard bouldering in the state. Making this one of the easiest places to find a project for anyone in your group.

Grab the paper guide from Cole Fennel here: https://www.naturalstatepublishing.com/product/arkansas-bouldering/

webSearchForLocation.name: Tulsa, OK
webSearchForLocation.description:
The city of Tulsa, OK sits amidst a region of rolling hills and dense forests on the west edge of the Ozark Mountains, otherwise known as Green Country. Beneath the canopy of trees lie hundreds of cliffs and boulders made of limestone or sandstone. 700+ established boulders and rope climbs are spread across almost 15 areas within an hour's drive of Tulsa with plenty more to be found and established. These guides cover 5 classic climbing destinations containing over 400 boulder problems and nearly 50 convenient rope climbs.

Weather/Climbing Season

Eastern Oklahoma is a very humid climate year-round and reaches temperatures of over 100°F in the summer. As a result, the ideal climbing season is usually only 4 months between late October and early March. Depending on the year, pleasant climbing can be extended into late April for a total of 6 months of solid climbing.

Sandstone makes up the vast majority of the rock in the area meaning that friction and conditions are critical. However, if its warm and you still want to climb hard, consider climbing on limestone. Veteran local climbers tell tales of hard sends on the slick limestone of Chandler Park even into the high 70s Fahrenheit.

Ethics

The main thing to know about climbing in the Tulsa area is that the sandstone is relatively fragile and soft. Regardless of the area, ALL climbers need to know that sandstone is weakened by the rain and will break if not given enough time to dry. This is especially true here. A general rule in the area is to give the sandstone 3 days to dry for every full day of rain. Moisture hides inside sandstone and will keep it wet even when it does not appear wet on the outside. This can be very inconvenient for the traveling climber and even the local climber, but when a climb breaks, it breaks forever. If it rained recently but you still want to climb, consider climbing at Chandler Park or visiting a local gym. Local limestone is totally fine to climb after a rain, only actively wet limestone will keep you from quality climbing.

webSearchForLocation.name: Mineral King
webSearchForLocation.description:
Mineral King is a subalpine glacial valley located in the southern part of Sequoia National Park. It is open seasonally from May through October, and is accessed by a long and narrow winding road. It is mostly and traditionally popular with backpackers and hikers, but the bouldering potential is just starting to be tapped. Most of the quality boulders are around lakes where the boulders are "pre cleaned" but there are some harder to find forested boulders as well. The rock is mostly granite but with a few exceptions. While there are a few stellar roadside lines, the bouldering here is not for the faint of heart, and a normal approach is 3+ miles, with some exceeding 8 miles. As such, take extreme caution when bouldering in the back country since all inherent dangers of rock climbing are amplified by the remoteness. Come here with a humble heart open to adventure, beautiful views and introspections. As an interesting fact, Disney once planned to make the Mineral King Valley a Ski Resort, but after long legal battles the valley was annexed to Sequoia National Park and the Ski Resort Project was abandoned. How different this area would have been. Silver City Mountain Resort is the one amenity in the Park. It is a seasonal resort offering cabins and a restaurant, which is a real treat after a long day on the trail. The restaurant also has low speed wifi which is the only place to get any sort of data. 

The camping in the park is Atwell Mill Campground and Cold Springs Campground. There is no BLM within reason and there are literally no places for unreserved "car camping" so be sure to secure somewhere to stay before making the long windy drive. Silver City Resort does have cabins if you wanted to splurge for a plush weekend. They are often fully booked but are often worth it for a group or a luxurious weekend. Since most of the best bouldering is around the lakes, it is worth getting a wilderness permit from the rangers and crash pad backpacking to a lake (I recommend Franklin or Mineral).
webSearchForLocation.description_bouldering:
Mineral King is a subalpine glacial valley located in the southern part of Sequoia National Park. It is open seasonally from May through October, and is accessed by a long and narrow winding road. It is mostly and traditionally popular with backpackers and hikers, but the bouldering potential is just starting to be tapped. Most of the quality boulders are around lakes where the boulders are "pre cleaned" but there are some harder to find forested boulders as well. The rock is mostly granite but with a few exceptions. While there are a few stellar roadside lines, the bouldering here is not for the faint of heart, and a normal approach is 3+ miles, with some exceeding 8 miles. As such, take extreme caution when bouldering in the back country since all inherent dangers of rock climbing are amplified by the remoteness. Come here with a humble heart open to adventure, beautiful views and introspections. As an interesting fact, Disney once planned to make the Mineral King Valley a Ski Resort, but after long legal battles the valley was annexed to Sequoia National Park and the Ski Resort Project was abandoned. How different this area would have been. Silver City Mountain Resort is the one amenity in the Park. It is a seasonal resort offering cabins and a restaurant, which is a real treat after a long day on the trail. The restaurant also has low speed wifi which is the only place to get any sort of data. 

The camping in the park is Atwell Mill Campground and Cold Springs Campground. There is no BLM within reason and there are literally no places for unreserved "car camping" so be sure to secure somewhere to stay before making the long windy drive. Silver City Resort does have cabins if you wanted to splurge for a plush weekend. They are often fully booked but are often worth it for a group or a luxurious weekend. Since most of the best bouldering is around the lakes, it is worth getting a wilderness permit from the rangers and crash pad backpacking to a lake (I recommend Franklin or Mineral).
webSearchForLocation.description_short_bouldering: Mineral King is a remote subalpine valley in Sequoia National Park, known for its rugged beauty and emerging bouldering potential. Most quality granite boulders are found around alpine lakes, requiring long approaches of 3–8+ miles, making climbs adventurous and committing. Camping is limited to Atwell Mill and Cold Springs campgrounds, or cabins at Silver City Mountain Resort. Due to its remoteness, preparation and caution are essential. Once nearly developed into a ski resort by Disney, Mineral King today remains a pristine wilderness for those seeking challenging climbs, stunning views, and backcountry solitude.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Mineral King Valley closes to public vehicles for the season beginning Oct 29 at noon (gate at the park boundary). It typically reopens the Wednesday before Memorial Day - unless there are delays due to winter road damage or construction. 

Head east on the 198 freeway which can be accessed via the 5, the 99 or the 65. Once on the 198, continue east past Lake Kaweah and into the small town of Three Rivers. The 198 turns into "Sierra Drive" when getting to Lake Kaweah. Follow Sierra drive for ~14 miles then look for a turn on the right for "Mineral King Rd". This is a long winding 24.5 mile one lane road so make sure your passengers take Dramamine if they get car sick. Most of the road is paved but there are dirt sections, but the dirt parts are usually well maintained so almost any car should be able to handle the road

NOTE: There is current construction on Mineral King Road and it may impact your trip. Please check https://www.nps.gov/seki/planyourvisit/road-construction.htm for the latest. Construction is expecteded until 2027

webSearchForLocation.name: Rocktown
webSearchForLocation.description:
Welcome to the South y'all!

Rocktown is one the the premier climbing areas in the Southeast and arguably Georgia's best climbing area.Home to hundreds of boulder problems from V-Fun to V-Hard. 
Rocktown holds a delightful approach, with many corridors that makes getting away from the crowds very easy. Camping is available on top of the mountain in designated areas only. There is no water, or electricity, so please plan accordingly. Pack out what you pack in. Please do NOT park in the Rocktown parking lot.

While the KAYA guide lists roughly 500 individual boulder problems, there are hundreds of more linkups that are not currently listed. While this area has been climbed by thousands of climbers, there are still projects for those yearning for FA's, particularly those who enjoy tall boulders with scary falls.

Dogs are allowed, please clean up after your pets, and please bring a leash. Cell service is very limited on the mountain, and access to EMS is 1+ hours away, so please climb within your limit. There are many unique sandstone holds and features that are fragile, climb at your own risk. There is no access to restrooms, so please bury things deep and only use biodegradable toiletry items. Do not use plastic or metal brushes on the sandstone.

Finally, this is a Georgia Wildlife Management Area, it is shared with hikers and hunters, please check the access info before your visit to make sure Rocktown is open for rock climbing.

Enjoy your time, be respectful to others.

Purchase the paper book here: https://www.brayackmedia.com/books/rocktown-bouldering-guidebook

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Rocktown, also known as Crockford-Pigeon Mountain, is a Georgia Wildlife Management Area that requires a pass or license to access the area. There is no front gate or information center to purchase a license on the property, so it is best to purchase a license online before you arrive, as there is limited cell service at Rocktown ( https://gooutdoorsgeorgia.com/ ).

The Public Lands Pass is the best for rock climbers at $30 per year or $60 per year and is good for all Georgia WMA properties. For Sportsmen, the Hunting license is also valid.

Rocktown does have weekend closures throughout the year for hunting, please check the official Georgia page for closures: https://georgiawildlife.com/crockford-pigeon-mountain-wma

The Rangers DO patrol the area and will give you a ticket if you are on the property without a license.

webSearchForLocation.name: Horse Pens 40
webSearchForLocation.description:
Once a great mountain range that would rival the Himalayas of today, the Appalachian Mountains that stretch from Canada to Alabama have fought an all out brawl with time and erosion for the last million or so years. The street fight was hard fought, but eventually the forces of nature won out, sculpting the hills, valleys, and the East Coast's versions of "mountains" that we know today. As the Appalachians fade in Chattanooga, TN, the Lookout and its sister mountains unveil the treasures of the battle with erosion with multiple world class bouldering destinations. Areas such as Little Rock City (aka Stone Fort) and Rocktown draw climbers from the world over to sample some of the best/most accessible sandstone in North America. Luckily for Alabama, it saves the best for last. Sculpted by the ravages of time, Horse Pens 40 is home to acres of bulbous faces, blunt prows, delicate slabs, crimpy overhangs, and water grooves. The owners, Mike and Gina Schultz, are models for southern hospitality. Mike is one of the best storytellers you will ever meet, while Gina slings some of the meanest country cooking you will ever encounter. HP provides the maximum amount of problems for the least amount of effort. If you are in search of the double digit line, you might want to "go west young man," because the area lacks the soft sends needed to pad the spraycard. With over 100+ lines from V3-V5 and the same amount from V6-V8, this is the moderate climber's dream come true. Horse Pens is the Fontainebleau of the South, without the arrogance and the stench. Either for a day, a week, or a season, your trip to HP will have you wanting of more. If the weather permits, this is as good as it gets.

RULES
In their administration of Horse Pens 40, the Shultz family has established some basic rules to protect the people and the park itself. Please show your respect for the Shultz family, Horse Pens 40, and your fellow users by following these rules. Also remember, HP40 IS A "LEAVE NO TRACE" PARK.

1. All guests must sign a waiver before entering the park or campground areas. Sign in at the Country Store. After hours sign-in is available in alcove at left of store. Minors not accompanied by parent or guardian must have a parental waiver on file. (Available by e-mail. Send request to horsepens40@aol.com)
2. No pets are allowed (outside your vehicle) on HP40 property except in the large grassy field outside the middle gate!!
3. Pets are totally prohibited at all scheduled events, rallies, comps, concerts, and festivals.
4. No glass is allowed in the park!!! Broken glass is a real problem for us and is dangerous to everyone. This rule is strictly enforced!!!
5. No open consumption or display of alcoholic beverages on HP40 property (as per AL. state law). Cups, huggers, bags or etc. are required in ALL areas of the park. If you have too much to drink and cause any problem, you will be removed from HP40 property!! No excuses will be accepted and no refund given!!!
6. All fires must be in existing fire rings only! No camping or fires in the rocks or in the nature areas. Do not move fire rings or build new ones!!!! Do not move any rocks for any reason!!
7. No cutting, breaking, or damaging of live plants or trees whatsoever. Do not pick flowers. For ecological reasons, FIREWOOD GATHERING IS NOT ALLOWED INSIDE THE PARK. You are welcome to bring all the firewood that you like, or we can sell you some here, reasonably priced and delivered to your campsite.
8. Do not feed, chase, harass, or harm any birds, animals, or reptiles.
9. No moving, marking, or damaging of the rocks whatsoever!!!
10. Respect your neighbor's campsite, property, and privacy. Foul language, loud noise, and offensive behavior will not be tolerated.
11. One vehicle per campsite. (Must have campsite permit displayed during festivals or when required).
12. No un-nessessary traffic in campground. Go slow and watch for children. Speed limit 5 mph.
13. Please stay on roads and trails. Watch out for plants and mosses.
14. Place all trash in proper receptacles or take out with you. All glass is prohibited outside of your vehicle and must be put in the dumpster, not the trash barrels!!!
15. Take nothing but pictures, and leave nothing but footprints. Do not remove anything from the park!!

ACCOMMODATIONS
Camping and rustic cabins are available. Visit http://www.hp40.com for more information.

and receiving clearance to enter.

webSearchForLocation.name: Santa Barbara
webSearchForLocation.description:
Sandy sandstone, sweaty slopers and beautiful views is the name of the game here. Though the rock quality can leave something to be desired, it's the overall experience of climbing here that's hard to beat. Sunny skies, miles of beaches, a chill downtown, and in just minutes you can be high in the mountains taking in the views, or wandering up shady canyons by the creek. 

Logistics: The prime season is late Fall, where the days are still long enough, temps finally drop, but before the rains. Winters are mild, with plenty of good temps, but **if it rains, it requires lots of waiting as the sandstone is very weak when wet**, and many of the areas are shaded and dry slowly. Spring is great as well, with water flowing through the canyons and a lushness



History: Santa Barbara has a long history of climbing. From Yvon Chounard setting up shop and starting Patagonia in Ventura, climbing all around the local region (with evidence of early pitons etc still to be found), to the Golden era of bouldering development with the Bob Banks/Steve Edwards crew. Wills Youngs put up many hard lines before moving on to Bishop and beyond. Development still continues to this day. While the main major areas have been poured over, there has been many new 'gems' unearthed, often more singular boulders hidden up side canyons or washes, like the great new Piper Bicycle Michaelson near Tangerine Falls, No Pigs For Rent up Rattlesnake, or Junglebook in Buena Vista.


Classics:
Dancing Outlaw
Yeti
She Made Me Do It
Trojan Arete
Heavy Traffic
Debra
Silent Observer

Some dense zones (Brickyard), some short approaches (Painted Caves), some rugged wild bouldering (Potters Point), easy access spots (Skofield Park, The Creamery) to more adventurous zones like Upper Cold Springs, there's something for everyone in the Gnarbra.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Santa Barbara is a small seaside city, nestled in between the Pacific Ocean on one side and mounains on the other. Highway 101 runs right through the middle, with San Francisco about 5 hours North and Los Angeles 1-2 hours south.

webSearchForLocation.name: Doyle
webSearchForLocation.description:
Are you looking for an alternative to the East Side when Tahoe is snowed in during winter? Located just 1 hour north of Reno, Doyle is a great change of pace and much closer than the Buttermilks or the Happy Boulders. Doyle kinda has a Joshua Tree look and feel to it. The rock is similar and the high desert setting is reminiscent of J-Tree as well. Doyle is divided into two main zones: the West Face Area and Fort Sage Mountain. The West Face Area tends to be more highball while Fort Sage is a little more friendly in that respect.

I really enjoy this spot; it holds a massive number of boulders with a wide variety of styles. Unknown to most climbers, this area has not seen much traffic. Hopefully with the publication of this guidebook Doyle will get the attention it deserves. It has become my favorite winter spot and is an easy hit for a day trip from Tahoe, especially if you live in Truckee or better yet Reno. Doyle is wide open desert and there are many primitive camping spots around if you decide to make a multi-day trip.

The area is in a bit of a rain shadow and when it’s raining and snowing in Tahoe it can be climbable at Doyle. But the conditions are best when high pressure moves in, and the weather is solid. At those times you will find cool, crisp temps, great friction and no snow on the ground. Be aware that when the really big storms hit and Reno gets standing snow Doyle is not good. General rule of thumb is if Reno is warm and snow free so is Doyle.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
DRIVING: From Reno drive north on Hwy 395 for 42 miles and turn right on Doyle Loop Road. The turn for Doyle Loop Road is at the end of a long sweeping corner, just after a bridge that crosses the train tracks. It’s not well marked and easy to miss. After turning right on Doyle Loop Road, go for 0.5 miles and turn right on Hackstaff Road. Continue for 0.8 miles until the pavement ends. Just past where the pavement ends is where you can turn right to The West Face Area or go straight to Fort Sage Mountains.

To Approach The West Face Area take the immediate right turn just past where the pavement ends and reset your odometer here. Drive for 4.2 miles on a semi rough dirt road passing many left turns along the way, some of which lead to smaller satellite areas. At 4.2 miles turn left up a steep canyon passing two old run down trailer/houses at the junction. From the junction go 1.1 miles and park in a pullout on the left below the obvious boulder cluster on you right, which is the Cow Skull Boulders. A passenger car can just barely make it here if you’re careful and this is a good place to start and get to know Doyle, especially if you don’t have 4wd. The road continues from here up a very steep road to many of Doyle’s finest boulders and a 4wd is pretty much mandatory.

To Approach Fort Sage Mountain take Hackstaff Road until the pavement ends and reset your odometer. Continue straight for 1.2 miles and turn right on Fort Sage Road. Continue for 1.0 miles and you will see a right hand turn which is the south entrance to a road that forms a developed so far are located along this roughly 6 mile loop. It’s a little confusing from here because some of the boulders are better approached by entering on the south side of the loop and some from the north. To me, entering the loop from the north gets you to the more obvious clusters quicker, so I will begin the Fort Sage Mountain section as if you are coming into the loop from the north. To get to the north entrance of the loop continue past the south entrance for 2.3 miles and go right into the loop road. Go for 0.9 miles, turn right at the fork, continue for 0.1 miles and park on either side of the road in a few small pullouts. The Rocky Ridge boulders will be visible on the hill to your left. The loop continues from here to the rest of the areas and you will find beta for the approaches in the Fort Sage Mountain section.

webSearchForLocation.name: Comox Lake
webSearchForLocation.description:
It is crucial to acknowledge that Comox Lake, and the entire Comox Valley, is the Unceded Traditional Territory of the K’ómoks First Nation, the traditional keepers of the land. The indigenous people have occupied the shoreline of eastern Vancouver Island for thousands of years. Traditionally know as “the land of plenty”.  We are lucky to live, play, and visit their traditional lands.  

OVERVIEW

Comox Lake is located just outside the town of Cumberland, British Columbia in the beautiful Comox Valley. Located approximately 215 km north of the provincial capital city, Victoria, located on Vancouver Island. The Comox Valley has a population of approximately 72,000 people. The Valley consists of three distinct communities: Comox, Courtenay, and Cumberland. 

The bouldering at Comox Lake takes place over a large collection of basalt boulders located in the lush temperate rainforest bordering a large damn controlled lake. The rock is slick, offering little in the way of friction. The climbing varies from gymnastic movement on large smooth blocky holds to heinous small sharp crimps. 

Comox Lake offers ideal bouldering during the spring, summer and fall months. The majority of the boulders are located in the forest and are shaded for most of the day. Their location within the Cumberland Lake Park Campground facilitates opportunities for camping mere minutes from the climbs. The campground offers concession stand snack options, including ice cream. The lake is the perfect place to take a post-climb dip to wash off the sweat, chalk, and to facilitate some muscle recovery.  

ETHICS/CLEANING

The boulders lay in a shaded and heavily forested temperate rain forest. Moss growth is a constant concern. Some quality problems are in need of a retro-scrub. Often “new problems” are uncovered only to discover they were previously climbed many years before. It is worth having a wire brush in your bag. Please feel free to give existing climbs a quick maintenance clean. However, care must be taken to not alter the climbs in any way.  There are ample opportunities to put up new boulder problems. If you have never developed boulder problems before please check out the following pages for tips/techniques: 
https://www.flashed.com/explore/article/advice-and-tips-on-developing-climbs/

The following rules must be adhered to: 

NO CHIPPING/ALTERING HOLDS ON EXISTING CLIMBS
BRUSH OFF YOUR TICK MARKS 
PACK IN/PACK OUT, PICK UP YOURS AND OTHERS TRASH
USE THE CAMPGROUND OUTHOUSES

The bouldering at Comox Lake takes place over a large collection of basalt boulders located in the lush temperate rainforest bordering a large damn controlled lake. The rock is slick, offering little in the way of friction. The climbing varies from gymnastic movement on large smooth blocky holds to heinous small sharp crimps. 

Comox Lake offers ideal bouldering during the spring, summer and fall months. The majority of the boulders are located in the forest and are shaded for most of the day. Their location within the Cumberland Lake Park Campground facilitates opportunities for camping mere minutes from the climbs. The campground offers concession stand snack options, including ice cream. The lake is the perfect place to take a post-climb dip to wash off the sweat, chalk, and to facilitate some muscle recovery.  

ETHICS/CLEANING

The boulders lay in a shaded and heavily forested temperate rain forest. Moss growth is a constant concern. Some quality problems are in need of a retro-scrub. Often “new problems” are uncovered only to discover they were previously climbed many years before. It is worth having a wire brush in your bag. Please feel free to give existing climbs a quick maintenance clean. However, care must be taken to not alter the climbs in any way.  There are ample opportunities to put up new boulder problems. If you have never developed boulder problems before please check out the following pages for tips/techniques: 
https://www.flashed.com/explore/article/advice-and-tips-on-developing-climbs/

The following rules must be adhered to: 

NO CHIPPING/ALTERING HOLDS ON EXISTING CLIMBS
BRUSH OFF YOUR TICK MARKS 
PACK IN/PACK OUT, PICK UP YOURS AND OTHERS TRASH
USE THE CAMPGROUND OUTHOUSES
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
ACCESS

The majority of the bouldering at Comox Lake is accessed through the Cumberland Lake Park Campground.  The park is open from April through October. During these months it is possible to park within the main parking area. Beware that during the height of the summer months the parking lot can be very full as it is a popular area for swimming and boating.  If full, it is possible to park along Comox Lake Road before the campground.  Do not block the boat ramp parking. The gate is locked later in the evening, so if you were planning to have a night session, it would be wise to park outside the yellow gate and walk the additional 1-minute to avoid being locked in. If climbing between November and April you will have to park outside the main campground parking lot but all the climbs remain accessible year-round. 

The Sherman Boulders and Upper Deck both lie on private forestry land, while many people use the existing trails and roads on this land, please be respectful of signage ad don’t block any gates when parking. The community of Cumberland has a good working relationship with the logging companies and landowners.  As climbers we don’t want to jeopardize that relationship.

webSearchForLocation.name: New York City
webSearchForLocation.description:
New York City: center of the universe. Home to the most diverse people and foods and cultures on the planet, and to top it all off, it's even got boulders - over four hundred of which have been documented in this guide. There's so much history in these polished blocs of schist dating back more than half a century. When you climb here, you're following in the footsteps of giants: John Gill, Lynn Hill, Nick Falacci, Koma, Yuki, Kevin Jorgeson, Ashima Shiraishi, the list goes on and on. NYC Bouldering is hard, polished, sketchy, anything but peaceful, occasionally disgusting, and to me, there's nothing else like it anywhere on earth.

If you venture into Central Park on any given weekend when the weather is good, you'll see that the scene is still very much alive and thriving. Full of very specific eliminates, link ups, and contrivances, NYC bouldering is not for the purist, but if you can let go and just enjoy the movement, there's a plethora of great climbing to be had.

Though it gets the most traffic, Central Park isn't all the city has to offer. Quality boulders can be found scattered in parks all across the island of Manhattan, from Lower Central Park all the way to 207th Street in Inwood. Some of the very best boulders in Manhattan get some of the least traffic, so it's worth hopping on the Subway and exploring them all!

ETHICS
- We are incredibly fortunate that the city of New York allows bouldering. Let's be great stewards of climbing and keep it that way! Be respectful and courteous of other park-goers at all times.

- The rock is quite polished and frictionless in many places, so grades here may feel hard compared to what you're used to in the gym. Even so, absolutely no chipping or manufacturing of holds. Period. If you're not strong enough, get stronger! Don't let your ego ruin the climb forever.

- Clean your shoes before pulling on! Dirt on shoes polishes down the rock. Please don't contribute to an already prevalent problem!

- No Resin. Please only use good ole regular chalk.

- Pack out your trash. Keep the boulders cleaner than you found them.

- If you see any hold breakage, please use the Report Content feature in KAYA to let us know!

HISTORY
For a deep dive into the history of the bouldering in NYC, check out the incredible resource and walk down memory lane that is Nick Falacci's Beta Boy website: http://www.beta-boy.com/nycboulderingguide/index.html

Before there were print guidebooks and climbing apps, there was Beta-Boy.com

PRINT GUIDEBOOK
The NYC Bouldering Guide by Gaz Leah is currently the only available print book for purchase. Head to https://stores.sharpendbooks.com/new-york-city-bouldering/ to purchase a copy.

The best way to access the boulders in NYC is via the Subway. Even though carrying crashpads on a crowded Subway car is quite the ordeal, it's definitely worth the effort. Pro Tip: The Subway station emergency exit doors are your friend!

All the Areas in this guide will tell you which trains are best to take in order to access them.

webSearchForLocation.name: Moe's Valley
webSearchForLocation.description:
--- OVERVIEW ---
Moe's Valley is nestled in the sandstone hills just west of St. George, Utah. Moe's has grown increasingly popular as a winter bouldering destination due to its easy access from the town of St. George and a plethora of classic climbs in a wide variety of grades. Many of the boulder problems in Moe's are also shorter, making it a great outdoor area for new outdoor climbers to test their topout skills. There are plenty of lodging and food options in St. George. Feellove Coffee is a great pre-climbing spot to grab a coffee and breakfast, with vegan options. On a rainy day, check out Contact Climbing Gym just off the Green Spring exit from I-15.

DO NOT CLIMB ON WET ROCK. The rock in Moe's is relatively fragile sandstone, making it extremely delicate after rain. Sandstone typically takes a minimum of 48 hours to dry if water has a chance to seep into the rock. Often more time is required to safely climb on the rock, the drying time depends on the amount of rain and the amount of sun/wind in the following days. If it has been raining within the last 7 days, check the rock carefully and avoid any holds that appear fragile or moist. If the ground is wet then it is very likely that there are wet and weakened holds. Try out the local  basalt or granite if you are in doubt or head to Contact Climbing for a great gym session. Only use soft bristled brushes and brush holds lightly to avoid damaging of removing grains of sand.

Stay up to date on the latest access issues by following the Southern Utah Climber's Alliance (https://www.instagram.com/southernutahclimbersalliance/) on Instagram!

Purchase the paper guide from Dallas Lasley here: https://stores.sharpendbooks.com/st-george-bouldering/

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
-- Getting There --

The main parking area for Moe's is adjacent to the Sentinal climbing area. Accessing Moe's requires that you drive through a neighborhood.  There are posted signs directing you to the dirt road entrance along Chandler Rd. To reach the main parking, follow the dirt road as it leads down through an open fence/gate. Take a left after the fenced area down through the wash to find the main parking area. 

The parking area for Super Mario Land can be accessed by taking a slight right turn before you hit the fenced area that takes you to the main Moe's Valley parking area. Continue along the main dirt road, following the power lines that lead northwest. After about 3/4 mi, you will reach the parking area. NOTICE: There are NEW PARKING RESTRICTIONS in place for Super Mario Land. You can no longer park in the circular pullout adjacent to Shell Rock. Please make sure that you park outside of the posted motor vehicle signage or you will be ticketed!

-- Camping at Moe's --

There is NO CAMPING in Moe's Valley. This is an incredibly sensitive topic with local homeowners near Moe's Valley and any camping in Moe's directly threatens future access and closure of Moe's. The Santa Clara Camping Area, https://www.blm.gov/visit/santa-clara-river-reserve , is the closest camping to Moe's and is on BLM land. Snow Canyon State Park, https://stateparks.utah.gov/parks/snow-canyon , has reserved camping and is another popular spot. There are many hotels and AirBnB's available if you prefer not to camp.

-- Climbing After Rain --

Moe's is home to amazing, but incredibly fragile sandstone. It is extremely important that climbers adhere to a policy of no climbing after rain or snow. Please protect this climbing area by respecting the general ethics of sandstone climbing after rain.
webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering: ***NEW PETITION***Moe's Valley is owned by the Utah Trust Lands Administration (TLA or SILTLA). TLA has agreed to cease development of Moe's if the Northern Corridor Highway is built, which is the current plan. However, there is a long history of lawsuits and other potential obstacles that could reverse this land swap. YOUR ACTION IS NEEDED. Please sign this NEW petition asking St. George City officials to create an Open Space & Recreation Preservation Committee to ensure long term preservation of important recreation spaces such as Moe's. Please take a few seconds to add your name using the link below.   https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfO68ldddJtRVMACoT0khNaQV9-4GlE_W8ExvUuPNDHWkL_aw/viewform?fbclid=PAZXh0bgNhZW0CMTEAc3J0YwZhcHBfaWQPNTY3MDY3MzQzMzUyNDI3AAGnMBKKNku6kalGLZRtESyivYYQG3iffkwZRZ4qMbEAzoZXxAzl-W-qN0MuNj4_aem_ytRTVI84vOfsEUNlBALWOg&utm_source=ig&utm_medium=social&utm_content=link_in_bio

webSearchForLocation.name: Gold Bar
webSearchForLocation.description:
The magical forests of Gold Bar (also known as the Reiter Foothills) are the sister area to the more popular Index Town Walls and all the same levels of quality within the rock climbing apply. Quiet shady locales peppered with imposing boulders dot the hillside below Zeke's Wall drawing climbers up the logging access road. The climbing covers all ranges of styles with predominately more 'holds' than the neighboring Index areas which allows for athletic and steep problems somewhat outside of the norm for granite areas. Comfortable rounded seams, protruding knobs, blocky pinches....it's all there in glorious abundance spread between the more exposed clearcut area and the forested upper portions of the hillside.

Season:
Gold Bar can be a year-round destination because of the variance in aspects and sun exposure between the clearcut and the forest. Cool, calm summer conditions can be easily found beneath the tree canopy in the forest while the winter sun and wind can dry the clearcut boulders quickly and provide the stickiest friction of the year.

History:
Climber's began exploring the Reiter Foothills in the early 1990's and the golden age continued into the early 2000's when it was still possible to drive up the logging road. This access allowed for extensive development as getting all the necessary equipment to clean the blankets of moss and manicure the detritus beneath the boulders much easier. Motorized access was revoked around 2010 due to years of abuse on the land from the off-roading crowd that also frequents the area. This change in jurisdiction has slowed the pace of development and cleaning though most of the classic problems remain accessible. Hiking the road is relatively easy in the grand scheme of climbing access and well worth the effort any time of year! The future access to the area may change as commercial logging operations occur in the area but the timeless quality of the boulders themselves will remain.

Paper Guidebook:
Purchase the paper guidebook from Pablo Zuleta here: https://westernwashingtonbouldering.com/guidebook

Gold Bar is about 50 minutes from downtown Seattle and an hour 20 from Leavenworth via Highway 2.

A Discover Pass is required to park at any of the parking spots along Reiter Road. This pass can be purchased at the General Store in Index, along with many outdoor gear stores throughout Washington, such as REI, Big 5 Sporting Goods, etc. The Discover Pass costs $35 for the year and must be displayed while parked.

Click here for more info: https://www.discoverpass.wa.gov/133/Where-to-Buy

webSearchForLocation.name: The Nooks
webSearchForLocation.description:
Welcome to the Nooks bouldering area. Found in 2019, the area has quickly become a talking point in Ontario climbing. The area is regularly visited by both Canadians and Americans calling it a home crag. Making this area very unique. The boulders sit along a paved road deep within the Canadian wilderness with little to no cell reception. Camping can be found along the entire stretch on different pull offs. Elliot Lake is the closest town to The Nooks and is located 30 minutes south with a hospital and all the amenities needed. The climbing exists on crownland, so please respect the wilderness and practice good outdoor ethics. We have striven to keep the area clean and attempted to make a minimal impact on the wilderness around us. This means the experience of climbing here is a great mixture of good trails with a wild experience.
Have a great time! Paper guide available here: https://ontarioclimbing.com/Guidebooks/the-nooks-bouldering/

webSearchForLocation.name: Stoney Point
webSearchForLocation.description:
Stoney Point is an iconic and historic climbing location, not just locally, but on a national scale. The pedigree of climbers that have cut their teeth on this local sandstone, is of the absolute highest regard. Climbers have been scaling at Stoney as early as 1935, when Glen Dawson and others of the Sierra Club trained for their mountaineering feats. Dawson and others went onto climb cutting edge routes in the High Sierra, including the first ascent of the East Face of Mount Whitney. The next notable group to follow came in the 50s, with legends and pioneers such as Royal Robins, Yvon Chouinard, TM Herbert, Tom Frost, Bob Kamps, and others, finding their footing on the same hill we play on today. These climbers not only pushed the climbing at Stoney Point to a new level, but they went on to raise the bar of climbing on a global scale. This pattern continues over the decades, seeing visits from the likes of climbers such as John Long, Lynn Hill, John Bachar, John ‘Yabo’ Yablonski, Mike Waugh, and so many others whom have left their mark in the world of climbing. Stoney is truly a special place, one that we are lucky to enjoy even to this day.

For an in depth look at the incredible history of Stoney Point, check out the online documentary “Stoney Point: Portrait of an American Crag” by Cole Gibson and Matthew Talesfore.

Today Stoney Point remains a popular climbing spot in the Greater Los Angeles area, and is often the introductory location for many gym climbers trading plastic for stone for the first time. While Stoney truly does have something to offer to climbers of all levels, newcomers are often humbled by the challenges the problems present. Though the area may be sandbagged, most landings tend to be flat, allowing for easy pad management. For those with a fragile head game, there are problems so close to the ground that you can feel the top out holds standing on solid ground; and for those seeking a thrill, there is an abundance of spicy, high off the deck lines, to be found. This guide is a documentation of the more direct and natural lines found on each boulder; Stoney has hundreds of variations and eliminates that have been standardized over the decades. Documenting these is far too great a challenge, so you will have to socialize with the locals to find these cryptic lines for yourself. 

It is important to know that the rock here is a very soft sandstone, which is fragile and therefore ever-changing. Due to the rock breaking throughout the years, many lines are quite different than they were when first ascended. I have done my best to update all lines to reflect their current state as of 2026, but unfortunately many of them will continue to change. 

IMPORTANT: Climbing is absolutely prohibited at Stoney when wet. You will typically hear that you should avoid climbing on sandstone for 48 hours after rain, but that is a bare minimum and it is not absolute. The timeframe is dependent on the amount of rain received, the amount of sun received, the wind conditions, the direction of the boulder, the amount of shade or exposure on a line, and so on. It’s very complex, so please consider each of those factors. After a bad storm followed by cloudy weather, it could be as long as a week before the rock is dry. If in doubt, please avoid climbing on the boulders to preserve the lines for as long as possible. Please use https://wetrockpolice.com/stoneypoint to check the latest rainfall.

Stoney is a wonderful place to climb, and a fantastic place to partake in community. It’s no secret that the area is a bit grungy, so lets do our best to clean up after ourselves, and facilitate a welcoming environment for everyone who visits.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Stoney Point lies just 30 miles NorthWest of downtown Los Angeles in the city of Chatsworth. It's just a mile South of the 118 on Topanga Canyon Blvd. The 118 can be accessed via the 405 or 5 North from most of LA, as well as from the 210 West if coming from further inland. As you approach the park from the North you will need to pass Stoney on your left and make a U-turn from a middle shoulder. This is a high traffic street so do so carefully. Park along the side of the road on the Northbound side of Topanga Canyon Blvd. Park as soon as you see the park for easy access to the West, South, and East areas, and drive a bit further up but before the traffic light to more easily access the North, Northeast, Canyons, and Summit areas.

The park is open from dawn to dusk every day.

webSearchForLocation.name: Adirondacks
webSearchForLocation.description:
The Adirondacks are a vast, 6-million-acre protected natural area in northeastern New York, featuring mountains, over 3,000 lakes, and extensive forests, including the "Forever Wild" Forest Preserve that comprises roughly half the Park. Geologically a dome, not a contiguous range, the Adirondacks offer unparalleled year-round bouldering with THOUSANDS of blocks strewn across this vast area - some developed, many yet to be found.

ETHICS
In the Southern and Northern Adirondacks, wet rock is no issue. In the Central Adirondacks, some flakes are more friable after wetness.

HISTORY
Bouldering in the Adirondacks has been slow to take hold compared to other regions in the world. People have been bouldering at McKenzie Pond since the 1970's but the Daks still held out as a Trad Climbers Stronghold. It wasn't really until the early 2000's that widespread searching and developing of boulderfields began in earnest.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Head to Northern NY and use the Area and Subarea approach instructions to find the crag you're looking for.

The Adirondacks has bountiful rock on public land. That being said we do have great boulders on private land that we have lost access to or that should be approached with care.  The most notable access issue is Gnarwall.  This boulder is on private land and the landowner does not want any climbing on their property.

webSearchForLocation.name: Eldorado Canyon
webSearchForLocation.description:
One of the world's famous climbing areas, Eldorado Canyon has played a role in the evolution of our sport since the beginning. Aid climbing in Eldo was quickly shoved aside by the dawn of free climbing, and some of the legendary free-climbing tales took place on the polished, hardened sandstone walls inside this small canyon.

Because Eldo was one of the earliest free-climbing destinations in America, some of the earliest bouldering also took place here. Roadside problems have ascents dating back to the 60s, and for over fifty years local climbers have tested themselves on the same lines. However, several decades of generations pushing the limits has yielded hundreds of new problems, many of them just as roadside as the first. The finest collection of elite-level bouldering around lies in Eldo. Old-school testpieces have seen a resurgence as of late, and often the best hard lines form a steady stream of traffic during the winter. 

The magic of Eldorado Canyon has captivated many pioneers of world-class first ascent bouldering. Dave Graham has made his mark on Eldo with  five star lines such as "Barrel Rider" and "Suspension of Disbelief." Kevin Jorgeson added "The Heist," which may be the state's best V12 outside of the alpine. Drew Ruana is hard at work filling in obvious gaps, with new lines like "Grinch SDS" and "Fort Knox." Lastly, Daniel Woods, Drew Ruana, and obviously Shawn Rabatou have made the most indelible mark in Eldo bouldering history by adding Colorado's first V17/9A. "Megatron" may be the hardest problem in the world. 

Whether you're here to push your limits in the crisp cold, or to simply enjoy sunny days in a beautiful state park, Eldorado Canyon will not disappoint.

webSearchForLocation.description_short_bouldering: Eldorado Canyon is one of the great bouldering destinations of Colorado. Bullet sandstone blocks line creek-beds, gullies, and hillsides, offering a brilliant day of climbing for all abilities.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Eldorado Canyon is located less than a mile west of Eldorado Springs; a small, peaceful town with few amenities. From the town, simply drive up Eldorado Springs Drive (a paved road that turns to dirt inside the town), until passing a ranger station and entering the canyon. 700 foot walls of sheer, maroon sandstone will mark the entrance. 

DO NOT SPEED THROUGH THE TOWN OF ELDO, AND PARK IN DESIGNATED SPOTS ONLY. Eldorado Springs has a dust issue and parking is very limited, so respect the locals.

webSearchForLocation.name: Stevens Pass
webSearchForLocation.description:
Stevens Pass is the alpine region located 4,061 feet above sea level and straddling the Cascade crest along Washington State Highway 2 between the Seattle metropolitan area, and Leavenworth to the east. Stevens Pass is named for brilliant engineer John Frank Stevens whose vision led to the Great Northern Railroads traversing of the Cascades in the early 1900's. Stevens also played a large role in the designing and completion of the Panama Canal! The area was originally known as Wellington but a devastating avalanche in 1910 wiped out the railroad and killed nearly 100 passengers in a story that shocked the nation! In order to save the local railroad business, rebranding was required and thus: Stevens Pass came to be. 

In recent years the 'Pass' as it's locally known has become a hub for winter time lift skiing and snowboarding, PCT hiking, downhill mountain biking and a slow but steady growth of alpine bouldering venues that provide summer season options when the rest of the valley floors are baking in the summer heat. 

The climbing in the Stevens Pass region is similar to the granite found to the west within the greater Skykomish River Valley though the grains and crystals tend to be a bit bigger and rougher on the skin. Many brilliant problems exist across a handful of areas; from roadside goodies along Smithbrook Road to secluded higher elevation clusters like Skyline Ridge, the Treasury or Lichtenberg Mountain, there is something for everyone here. 

Beware of biblical swarms of mosquitos in early summer months! Windy days and late summer provide respite from arguably the areas biggest detractor......

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Coming from east or west; follow State Highway 2 to the apex of the pass then choose your parking location based on your climbing destination for that day! The various areas and subareas all have their own differing parking locations.

webSearchForLocation.name: Uintas
webSearchForLocation.description:
The Uinta Mountains in northeastern Utah offer a rugged and beautiful setting for bouldering, with remote, high-altitude zones that come into condition mostly during the summer and early fall.

Rock Type:
The boulders in the Uintas are primarily quartzite, which is dense, sharp, and highly featured. It offers great friction, though it can be skin-intensive. There are also some areas with granite and other metamorphic rock types depending on the exact location.

Quality:
The quality ranges from good to excellent, with many classic problems that have seen increasing development over the last two decades. Expect everything from highballs and technical slabs to steep, powerful overhangs.

Elevation & Season:
Most of the climbing is between 8,000–11,000 feet, so conditions are best from late June through early October, depending on snowmelt and weather. The higher altitude makes it an ideal escape from the heat of Salt Lake City in summer.

Access & Ethics:
Many areas require hiking in (some quite far), and weather can change quickly. Leave No Trace principles are especially important here. It's relatively undeveloped compared to places like Joe’s Valley or Little Cottonwood, so expect solitude and a bit of exploration.

webSearchForLocation.name: Holy Boulders
webSearchForLocation.description:
This guide was produced by and supports the Illinois Climbers Association. For more information or to support the ICA, visit https://www.ilclimbers.org/

The Holy Boulders is the largest concentration of boulders in Southern Illinois. There are 350+ developed boulder problems from V0 to V13 and has the potential for hundreds more. The sandstone boulders and cliff line are known for their Fontainebleau-like perfect friction and aesthetic lines.

Special thanks to Kevin Sierzega for all his work compiling and contributing photos & topos for this guide.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
As of 2024, parking is limited and can become congested during peak climbing months. The Illinois Climbers Association asks all who visit to be as courteous as possible when looking for a place to park, and to make sure to pull your vehicle as far off the road as possible so as not to constrict traffic.

To get to the Holy Boulders, it is recommended to use your GPS to guide you to the parking off of Macedonia Road. At the Holy Boulders, there is limited parking located at the bottom of the hill, with the majority of vehicles parked higher on the hill, just on the edge of the road, close to what has become the climber access trail. However you decide to park, please do so with others in mind.

Once parked, you need to use your trained eye to locate the unmarked old forest logging road located on the South side of Macedonia Road. It is distinguishable by it being about the width of a modern car with a well trodden foot path guiding the way. As you begin hiking South on the approach trail (logging road), you will quickly see a tall boulder uphill and on your left. Continue past this unnamed boulder and eventually crest over a hill that will descend directly to the Open Gates Boulder, distinguishable by the short, West facing overhang. From Macedonia Road to the Open Gates Boulder, depending on your hiking pace, the approach should take 5-10 minutes.

Please leave no trace and do not improve the trail. Not all local roads are clearly marked in the area and cell service can be spotty, so research driving directions beforehand.

webSearchForLocation.name: Gunpowder Falls
webSearchForLocation.description:
Gunpowder Falls State Park is home to some fantastic bouldering and lovely isolated wilderness. It is easy to forget that you are only a 15-30 minute drive from downtown Baltimore. 

Although at first the crags within the state park may seem isolated and disjointed, once you spend some time climbing here you will realize they are all within a 15-20 minute drive from one another. Hitting one crag in the morning, taking a lunch break, then going to another crag in the afternoon is how I love to spend my days off. Or after work, if the weather is nice, getting outside instead of the gym couldn't be easier with most of the boulders at Gunpowder being 10-15 minutes away from the Movement gyms in Baltimore.

Most of the crags at Gunpowder Falls are excellent areas for climbers venturing outdoors from the gym for the first time. There are many boulder problems in the lower grade range that are not too tall and have good landings.

That being said there are certainly boulder problems for the local crushers too. The V5-V8 range really shines at Gunpowder and if you are looking for something harder there are several high quality open projects in the double digit range waiting for first ascents!

This guide was written to document the local boulders and increase accessibility to the growing climbing community in Baltimore. Many of the boulders have likely been climbed long before the first known or documented ascents listed in this guide. Please reach out to the authors if you know more accurate history! 

Special thanks to Mark "Indy" Kochte, Justin Piteleski, John Brunson, Mark Profeta, Rob B., Justin Meserve, Robin Close, Dana Miller, Mike Kremer, and many other local MD developers who have done much of the early climbing at Gunpowder and have served as inspirations for the authors of this guide.

webSearchForLocation.name: Boat Rock
webSearchForLocation.description:
It is quite clear that there would be no bouldering at Boat Rock at all were it not for the foresight of the Southeastern Climber’s Coalition (SCC) and the many generous donations received from climbers like you. If you are not a member of the SCC, you should be. 
While you’re at it, join the Access Fund, too. The Access Fund is a major supporter of the SCC, and they work hard to keep many excellent climbing destinations open nationwide.
