webSearchForLocation.name: Reynolds Creek
webSearchForLocation.description:
Reynolds Creek is one of Boise's top bouldering areas and for good reason. Generally good rock, a diversity of not only grades but styles as well. One side of the Upper Reynolds Creek Road is littered with granite boulders that tend toward the gritty and technical side. The other side of the road is filled with rhyolite boulders that tend toward steep faces, large holds, and gymnastic moves. Most people thrash their skin on the granite to start the day and finish on the rhyolite.

Bouldering History – Although the early climbing history in Reynolds remains a mystery, Leeper hangers have been found on top of many boulders indicating people may have been climbing there as early as the 1960s or 70s! Regardless, modern bouldering began out there in the mid 90s when Chris Cahoon and Sean Birt began establishing a few problems near the main area. Shortly after Miguel Reynoso, Jordan Forrest and Mike McClure began systematically climbing everything within their realms. Jordan’s bold head lead to some early ascents of some of the most terrifying and futuristic, for the time, highballs such as Meat Grinder (without pads) and Rodents of Unusual Size. By 2002 Sus Edmundson, Jamey Srpoull, John Who and others began development of the Rhyolite side of the road establishing the majority of the climbs in the Boneyard area as well as many overlooked classics in the 

Climate/Season – Reynolds Creek is a true year-round climbing area. Obviously it can get hot in the summer, although a reliable afternoon breeze cools it down quickly. In fact some of the harder problems, Absolution and Ride the Lightning for example, were established during the summer months. Wintertime can be excellent as well since Reynolds is typically above the fog inversion that socks in the valley below. Allowing sunny skies and warmer temperatures than the valley. With that being said, prime season is typically March-May and September-November.

webSearchForLocation.description_short_bouldering: Reynolds Creek is home to some of the Boise area’s most classic climbs such as Miguel’s Finger Crack (V3), Cosmic Squirrel (V4), Peaches (V7), Catalysis (V9), and Absolution (V11).
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
To access Reynold’s Creek from Nampa head south on 12th Ave/Highway 45 for approximately 15 miles. The road will drop into the Snake River Canyon and cross the river. To access the Wilson Creek areas, veer right after crossing the river and make a right on Highway 78. Continue west for 3.2 miles to make a left on Wilson Creek Rd. After 2.5 miles veer right onto the dirt road to avoid driving into the feedlot. Another mile will get you too Wilson Creek Trails where individual area directions will start from. The roads in Wilson Creek are all dirt although generally passable in a 2WD with moderate clearance. Always use good judgment and just walk a bit further if the road seems muddy.

Lower Reynolds (Peaches) and the Windy Point zones are accessed by veering left after crossing the Snake River to merge with Highway 78. After just under 1 mile make a right on Upper Reynolds Creek Rd. In about 1.5 miles the road will pass through a feedlot. The parking for the Peaches Boulder will be on a small hill overlooking a side canyon on your right after approximately 4.5 miles. The Windy Point area is reached at about 10 miles, follow individual zone directions for more details. Generally a 2WD with moderate clearance will access most areas at the Windy Point Boulders although some boulders like Absolution and Brain Teaser may require an additional 5-10 minutes walk depending on road conditions.

webSearchForLocation.name: Triassic
webSearchForLocation.description:
Triassic is a great zone that hosts tons of sandstone boulders in a very condensed area. The boulders are accessible year round, except for rare occasions after a heavy snowfall. The best climbing seasons are Fall, Winter, and Spring. The majority of the boulders fall within the easy to moderate grade range, and many of them can be climbed with just one or two pads. This, coupled with the area’s short approaches and high concentration of boulders, make it a great spot for beginners and families. But for the hard-bodies out there, don’t worry- there are several double digit boulders scattered around, as well as many hard projects yet to be climbed. Because of its proximity to Joe’s Valley, climbers sometimes travel to Triassic for the day when Joe’s has inclement weather, since Triassic often remains dry and sunny. This area is also much less traveled than Joe’s, so it can offer a nice secluded reprieve from the Joe’s crowds.

The Triassic boulders were found by Darren Knezek in 2002, and a wave of development quickly ensued. Since then, further development has been slow, and some hard projects are still waiting for ascents.

If you continue down Dinosaur Quarry Road, you will reach the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry, which is still actively excavating fossils to this day. Bones from this quarry can be found in museums around the world.

Though it may feel like you’re out in the middle of nowhere, don’t forget to treat the land with respect and practice Leave No Trace ethics. As the number of climbers visiting this destination continues to grow, it is more important than ever that we give climbers a good reputation as stewards of the outdoors.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: The interwoven dirt roads can get you to the parking pins several different ways. The recommended roads to take are highlighted as trails in the app. Some of the dirt roads require decent clearance, but most cars should be able to get to the parking pins. If it is snowy the roads may not be accessible, though this is rare. If this is the case, it is still possible to park on Dinosaur Quarry Road and make the slightly longer approach into the boulders. Also, be aware that if it starts raining hard the roads can become muddy and difficult to drive on.

webSearchForLocation.name: Needle Peak
webSearchForLocation.description:
Needle Peak is an iconic Wyoming Bouldering area nestled within Saratoga Valley and framed between the Snowy Range to the east and Sierra Madre to the west. As such, it is part of a classic western landscape; an area enriched with the scent of sage and scattered with antelope, deer, coyote, and a variety of birds. The rock is excellent and abundant, consisting of compact Archean gneiss that has been cleaned and sculpted by wind and water over eons. The entire area is concentrated on a single mountain as an island in the sky, despite a few small outliers along the broad edges of the peak. 
Located between the towns of Saratoga to north and Riverside and Encampment to the south, the area provides many comforts in the neighboring towns. Saratoga is the largest of the towns and provides a grocery store, restaurants, lodging (no tent camping), fuel, and of course the free hot springs at the “Hobo Pool”. Riverside and Encampment are closest to Needle Peak and provide a rural assortment of options with a small bar or two, fuel, a small store, and a café or two. Riverside has a good campground, The Lazy Acres, should the free camping on BLM land at Needle Peak not provide adequate comfort.

It is possible to boulder at Needle Peak during any part of the year. The end of June through August is usually too hot, though morning and night sessions may be cool enough for good conditions. The end of November to the end of February is often cold in the middle of Wyoming winter. That being said, some perfect winter days occur if the wind behaves. and the road isn't completely drifted in. The back half of September into December is a long period of stable weather and more often than not, the best conditions for holding on to Needle Peak grips. Alternatively, March through May is also an excellent time for bouldering at Needle Peak. Wet days are more likely in the spring, but a cold wind often blows. Needle Peak sits in a small rain shadow created by the Sierra Madre to the west. Often, it is the only dry place to boulder during periods of bad weather in southeast Wyoming.

ETHICS:
Enjoy the boulders of Needle Peak. Treat the place as a sacred mountain. It is sacred for many of us. History is ongoing and the future is always near. Please add your own chapter to this mountain and revel in the process of it. NOTE: We do not chip or modify the rock at Needle Peak. It serves perfect grips as is! You will notice some landings built. Please be awarwe of the potential impact this has on the landscape. Organize and make it look natural (lichen up, soil and plants preserved), and do with a long term future in mind. It is better to have a level deck that last for generations than to have an eroding slope of dirt that gets worse every season.

HISTORY:
The history of Needle Peak is as common as most other places in the annals of Wyoming climbing. The first routes were done by Saratoga and other Wyoming locals during the initial waves of American free climbing (1950s-1960s). Later on, the steeper lines gained interest and bolts were added to a few small towers. In the early 2000s, bouldering began. Though boulder problems have been contributed by many, the majority of problems were cleaned and climbed by a few locals. Bryan Vansickle, Guilherme Zavaschi, Ethan McMahan, and the author spent too many days, over several long seasons, developing the majority of problems at Needle Peak. Other significant help in development came from Josh Helke, Liz Hajek, Bob Proffit, Josh Thuier and others. From 2016 onward, after the first edition of a PDF guide was released several of the last great projects were completed. Andrew Hudson and Sam Berg led this next generation with new problems being developed and new projects being cleaned. Some incredible projects remain with a few getting done each year. A generation of high end double digit problems await.

Enjoy the boulders of Needle Peak. Treat the place as a sacred mountain. It is sacred for many of us. History is ongoing and the future is always near. Please add your own chapter to this mountain and revel in the process of it. NOTE: We do not chip or modify the rock at Needle Peak. It serves perfect grips as is! You will notice some landings built. Please be awarwe of the potential impact this has on the landscape. Organize and make it look natural (lichen up, soil and plants preserved), and do with a long term future in mind. It is better to have a level deck that last for generations than to have an eroding slope of dirt that gets worse every season.

HISTORY:
The history of Needle Peak is as common as most other places in the annals of Wyoming climbing. The first routes were done by Saratoga and other Wyoming locals during the initial waves of American free climbing (1950s-1960s). Later on, the steeper lines gained interest and bolts were added to a few small towers. In the early 2000s, bouldering began. Though boulder problems have been contributed by many, the majority of problems were cleaned and climbed by a few locals. Bryan Vansickle, Guilherme Zavaschi, Ethan McMahan, and the author spent too many days, over several long seasons, developing the majority of problems at Needle Peak. Other significant help in development came from Josh Helke, Liz Hajek, Bob Proffit, Josh Thuier and others. From 2016 onward, after the first edition of a PDF guide was released several of the last great projects were completed. Andrew Hudson and Sam Berg led this next generation with new problems being developed and new projects being cleaned. Some incredible projects remain with a few getting done each year. A generation of high end double digit problems await.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
All bouldering is on public lands of both the BLM and State of Wyoming. However, all sides of the public land at Needle Peak are bounded by private ranch lands. Respect those landowners and do not access private lands. No, they are not interested in talking to you or allowing access to rock behind their fences.

Needle Peak is located a mile east of Highway WY 230, 14 miles south of Saratoga and 4.5 miles north of Riverside and Encampment. Baggott Rocks Road (Carbon County Rd. 680) leaves WY 230 going eastward. Follow the county road for less than a half mile to the first north going dirt road; just before the second cattle guard since leaving the highway. The dirt road follows a fence around private land, first northward, then eastward before going directly to Needle Peak. The “Central Parking” is the main parking for Needle Peak, but various other parking spots abound and make approaches pretty minor. Central parking is found by a quick left, then immediate right where the dirt road splits at the first fork (four-way fork) since leaving the fence line along the property boundary. 
The west side of the mountain is the “front side”. It is seen from the highway and the side accessed while driving in. The east regions are the “far side” being the side you walk farthest to. North and south sides are equally accessible. An abundance of small side roads provide parking and access points. Be aware that private land surrounds the entirety of Needle Peak, though Needle Peak and the outlier Silver Spur are on BLM or State of Wyoming lands.

NOTE: The main dirt road from the the country road onward can be very poor in wet conditions, even for an off-road vehicle with good tires it may become a challenge to drive on.

SECOND NOTE: along the northern end of the peak is a 4wd road that is referenced several times for approaches. It has a nice and easy parking spot for any vehicle near the bottom of the road. After that parking spot, it gets rugged and steep. It requires not only significant clearance and 4wd low, but an experienced driver. Proceed at your own risk if you choose to drive up there.

THIRD NOTE: The long and bumpy road that takes you to the Silver Spur outlier traverses northward around a long distance shooting range (welcome to Wyoming). You will see large gongs on the private side of the fence. The range is run by responsible adults and they are aware of the public land behind the targets. Do your part and make yourself visible as you drive around the north end of the peak and across the broad field. Turn on headlights and drive safely!

webSearchForLocation.name: Box Springs Mountain Reserve
webSearchForLocation.description:
Box Springs Mountain Reserve is a 3,400-acre park in Riverside County. These coastal sage scrub and chaparral hills stretch across Riverside and Moreno Valley. The area is a mix of public land, private land, and conservation areas. Reaching some of the climbing areas can be challenging as the hills are steep. During dry seasons, the trails are dusty and may be difficult to distinguish or navigate. However, during wet seasons, the trails clear up significantly as the brush greens and the trails become more visible.

Like much of Southern California, Box Springs will transform into vibrant rolling green hills after a good rain. The best times to climb are in the winter and spring. While Box Springs is quite accessible, it is surprisingly not heavily impacted by trash and graffiti in most spots. The hills also host trails for hiking, biking, and donkeys.

DO NOT FEED THE DONKEYS

The donkeys are endless. They are wild animals. While not native, they exist in abundance. Do not feed or approach the donkeys. If anything, try to discourage them from becoming familiar with humans. There will be donkey poop everywhere. If you're climbing in Box Springs, be prepared.

webSearchForLocation.name: Horse Flats
webSearchForLocation.description:
From author and original Horse Flats developer, James March: Horse Flats has been a unique bouldering destination for Southern California for over fifty years. It consists of a boulder-strewn mountainside above an idyllic campground with the summit of Mt. Hillyer, just over 6,000 feet.

I first visited Horse Flats in the fall of 1992 while living in L.A. I came armed with my first edition copy of the Southern California Bouldering Guide, a few apples, trail mix, water, shoes and chalk bag (no crashpad). I had no expectations for the area aside from some vague directions to the boulders and grainy black and white photos. But as soon as I emerged alone from my car I was hit with a sudden sense of peace and beauty. The wind seemed to whisper melodies through the Jeffrey Pinetrees and I took a rewarding breath of smog-free air.

As I walked up the steepening trail from the campground, the boulders started to reveal themselves as statuesque granite sentries protecting a hidden mountain garden. Their colorful granite hues and multi-featured edges, created a perfect bouldering garden for me that day to explore, climb and simply kick back and give thanks.

Located at the far Northeast end of Los Angeles County, Horse Flats is a popular hiking, climbing and mountain biking area in the San Gabriel Mountains. The area is also known for its high quality granite bouldering with a concentrated circuit of boulders and problems of varying style and difficulty.

Remember that the Stonemasters who developed Horse Flats, brought with them no crash pads, only the skills and bravado for climbing the classics. Many of these original problems and boulders were not named so I have titled them with self-explaining references such as East Face or Right Arete, in an effort to make this guide easier to navigate. 

The early 90’s had the first crash pads available, but bouldering was not popular then and for me I practiced alone mostly because I couldn’t find others as psyched. After climbing alone for a while I came to prefer it. I was on my own time and rhythm. I meticulously brushed holds and thought through sequences and down climb scenarios, risking an unspotted fall, the rewards of my ascents were amplified and often mystical.

With the advent of larger crash pads and climbing gyms, standards rapidly evolved and the potential for higher and harder boulder problems still exist. Many of the older highballs were established on top rope but are typically bouldered now. Please keep safety in mind on your visit, and remember the closest hospital is more than an hour’s drive away.

Apart from the bouldering, the Top Rope Wall and the Pie Slice has a collection of nice routes, a few of which can be led on traditional gear. Not many bolts exist so most anchors need to be natural, (ie. sling trees and rocks).

The first humans to live at Horse Flats would be the Gabrileno Indians. They frequented the area using the now famous Silver Moccasin Trail which now starts in Chilao to the South and becomes the Main Trail to the boulders at Horse Flats Campground. In those days both the Black Bear and the long extinct California Grizzly were at the top of the food chain.

The name Horse Flats is in reference to the land being used in the late 1880’s by Horse thief and bandit, Tiburico Vasquez. He and his band of outlaws used the hidden meadows as pasture for their stolen horses. With the boulders surrounding Tiburcio like a fortress, he terrorized the lowland ranches for years until his eventual capture and hanging in 1875.

CAMPING:
The yellowish-orange and gray boulders lie above a shady campground with 26 sites; each has fire rings, picnic tables, communal restrooms, but no water. There is a 14 day limit to the unreserved camping and the cost is $12 a day. Senior or Access Interagency Pass discount $6.00. Additional vehicles add $5.00. The day use fees are the same as camping. If you don’t want to pay then you can park outside the campground and hike an extra ½ mile. Note: The campground is closed and gated through the winter months so this is the approach.

SEASON:
Horse Flats is typically known as a cooler season destination for bouldering. It can be hot in the summer days and buggy, though evenings and early mornings are still pleasant. The nights can be very cold as well so prepare appropriately.

ETHICS:
Horse Flats is home to many species of plant and wildlife so be aware of your impact. Please pack your trash and brush your tick marks, come in peace and leave rejuvenated.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Horse Flats is accessed from Los Angeles from the 210 freeway. In La Canada take the 2 (Angeles Crest Highway) for 27 miles taking a left on Sulphur Springs/Santa Clara Divide Road. Drive another 2.5 miles until the campground entrance appears on your left. The Top Rope Wall Area can be accessed also by driving another 0.5 miles up the road to park at Rosenita Saddle and hike in from the broad summit of Mt. Hillyer (about 20 minutes).

Parking is not allowed along the road past the Horse Flats Campground entrance gate. Do not park in campsites unless you have paid and are camping there.

Park at the Rosentia Saddle Trailhead, then either take that trail to the northern boulders, or walk back down to the Horse Flats Campground to access the main boulders.
	
Currently there are no access issues to Horse Flats but remember you are sharing the land with others so be mindful of mountain bikes and runners on the trail. The erosion has gotten worse following Hurricane Hilary in 2023 and the base of many problems have receded, so pad up accordingly. Also please respect your surroundings and don’t garden or overtly alter the landing zones. You may notice a few holds on boulders have been reinforced with glue. This was a method for keeping key holds from breaking, and used in the early days but not anymore.

webSearchForLocation.name: Mt. Blue Sky
webSearchForLocation.description:
Lincoln Lake Guide:
https://app.kayaclimb.com/share/location?id=14434&childId=undefined&suid=34829

Guanella Pass Guide:
https://app.kayaclimb.com/share/location?id=2033&childId=undefined&suid=34829

Idaho Springs is the closest town to the bouldering. It is a small mining community and ski-town gateway with a population of 1,889. It sits at an elevation of 7,526 ft. There isn’t much in Idaho Springs, but it does serve as the last stopping point for many who visit the Mt Evans Wilderness Area.

ACCOMODATIONS:
Idaho Springs has several hotels, and you can always find everything you need just 30 minutes down I-70 E in Denver. Expect to pay $100 a night for a hotel room. For many climbers on a budget, this is simply not an option. There are, however, several places in the area to camp.

CAMPING:
There are several pay sites near the bouldering on Mt. Evans:
Echo Lake Campground: 18 sites | $10 a day | Elevation 10,600 ft 
West Chicago Creek Campground: 18 sites | $10 a day | Elevation 9,600 ft 
Guanella Pass: 18 sites | $11 a day| Elevation 10,900 ft

Camping is permitted in the boulders at Area A and B, provided a free permit is filled out at the kiosk near the entrance of the Mt. Evans Wilderness Area, just beyond the Idaho Springs Reservoir. Campers must be 100 ft from rivers, lakes, trails, or streams. Fires are allowed here as well, and they too must be 100 ft from rivers, lakes, trails or streams. It is best to use an existing fire ring. Dogs are welcome in the Wilderness Area so long as they are on a leash at all times. Waking up in the boulders and having a quiet morning session can be a rewarding experience. Please be respectful and appreciative of this special opportunity.

In the summer, food and drinks can be purchased at the Echo Lake Lodge, which is 0.25 mile beyond the Echo Lake Park (14 miles from Idaho Springs). There is no gas station at the Echo Lake Lodge. 

Mt. Evans Elevation: 14,265 ft.
Area A: 10,960 ft.
Dali Wall: 11,123 ft.
Area B: 11,217 ft.

Buy the paper book: https://stores.sharpendbooks.com/mount-evans-bouldering/

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Climbers visiting internationally should use Denver International Airport (DIA). From DIA follow Peña Blvd for 3.5 miles to I-70 and Denver. From Denver continue west on I-70 39 miles to Idaho Springs. Take Mt. Evans exit 240 and turn left, onto CO 103. If approaching from the west, take I-70 E to the Mt. Evans exit 240 and turn right onto CO 103. Just south of I-70 is the Clear Creek Ranger Station, on the right. Idaho Springs is on the north side of the freeway and is the last place to get groceries or gasoline before driving to the bouldering area.

To continue on to the bouldering areas take CO 103 south (away from Idaho Springs) for 14 miles to Echo Lake Park, on the right. There are two places to park here, the first being the gravel parking lot on the right, adjacent to Echo Lake (see map on page 31). The second area, which makes for a slightly shorter approach, is accessed by turning right down a dirt road at the close end of the parking lot and following this for a quarter mile to another smaller parking area. Either one is good for parking, although the smaller lot at the end of the dirt road can fill up on a busy summer weekend. It is also possible to approach from the east on CO 103 out of Bergen Park, although this route is winding and slow.

It is free to park at Echo Lake, and there is no fee required to hike to the boulders.

webSearchForLocation.name: Smugglers' Notch
webSearchForLocation.description:
Tucked into a beautiful, forested, alpine valley, Smuggler's Notch is one of the best bouldering destinations in Northern New England. I would even go so far as to say it is one of the best summer bouldering destinations on the entire East coast. It sits right about 2100 feet of elevation and can be 10-15 degrees cooler than lower elevation areas. On warmer days Smuggs can be good in the morning and evening or in the Green Cave area which generally stays cooler. The rock dries extremely quick after rain, other than a few seepy boulders. You can arrive at Smuggs in pouring rain and have it be climbable just an hour or 2 later. This is particularly important because Smuggs has its own unique weather. Some days it can be pouring rain just a few miles down the road in Stowe, while its bone dry at the boulders in Smuggs. But unfortunately the opposite is also true and it can have its own personal rain cloud sitting just over the notch with the rest of the state mostly sunny. Additionally, watch out for humidity in the spring and fall, it can cause the boulders to become soaked with condensation in the morning. This doesn't happen nearly as often in the middle of summer. Even if it doesn't rain, they may be wet from this. This generally only affects the bottom half of boulders near the ground and generally affects overhangs and roofs worse. If you get rained out of Smuggs check out the nearby board gym Burly Bloc about 30 minutes away from the boulders in Essex, VT. Right on the way to Burlington.

The Smuggs season lasts from about May to November coinciding with the status of route 108 that runs through the Notch. 108 is a seasonal road and the gates will close around the first snowfall where snow sticks to the roads in early November. I've seen it close as early as just before Halloween, and seen it stay open as late as just before Thanksgiving. The gate generally opens around the first week of May but may open in April following a mild winter or later in May if there was significant snowfall in the late winter/early spring. Fret not, however, because the climbing is still accessible, depending on snow/ice at least. Whenever 108 is closed you can park in parking lots at either of the gates and hike in. The hike is significantly quicker and easier from the North side. While Smuggs is an excellent summer option, its best climbed in late April, May, October, and early November when temps are low and friction is high.

There are 2 main parking lots in the main areas and 2 parking lots for the Stowe-side satellite areas. An additional parking lot is currently under construction below the King and Queen area. At the main area the main parking lot is the one with the outhouse and info hut it is gravel and not paved. The top of the notch parking lot is found on the opposite side of the road just south of the main lot. There are also some spots to park up the north side of the road around and just past the outhouse. Approach directions are written based on coming from either of the two main parking lots. The approach times reflect coming from the two main lots. They will differ if parked down the Stowe side.

Local Ethics:
The park is focusing on allowing some eroded areas to regrow. Most of these are along the sides of the road and parking lots. If you find sticks, branches, or logs crossed over what looks like a trail do not walk that way, they are left there as a barrier. Stick to trails or the side of the road to get around. There is a trail to nearly every single boulder in this guide. There are also some new signs pointing these areas out. Also please make sure that if you need to park along the side of the road that you keep your tires away from any plant life.

History:
Smuggler's Notch gets its name from its historical use as a smuggling route between Canada and the US. During these times smuggled goods were hidden in the various caves and crevices formed by the boulders that fell off the main wall above. Some of these caves even have ice nearly year round allowing them to preserve some goods in the summer months.

Smuggler's Notch is actually one of the oldest developed climbing areas in all of the Northeast. After the ski resorts were built and subsequent road infrastructure was built in the 1960s, accessing the notch became much easier and climbing development accelerated. The famous German climber Fritz Weissner even had a hand in development of Smuggs climbing after he moved to Stowe in 1952.

Most of the bouldering we know and love in Smuggs today was developed by Bill Patton and his crew consisting of people like Marc Troob, Benny Harlow, Kyle, John Tomes, and Marlon Campos in the 90s and early 00s. During this era even the famous John 'The Vermin' Sherman climbed at Smuggs.

A new wave of development has also been seen in the 2010s and 20s by Brad Fauteux, Troy Fauteux, and Jake Perry.

Access:
There are no real access issues. Some park rangers have an issue with night climbing but not all of them. If they find you climbing at night and ask you to leave please respect that. They may also just tell you that you can climb as long as you want as long as you aren't planning on camping overnight there.

There are no real access issues. Some park rangers have an issue with night climbing but not all of them. If they find you climbing at night and ask you to leave please respect that. They may also just tell you that you can climb as long as you want as long as you aren't planning on camping overnight there.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
From the south get on interstate 89 North til exit 10 Waterbury. Take a right onto route 100 off the interstate and drive til route 108 in Stowe. Take a left onto 108 and continue until you reach any of the various parking areas in the Notch. You will find them just after the Stowe ski resort. You can also take a shorter route by turning left on Moscow Rd before you reach Stowe. From Moscow Rd continue for a couple miles til you reach Barrows Rd. Turn right onto Barrows Rd and continue til the end of the road. At the end, turn right on Luce Hill Rd and continue til the end of this where it connects with 108. Take a left onto 108 through a funky intersection, watch out for cars on 108 turning left onto Luce Hill road!

From Burlington take 89 South to Waterbury and use those directions. Alternatively you can take exit 11 in Richmond. Take a left off the interstate onto route 2 then immediately take a right onto route 117 at the intersection. Take the very first immediate right off 117 onto Governor Peck Highway. Drive til the end and then take a left onto Browns Terrace. Proceed through Jericho Center and past the high school til you reach route 15. Take route 15 til Jeffersonville where you will see a Mobil gas station. Turn right here onto Church St. At an intersection soon after go straight onto Mill St which is route 108. Take this all the way up the mountain to the parking areas.

From the north if coming directly down from Canada you can cross the border in Frelighsburg which will put you on 108 and take you directly there.

From the north but coming from 89 get off exit 18 in Georgia and turn left onto route 7. Just past the mobil gas station turn left onto Highbridge Rd route 104A. Continue on 104A til the end and then turn right on Main St route 104. Continue for a while on 104 until it meets up with route 15. From here you can follow the directions found in the 'From Burlington' section.

webSearchForLocation.name: Rock Shop
webSearchForLocation.description:
A percentage of revenue from this guide directly supports the Central Wyoming Climbers Alliance.

The Rock Shop is a beautiful, quiet refuge of boulders tucked in the forest right off the highway about 30 minutes south of Lander. The easy access, remote feeling, high rock quality, and density of climbs make it one of the best bouldering areas in Wyoming. The granite found throughout the forest is often bullet hard, very featured, and colorful, making it perfect for climbing.

The Rock Shop bouldering season is best in Spring and Fall, but decent conditions can be found all Summer long if you stick to the shade. When the weather is nice it’s a great place to car camp and spend a long weekend. If you’re living in Lander, these boulders are the local stomping grounds that can easily be accessed on a workday. After a snowfall, the road up to the boulders can get a little squirely, but for those desperate for good temps it can be navigable.

Special thanks to David Lloyd and Zach Alexander, whose previous documentation efforts were an invaluable stepping stone for the formation of this guide. David Lloyd has published a paper guide for the area that is available for purchase for those who prefer the feel of a physical guidebook. Additional thanks go to the many climbers who have contributed to the development of this area such as Chris Marley, Jesse Brown, Justin Iskra, David Lloyd, Jon Glassberg, Griffin Whiteside, and many more. Chris Marley in particular is responsible for a large share of the development. Chris found, cleaned, built landings for, and FAed many of the hardest and best boulders in the area in the early to mid 2010s. Some of his testpieces still have very few repeats.

There is still plenty of potential to explore and develop new boulders at the Rock Shop if you’re willing to walk, but if you choose to develop do not chip or reinforce holds. Many of the rocks in the area may have been climbed at some point and then reclaimed by lichen, so the developing experience can be enjoyed more than once! All of the established trails and climbs are on BLM and National Forest Land, but make sure to stay clear and be respectful of the private property that lies southwest of the main UFO zone.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: Heading out from Lander, look for a sharp turn off Highway 28 to access the Rock Shop. The "Low Clearance Parking" pin in this guide will take you directly to this turn. Shortly after turning off the highway you’ll encounter a large gate that you will have to open. Make sure to chain the gate closed behind you! From this point, the road becomes somewhat rough and rocky; low clearance vehicles may want to park here and hike into the climbing area. Otherwise, continue up the rocky road to the designated parking pins. The trails at the Rock Shop can be difficult to see and winding, so it is very easy to get lost. Downloading the trail data and boulder pins ahead of time can save you a lot of wandering! You will most likely not have service at the boulders.
webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering: Please note that the boulders in the “Property Line” area west of the UFO zone lie very close to private property to the south, and the landowner has a history of being aggressive towards climbers. However, all of the established trails and boulders are on BLM / National Forest land, so as long as you stay on the trails shown in the guide you will not be trespassing. DO NOT VENTURE SOUTH OF THE PROPERTY LINE TRAIL.

webSearchForLocation.name: Miller River
webSearchForLocation.description:
A vast river valley full of dense forests, tranquil streams, open talus and hidden behemoth boulders. Old mining era trinkets provide insights into a bygone era when these forests were first explored; the abandoned road grade from this era is perhaps the main reason any of these wondrous boulders were ever found in the first place. Rock quality is top-tier, movement is sublime and the setting is indescribably beautiful.

Purchase the paper guidebook from Pablo Zuleta here: https://westernwashingtonbouldering.com/guidebook

Look for signage indicating the Money Creek Campground for this turnoff. Follow the Old Cascade Highway past the campground and over the railroad tracks and continue for just a minute or so. Just before the washed out bridge and 'Road Closed' signs you'll turn right onto Miller River Road which will take you deep into the river valley and provide access to all the area and subarea parking and approaches.

webSearchForLocation.name: Berkeley
webSearchForLocation.description:
Overview: The boulders of Berkeley are the heart and soul of Bay Area climbing. Occasionally, in the history of American climbing, an area displays a unique charisma that reverberates across the country. This happened during the golden age of big wall climbing in Yosemite and again at Smith Rock with the development of sport climbing in the 1980s. These moments were only possible because Berkeley climbers, such as Dick Leonard, developed the dynamic belay at Indian Rock in the 1930s. Softer falls on a rope make it safer to push the boundary of what is possible. 

The rock is northbrae rhyolite which was thrown into the area by volcanic explosions about 10 million years ago. This explains why Berkeley is full of small, discrete clusters of boulders. These scattered areas were the “gym” before gyms existed. Over the decades, climbers have gotten creative with their options on limited real estate, leading to a long tradition of variations and linkups. The practice of making climbs harder – or simply different – by eliminating holds is something of a ritual that continues today. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the boulders of Berkeley served a home base for climbers in a chaotic and uncertain time. If you want to challenge yourself at these outdoor gyms, do the classic triple crown by climbing Nat’s Traverse, Grizzly Peak Traverse, and Gomer’s Pile in a single session. 

Conditions: You can climb in Berkeley all year. The weather never gets too hot or too cold, and the rock dries quickly after a storm. 

Rules: The bouldering is in city parks. They’re open from sunrise to sunset, and dogs need to be on a leash. Houses surround most of the bouldering, so be respectful of neighbors. 

Bathrooms: Do your business before heading out to climb. Only Cragmont Park has a porta-potty (wheelchair accessible). Don’t go to the bathroom in the residential neighborhoods.

Land Manager: City of Berkeley, Parks Division

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Approach: All of the boulders are near each area’s parking. In fact, the longest hike is a mere 200 feet. 

Accessibility: This is one of the most accessible areas in the Bay. Indian Rock, Great Stone Face Park, and Remillard Park are wheelchair accessible, and the parking is only 50 feet from the boulders. However, Mortar Rock has a handful of steps to access the climbing, and Grizzly Peak is along a single-file dirt trail.

webSearchForLocation.name: Mount Rubidoux
webSearchForLocation.description:
Overview Description

Mt Rubidoux is a regional park in Riverside CA just 5 minutes from downtown and nestled amongst beautiful Victorian houses. This boulder strewn hill has a deep history in Riverside and in climbing. Having been established for decades, this stomping grounds for the original Stonemasters is characterized by numerous slabs, cracks, and a surprising amount of highballs. The area saw a surge during the 80s due to outdoor bouldering competitions and is often the first taste of real rock for many new, local climbers. Rubi is also often used to practice placing gear and building anchors. It is great for beginners in boulders and routes alike as there are plenty of lower grade climbs and the hill is easily accessible. But, don't let the grades fool you. Many of the climbs can still pack a punch with more complex movement than you anticipate.

The best time to climb Mt. Rubidoux is Fall to Spring. With low elevation and not much tree cover, summer is exposed. Early morning sessions until midday are still possible during the summer if you have a half day and want to stay near home.

Local Ethic
Mt. Rubidoux is a highly accessible regional park. As with many areas with such open access, there is also litter and graffiti. Please be kind to the park. Pick up trash and clean up after yourself. Trash cans are available around the hill along the main trail. Doggy bags are available at the park entrance. Please be a leading example to others of the care and gratitude that should be given to outdoor spaces, however small.

I hope that, with more climbers on the boulders, the boulders will see less graffiti. Maintenance and oversight of an area is difficult and resources are limited. Please connect with local organizations and become a steward of your local outdoor spaces.

Restrooms are available at Ryan Bonaminio Park
Additional Info/History
Mt. Rubidoux is a staple for Riverside locals. If you grew up in Riverside, you probably spent time at Rubi late at night with your friends overlooking the cityscape. If you have spent time at Rubi after sunset, you have probably also heard the rumors that there are tunnels that run beneath the hill to the Mission Inn. Some speculate that these were used to move alcohol during the Prohibition. Now the rumored tunnels are for those fond of ghost stories and mysterious lore.
Over the past several years Mt Rubidoux has become a very popular place for fitness and health enthusiasts. On any morning you are likely to find families and pets, bikers, runners, yogis and more. When you are done getting your morning workout, the hill is just a few minutes from multiple other attractions such as Fairmount Park, the historic Mission Inn, and the museums and galleries of downtown Riverside. While downtown has seen a surge of delicious niche eateries, don’t overlook the classics. Hit Back to the Grind for coffee, art, board games, and open mic nights. Visit Tios Tacos for Mexican food, beautiful, bizarre junk art, and strawberry horchata.

webSearchForLocation.name: Index
webSearchForLocation.description:
The tiny mountain town of Index needs no introduction for Washington climbers as it's home to arguably the highest quality granite in the state (if not the world!). Climbers have cut their teeth for decades here on the notoriously sandbagged routes of the Upper and Lower Town Walls. Besides the legendary rope climbing, Index is home to numerous small bouldering clusters with equally high quality problems across a wide array of grades.

Purchase the paper guidebook from Pablo Zuleta here: https://westernwashingtonbouldering.com/guidebook

webSearchForLocation.name: Purgatory
webSearchForLocation.description:
What it might feel like to go bouldering on the moon. Blocks ranging from lowball traverses to dramatic highballs dot the hillside of this surprisingly decent desert area out in the middle of nowhere.

THE GOOD: Fairly Short Approaches, Some Roadside Boulders, No People
THE BAD: Long Drive, Very Sunny Exposure

The Purgatory Boulders float in a state of limbo somewhere between the biggest little city in the world and the edge of nowhere. This place is remote—there isn’t much else out here besides sagebrush and boulders. If you live in Reno and you’re looking for a fun winter day trip, Purgatory will help you get your fix. If you live further than Reno it’s a pretty long ways to get here, although some may prefer the remote location.

On any given day you will likely have the place all to yourself. The rock is featured granite and it varies in quality from good to fairly chossy. Some of the boulders are big, but most of them are average to small. There is a good variety of climbs up to V6 and a handful of harder problems for the stronger climber. Please be aware that fur trappers use the area as well and you may come across their traps at the boulders. If you do find traps, simply leave them alone. You probably won’t see rattlesnakes in the winter, but I’m sure in the spring there is a fair amount of snakes, so watch your step.

All the boulders are very obvious sitting in the open on the exposed hillside. Navigating can be a little tricky because there are so many smaller, chossy boulders mixed in with the good ones. You will need to spend a little time sorting it all out before you become familiar with the boulderfield. One key point is to remember that most of the boulders sit about 1/2 way up the hill, so traversing across the hillside at about that level should bring you through most of the
goods.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
DRIVING: Before leaving town, top off your gas tank as there is no reliable source of gas in the desert. From Reno take I-80 to Pyramid Hwy (Hwy 445) and follow it to Pyramid Lake. At the lake turn right on Hwy 446 and follow it to Nixon. Alternately take I-80 east out of Reno to Wadsworth, take the #43 exit then follow Hwy 447 to Nixon. From the Nixon store follow Hwy 447 for 41 miles and turn right onto a dirt road that is underneath large power lines. Drive under the power lines for 0.8 miles and turn left on a smaller dirt road. Continue for another 0.8 miles, turn right and drive for 0.6 miles and park at the boulders in the Main South Parking Lot. You will be looking at the boulder named “Welcome To Purgatory.” If you wish, continue on this road a short distance as it goes uphill and wraps around the boulders to the Upper South Parking Lot. This is a good way to access some of the boulders that sit higher up on the hill. Taking a look at the main overview before you head out the dirt road will be helpful.

For the North Parking Lot: From the highway drive under the power lines for 0.8 miles and turn left on a smaller dirt road. Continue for another 0.8 miles, stay left here, drive for 0.1 miles, turn right and park up on the hill at the end of the road after 0.2 miles.

APPROACH: From the South Parking Lot, walk north across the hillside through the boulderfield. Or, from the North Parking Lot walk south across the hillside through the boulderfield. Again, using the overviews is a great way to get started. Once you find the first boulder, use the boulder descriptions to find your way through the circuit

webSearchForLocation.name: Vernon
webSearchForLocation.description: Vernon, British Columbia offers a quieter climbing experience in the North Okanagan, with a handful of local crags that provide a good mix of sport, trad and bouldering options. While the climbing scene here isn’t as extensive as in nearby Kelowna, Vernon’s crags are easily accessible and see less traffic, making them a solid choice for those looking to avoid the crowds. The area’s dry climate and long seasons are a plus, and its proximity to Kelowna’s renowned Boulderfields adds variety for those willing to make the drive. Outside of climbing, Vernon has a relaxed, small-town feel with access to lakes, trails, and a local spots to grab a bite or a beer. It may not be a major climbing hub, but for locals and road-trippers alike, Vernon offers a low-key base with enough rock to keep things interesting.

webSearchForLocation.name: Castle Rock State Park
webSearchForLocation.description:
Before he was known for the world’s hardest deep water solos, or the world’s hardest sport climbs, or the world’s hardest boulders... Chris Sharma was just a local Santa Cruz kid, psyched on the sandstone of Castle Rock. We like to think there's a 90s Santa Cruz dude in all of us, and when you’re feeling demoralized, you can tap into his endless fount of psych. If you listen real close, he’ll tell you about Castle Rock:

... it’s good yo. You can grab the slopers and squeeze juice right out the rock, like this... pszaaa! Then you jump to the gaston like bhaaa! …

He goes in like this, without pause, so he's always there when you need him. The vaqueros sandstone of Castle Rock is reminiscent of Fontainebleau, and although the comparison is rather generous, it gives you the general vibe. With friendly rock, a range of difficulties, and flat landings, this might be the best climbing in the Bay Area.

Head out of the new parking lot and walk right (south) on Skyline Blvd. for 0.2 miles to the old parking lot. From here, walk uphill (south) along the Castle Rock Trail. Either make an immediate right onto a single file trail to pass by Parking Lot Rock, or continue along the main trail.

Conditions: Slopers like the cold, so a chilly day is going to be best. Otherwise, summers are hot but doable. As with all sandstone, the rock needs 3-5 days to dry after rain. If you climb on damp rock, you’re likely to break a hold, permanently changing the climb. Don’t do that.

Parking: Make your way to Saratoga Ave. in the quaint town of Saratoga. Follow CA-9/Big Basin Way up the mountain to the west for about 7 miles. Turn left on Skyline Blvd. once you reach the top. In 2.6 miles you will see the new parking lot on your right (west). The ideal parking is along the road 1/4 mile farther along Skyline Blvd. near the old parking lot, but these spots fill up fast.

Rules: Open 6:00am to sunset. No furry friends allowed. No wire brushes, glass bottles, picking plants, or smoking. No climbing for 3-5 days after rain. Visit wetrockpolice.com/castlerock or call (408) 868-9540 for conditions.

Accessibility: This is one of the most accessible areas, and while the climbing isn’t right near the parking, industrious wheelchair users have made the approach. From the old parking, go south on the main Castle Rock Trail for 1/3 mile. It is wider and not as steep as the common approach via Parking Lot Rock. This information is confirmed by ParacCiffHangers.

Bathroom: There is a wheelchair accessible bathroom at the old and new parking lots, and another accessible bathroom at Castle Rock itself.

Land Manager: Castle Rock State Park

webSearchForLocation.name: North Bend
webSearchForLocation.description:
North Bend sits at the western edge of the Cascades in the lush Snoqualmie Valley, just off I-90. The area is surrounded by steep forested hillsides, river valleys, and rocky ridges, giving it a rugged, alpine feel. Many bouldering spots are tucked away along rivers or creeks, especially in the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Valley, which is home to some of the most popular clusters of boulders. Closer to town, areas like Little Si are better known for sport climbing, but there are also scattered bouldering opportunities mixed in.

The rock in the North Bend area varies depending on location. In the Middle Fork Valley, the boulders are mostly granite, offering solid, clean climbing with good edges and friction. Closer to Little Si and Exit 32, the rock shifts to volcanic metamorphics, which can feel grittier and sometimes more polished, depending on traffic and exposure. Most problems are on low to medium-height boulders, with a mix of slabby faces, delicate crimps, and friction climbs. Overhanging or roof climbs do exist but are less common. The dense forest setting means that many problems are shaded and can take time to dry out after rain.

The Pacific Northwest climate plays a big role in climbing conditions around North Bend. Frequent rain and cool, shaded forests mean that rock can stay damp or mossy for long stretches, and some problems seep water well after storms. The best season is typically late spring through early fall, when dry stretches allow boulders to clean up and stay climbable.

Access is relatively straightforward, with forest roads leading to most trailheads, but conditions can vary — some roads are gated, rough, or washed out in places. The Middle Fork Trail is a main access route, so expect to share the area with hikers and other recreationists.

Please see the specific Areas and Subareas for approach beta.

webSearchForLocation.name: Sam's Throne
webSearchForLocation.description:
Sam's Throne  is the most unique region in the state. Hosting some of the best and varying types of sandstone in the state. With many crags to choose from and many of them being relatively small, planning ahead is important if you are heading to these areas. But man are they so so good!

Grab the paper guide from Cole Fennel here: https://www.naturalstatepublishing.com/product/arkansas-bouldering/

webSearchForLocation.name: Patapsco Valley State Park
webSearchForLocation.description:
The Patapsco Valley State Park encompasses 16,000 acres of protected land that follows 32 miles of the Patapsco River. The park is frequented by hikers, fishermen, mountain bikers, kayakers, bow hunters, horseback riders, and of course rock climbers!

Climbers have been visiting Patapsco for decades. This guide is only possible due to the many years of hard work by local developers, first ascentionists, and crag stewards who have found, cleaned, climbed, and secured access to the rocks listed here. Mark "Indy" Kochte's "Climb Maryland" guides are invaluable resources for any DMV climber. Go buy them now. https://nextascent.com/maryland-climbing-guidebook/ John Kelbel aka "Mr. Patapsco" has created an incredible resource which documents nearly every gosh darn hunk of rock in the park in google maps along with photos. The Kelbel guide is a treasure map for anyone wanting to do future development at Patapsco and can be found here. https://patapscorock.blogspot.com/ Justin Piteleski, John Brunson, Robin Close, and Mark Profeta deserve special mention for their initial wave of bouldering development. Their love for choss hunting is inspirational. Because of these motivated climbers, the phrase "There's no climbing in Maryland." is heard less and less these days. 

Finally, many of these crags are also used by graffiti artists and rapscallions who like to smash glass bottles and leave trash everywhere. Anytime you visit Patapsco bring an empty trash bag and try to leave with it full. The good karma will help you send your proj. Even better, volunteer with Mid Atlantic Climbers Adopt-A-Crag events to clean graffiti, broken glass, and trash. The authors of this guide have elected to donate the proceeds to Mid-Atlantic-Climbers to help fund these clean-ups.

webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering:
Much of the land within Patapsco Valley State Park is open to seasonal bow hunting. Consider wearing bright neon clothing. To learn more, visit: https://dnr.maryland.gov/publiclands/Pages/central/PatapscoValley/Hunting.aspx

Many areas have limited parking with no parking signs posted outside of the lots. Please follow all parking rules and if a lot is full, go to another nearby crag.

Numerous crags sit near the train tracks. Walking on the tracks is not permitted so stick to the trails! For more information please visit midatlanticclimbers.org

webSearchForLocation.name: Dixon School Road
webSearchForLocation.description:
Convenient to Charlotte, North Carolina, as well as the Upstate of South Carolina, Dixon School Road Boulders is a storied part of Crowders Mountain State Park in Gastonia, NC. While the park itself was founded in the 1970s, the rocks here have been climbed in some form or fashion since the 1980s. Most of the hardest and most famous of the established boulder routes went down in the 90s and 00s thanks to Doug Reed, Diab Rabie, Jr., and Gus Glitch.

Boulder Field Details:
This guide currently contains more than 200 problems. There are certainly more problems out there to be (re)established. If you have information on additional routes, add them with supporting footage. As they can be vetted, they'll be verified as part of this guide. In that same vein, I'm aware of still-open projects at Dixon. The RIC (Risk, Intensity, and Complexity) rating on some of these is extremely high. Feel free to try your hand at them, but do so at your own risk and with respect to the rules and regulations of the North Carolina State Parks system. Know your own limits and remember that no boulder problem is worth your life. Having said that, a route is eligible for inclusion in the verified guide only once it has been confirmed as sent.

The boulders are accessible all year long. You will stumble on folks working problems regardless of what the calendar or thermometer reads; however, prime climbing time is between October and February. More rainy days creep in during March and April. When the heat and humidity settle in with the approach of summer, the resulting reduced friction makes higher grade problems extremely difficult to work. Though, the combination of sharp holds and the abundance of shade at Dixon does provide for any outdoors trip to be successful.

As a smaller boulderfield (relative to those you'll find out West), Dixon is historically split into two main areas - Lower and Upper. Lower Dixon contains the boulders SW of the Ridgeline Trail Boulders Overlook access and Upper Dixon is roughly everything located NE of that point. The Ridgeline Trail runs just about parallel to the main boulder trail on the Eastern side in Upper Dixon, so you'll find most all of the boulders to the West of the main bouldering trail. Take note on the map of the paths that lead to some of the boulders that are downhill and away from other boulder clusters. 

If you are planning a trip to stay overnight, search local listings for more details. Nearby, construction is underway on a premier RV park and a large Casino resort.

Acknowledgements:
I'd like to shovel praise and appreciation to the area's original guidebook author, Matt Bielejeski. When I approached him for assistance on building this digital guide, he was ready with encouragement and accommodation. My only regret is that we didn't meet sooner. Thank you, Matt!
Additional gratitude is due to Mike Reardon, Executive Director of the CCC, and to Glen George, the Crowders Mountain State Park Superintendent. Both of these men's input and counsel have proven invaluable. Thanks to you both.

Finally, bouldering at Dixon would not be possible without all the support from the Carolina Climbers Coalition (CCC), the NC Division of Parks and Recreation, and the Friends of Crowders Mountain. If you enjoy any part that the park and/or boulder field has to offer, I highly encourage you to follow the links provided below to show your appreciation with a donation of any amount:

CCC
https://carolinaclimbers.org/donate

Crowders Mountain State Park
https://www.ncparks.gov/state-parks/crowders-mountain-state-park

Friends of Crowders Mountain
https://friendsofcrowders.com/donate/
>FOCM host a Saturday morning work day once a month at Crowders. If you want to give back and/or are heading out to climb anyway, why not join us for some park maintenance and refreshments?

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
The park's hours of operation coincide with Daylight Saving Time: 8AM-6PM EST; 8AM-9PM DST.

Contact the parks department using the information at the following link for more details: https://www.ncparks.gov/about-us

Crowders Mountain State Park - Directions and Area Description:
To access the boulders, head to 108 Van Dyke Road, Kings Mountain, NC 28086. There you'll find an outfitted ranger station (that was established in large part to the efforts of the CCC) with a blacktop parking lot, free parking, bathrooms with running water, office, and a boulders registration box. Whether you're hiking the Ridgeline Trail or bouldering, don't neglect the registration box - fill out the form before heading out to the field. Good record-keeping helps when budgetary evaluations come up for consideration. 

From the boulders registration box, you have three options for approaching the boulderfield:
1. You can hit the Ridgeline Trail straight away out the back of the ranger station. This is the most roundabout way to reach the boulders but a pleasant hike nonetheless. Follow this trail 1.1 miles to reach the boulderfield. If you do opt for this route, know that bouldering in the area behind the ranger station is strictly off limits. Discussions have been had about changing that. As of now, however, climbing outside of the boudlerfield proper is prohibited. Climb boulders only once you have crossed over Bethlehem Rd.
2. Head back out the entrance driveway toward Van Dyke Rd. Turn left and walk toward Bethlehem Rd, taking it down to the crosswalk. When you reach the crosswalk, hit the crossing button, turn right, and cross over the road to join the Ridgeline Trail. Follow this trail .3 miles to the Boulders Overlook. This will bring you to the back of the TMI and Incinerator boulders. Head SW for Lower Dixon and NE for Upper Dixon. This is the approach method endorsed by the rangers.
3. The most most common approach (although somewhat discouraged due to erosion concerns) is heading directly to the main boulderfield trail. Head back out the entrance driveway toward Van Dyke Rd. Turn left and walk toward Bethlehem Rd, taking it down to the crosswalk. When you reach the crosswalk, hit the crossing button, turn right, and cross over the road. Instead of continuing onto the Ridgeline, turn left and walk down a couple hundred feet to the power pole. You'll see the path that has been worn to make the main trail. Enter the field, look up to your left, and you'll see Zeus Eye almost immediately.
webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering:
Consider others before acting solely in your own interests. If you notice graffiti or other defacement of the boulders, message me directly so that I can coordinate cleanup efforts.
ETHICS: As the boulderfield is located on state park land, the following is a list of the most relevant (although not exhaustive) guidelines to follow for proper use:
-Roped climbing is explicitly prohibited at Crowders. While it was once permitted everywhere in the park, that is no longer the case.
-Do NOT uproot any vegetation or remove it from the park. You may carefully snip green briar stems and dead trees that have fallen over paths to make for safe access, but do not cut down living trees or uproot any vegetation.
-Do NOT create new foot paths, as it is unsafe and leads to erosion along elevation lines.
-Do NOT build landings. Chopping down trees to make a flatter plane is not only unethical but illegal.
-Do NOT clear brush the boulders. Brushing essential holds and only those spots that would be worn clean through normal climbing activities is permitted. Let the lichens be.
-Practice "Leave No Trace."

Violating these rules WILL create a hazardous environment and jeopardize the public's access to bouldering in the state. 
For more guidance on regulations at Crowders Mountain State Park and the Dixon School Road Boulders, visit https://www.ncparks.gov/about-us/guidelines-park-rules-and-regulations

webSearchForLocation.name: Porcupine Hills
webSearchForLocation.description:
The Porcupine hills are a large hilly area just East of the Front Ranges of the Rocky Mountains. There are a handful of rock outcroppings nestled in the forested hillsides, some of which have quality sandstone bouldering. The Skyline Boulders and The Beach Boulders are the most notable sections.

The boulders Skyline boulders are one of the most popular bouldering areas in Alberta and sees traffic mostly in the summer on weekends. The rock is generally quality sandstone that has formed large angular blocks although there are sections of more eroded boulders with bulbous features.

The most popular subarea is immediately around The Icebox boulder which hosts a high density of classic lines with approachable beginner and moderate lines to challenging test pieces.

There is a junction about halfway, the left trail leads more directly to the boulders especially the Middle Forest and Sunspot subareas, while the right trail leads directly to The Icebox subarea.

webSearchForLocation.name: Barton Creek Greenbelt
webSearchForLocation.description:
The data and descriptions for this guide are generously provided by Jeff Jackson, former editor of Climbing Magazine, the author of Texas Limestone Bouldering, and one of the original developers of Texas bouldering.

35% of the revenue from this guide supports the Texas Climbers Coalition.
https://www.texasclimberscoalition.org/
--

The Greenbelt refers to the seven and a half mile natural sanctuary that protects the Barton Creek watershed. This continuous park system starts at Barton Springs and continues well beyond Mopac. The Greenbelt offers hiking and mountain biking trails, and, when the water is up, swimming, kayaking and canoeing. There are five cliffs that have been developed for sport climbing and an abundance of good boulder problems with many more undeveloped areas waiting for motivated scrubbers.

- Jeff Jackson

webSearchForLocation.name: Utah Hills
webSearchForLocation.description_routes: The Utah Hills are the mountains to the West of St George, UT. They are officially named The Beaver Dam Mountains, but locally referred to as the Utah Hills, because they are the last range of mountains inside Utah before you cross into Arizona traveling South on Old Highway 91. There are over 20 outstanding limestone crags in the Utah Hills, containing hundreds of routes, with grades ranging from 5.6 to 5.15b. Rock climbing development began in the late 1980's, and continues to this day. The styles range from short and bouldery, to long endurance test pieces, to adventurous 5-pitch sport routes on overhanging rock.

webSearchForLocation.name: Price Canyon
webSearchForLocation.description:
Price Canyon offers some nice sandstone bouldering about an hour and a half from Salt Lake City. The majority of the climbing can be found in the Price Canyon Recreation Area, although more recent development has brought to life more boulders in the surrounding area. The best climbing conditions are typically found in Spring and Fall. The Recreation Area stays about 10 degrees cooler than surrounding areas, making the Price is Right and Wheel of Fortune zones a nice early Fall / late Spring option. The Sun Gulley and Holy Grail zones get a lot of sun, making those areas accessible for most of the Winter.

Many of the boulders are small and can be climbed solo with just a couple pads. However there are a few high quality highballs that you’ll want to rally the crew for. Grades range from v0 to v12, with a handful of harder projects yet to be done. If you climb the grade, Turtle Head (v8) is a must do for the area.

If you are coming from Salt Lake City, Price Canyon could be a more “Day Trippable” option than Joe’s Valley when you’re craving some sandy grips. The Recreation Area is en route to Joe’s, so it could also be an easy pit stop if you’re headed to Joe’s for a longer trip.

Follow leave no trace practices when you visit. Particularly when in the Price Recreation Area, be respectful of the land and your impact. Park in designated pull-offs only. Climbers currently have a good relationship with the Recreation Area management and we want to keep it that way. Car camping is not permitted in the Recreation Area at the climbing pull-offs - however a nice paid camping area with water and bathrooms is available at the end of the recreation road.

Banner photo was taken by Martin Bigatti of Weston Gastrock on "Off the Couch" (v9, Price is Right sub area)

webSearchForLocation.name: Catoctin Mountain
webSearchForLocation.description:
Catoctin Mountain National Park is a true Maryland gem. While there aren't THAT many problems here, each area has one to two really highly classic problems on good stone. Standouts include: Bullfrog Arete, Neon Pit Stain, Walk into the Sky, Next Gen, Boss Hog, Slippy Toad, and The General. 

A big wave of development hit Catoctin in the early 2000s by the usual characters: Tim Rose, Travis Gault, ChetRoy, Kyle Stapp, Smitty, Brian Brotherton, Matt Bosley, Chris Bursey, and others. The park was then closed, tragically, until 2016 when it was reopened to the rejoice of Maryland climbers everywhere. 

What followed was a secondary wave of development from myself, Eric Jerome, and friends John Brunson, Robin Close, Justin Pitelski, CGIII, and more. 

While it appears most of the best climbing in Catoctin has been found and climbed, a newer community has continued to fill in the gaps and climb the less desirable lines throughout the park, often adding them to Mountain Project. While I don't always "agree" with some of the more contrived and link-up lines, I can appreciate that with limited outdoor bouldering resources in the state, it can be fun to move on rock, and I have included a good number of these problems (even though it pains me at times). 

The Future Roof Project awaits for anyone strong and motivated, and it will surely be the hardest problem in the park. 

This guide was created in collaboration with Mid-Atlantic Climbers and Catoctin Park Service. 50% of all revenue generated will be donated to MAC. Please be respectful of the boulders that the park has asked climbers to avoid (they aren't the good ones anyway). We want to climb here for decades to come, and being good stewards is a crucial part of the equation! 

Enjoy, thanks, Eric.

What followed was a secondary wave of development from myself, Eric Jerome, and friends John Brunson, Robin Close, Justin Pitelski, CGIII, and more. 

While it appears most of the best climbing in Catoctin has been found and climbed, a newer community has continued to fill in the gaps and climb the less desirable lines throughout the park, often adding them to Mountain Project. While I don't always "agree" with some of the more contrived and link-up lines, I can appreciate that with limited outdoor bouldering resources in the state, it can be fun to move on rock, and I have included a good number of these problems (even though it pains me at times). 

The Future Roof Project awaits for anyone strong and motivated, and it will surely be the hardest problem in the park. 

This guide was created in collaboration with Mid-Atlantic Climbers and Catoctin Park Service. 50% of all revenue generated will be donated to MAC. Please be respectful of the boulders that the park has asked climbers to avoid (they aren't the good ones anyway). We want to climb here for decades to come, and being good stewards is a crucial part of the equation! 

Enjoy, thanks, Eric.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
I doubt anyone will read this, since fortunately, Google Maps exists! Do note, Park Central Road often closes seasonally. I will do my best to update this guide with an access banner when applicable, but please do check the NPS website before making the journey in the winter! 

Directions from Major Population Centers

From Washington, D.C.:

Take the George Washington Memorial Parkway North to I-495, then I-270 North toward Frederick (about 27 miles).

Continue on U.S.-15 North ~17 miles to Thurmont, MD.

Exit onto Route 77 West (signed for Catoctin Mountain Park) and drive ~3 miles.

Turn right onto Park Central Road to the Visitor Center and main access areas.

From Baltimore, MD:

Take I-695 to I-70 West toward Frederick.

Merge onto U.S.-15 North to Thurmont, then follow Route 77 West and Park Central Road as above.

From Hagerstown, MD:

Drive I-70 East to Route 66 North, then right on Route 64 to Route 77 East.

Continue ~7 miles and turn left on Park Central Road.

From Gettysburg, PA:

Take U.S.-15 South to Thurmont, exit toward Route 77 West, then right on Park Central Road.

webSearchForLocation.name: Big Rock, SC
webSearchForLocation.description:
Located near Pickens, SC, and owned by Naturaland Trust, Big Rock is the only significant cliff open year-round in SC. Naturaland Trust purchased the 1,648-acre property in 2013. Through a partnership with Naturaland Trust, the Carolina Climbers Coalition was able to officially open this wonderful place to climbers in 2017.

Big Rock faces south and is primarily a Spring/Fall/Winter destination. In 2017, the CCC funded part of the current parking lot construction thanks to a grant from REI. In 2019, the CCC contributed $5,000 to Naturaland Trust to secure a 1-acre lot north of the new parking lot, creating a buffer for expanded access.

There are around 50 routes and several hundred boulder problems spread out across the pinnacles and boulderfields, all overlooking upstate SC. All guidebook author proceeds for this KAYA guide are donated directly to the Carolina Climbers Coalition.

Please support this organization, become a member, and join a trail day! You can donate to Naturaland Trust's work at www.naturalandtrust.org

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Main Parking Area: The gravel parking lot with a paved entrance on Big Rock Lake Road, Pickens, SC. It is labeled with a ""P"" on a post on the road and is located just past Charles Towne Rd. DO NOT PARK ON THE ROAD IF PARKING IS FULL!!! DO NOT PULL DOWN CHARLES TOWNE RD!  The CCC funded part of the parking lot thanks to grants Trailhead location from REI and help from Naturaland Trust. Follow the trails from the lot to the cliff and the boulders.

Alternative Parking: If you discover that the Main Parking lot is full, exit the neighborhood and drive to the intersection of Preston McDaniel Road and Nine Times Road. Here there is a gravel parking lot and a large grassy lot.

From the alternate parking lot, walk across E Preston McDaniel rd and follow the gravel road for 0.1 mile. Once you are beneath the power lines look for a trail sign on the right side of the road. Take the path to the right to begin the Big Rock Mtn Summit trail, which has green blazes.Follow the obvious trail with green blazes uphill for 0.4 miles to reach an old logging road. Continue to follow the green blazes on the logging road for 0.2 miles. At the next trail sign, make a right turn to continue on the Big Rock Mtn Summit trail. Continue to follow the green blazes for 0.1 mile to reach the left shoulder of big rock, near the inversion wall.  ~1.25 miles
webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering: Only use the existing trail system. Camping is not allowed. No alcoholic beverages. Please be respectful of local residents - keep a low profile in the parking lot, keep the noise down and drive slowly on the road. Do not turn into driveways of nearby homes to turn around.                                                        Any commercial guiding outfit wishing to guide at Big Rock Mountain must obtain permission from the landowners, Naturaland Trust.

webSearchForLocation.name: Rogers Park
webSearchForLocation.description:
The data and descriptions for this guide are generously provided by Jeff Jackson, former editor of Climbing Magazine, the author of Texas Limestone Bouldering, and one of the original developers of Texas bouldering.

35% of the revenue from this guide supports the Texas Climbers Coalition.
https://www.texasclimberscoalition.org/
--

God made a fine little Klettergarten. Why did he have to put it in Belton? Ever since a local Bible thumper plugged my truck with a .22 caliber rifle and scribbled "Devil Worshipper" in the dust on the front door, I've been down on the pervasive fundamentalist attitude that permeates the Temple/Belton area like a stinky fart. Sure, I wired a goat skull to the grill of my truck. Does that make me Satanic? I don't think so. The quality and difficulty of some of the problems at Rogers Park might have you making deals with the devil, howev-er. This mile or so of perfect pockets is, arguably, the nicest limestone pocket bouldering in Texas. There is something for everyone at Rogers. Steep lines, vertical lines, highballs and dumpy little grovel-fests will nurture your every fetish. Be sure to spend some time at the Billiards Wall, and if you're having trouble sending, don't hesitate to kneel down and call on Jehova for help. He might actually hear you, given the number of churches and blue-hair Baptists per square foot in Belton. I think the devil has moved to Austin for the booze and weed. Wait a minute, is that the devil? Or is that Dave Phillips?

Give thanks to the Phillip's brothers for unveiling Rogers Park. One night in 1979 Russell Tullick wandered away from the campfire and fell off the top of the Flake Wall. Luckily, his joints were well oiled with beer and he hit like a sack of beans. It took him most of the night to crawl back to the rim. The Phillips' brothers were quizzical. Where had Russell been? They've been bouldering at Rogers ever since.

- Jeff Jackson

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: From Austin: Drive north on 135 for 60 miles to the outskirts of Belton. Exit 293A "Central Ave. Downtown" and turn left (west). After passing down-town, turn right (north) onto 317 (Main). Turn left on FM 439. Turn right on FM 2271. Cross over the Belton Dam and continue for a couple of miles Turn left on Morgan's Point Rd (F.M. 2483). Right on Rogers Park Rd. Park at the Rodgers Park boat ramp area. From here, walk along the asphalt road which parallels the shore. When the road cuts up the hill look for a faint climbers trail off right which follows the base of the cliff band. Some climbers have been parking at a dead end and approaching the cliffs from the top. This has resulted in a few run-ins with the local fuzz.

webSearchForLocation.name: Salt Point
webSearchForLocation.description: Salt Point State Park is an otherworldly environment. The boulders are exposed along the coast, and you might feel like a small speck beholding the grandeur of nature. You will come to appreciate the tides, since the power of the ocean is always within sight, sometimes even lapping at your crash pads. Each small area has its own charm, from the tide-pool landing of Gerstle Cove to the territorial sea lions of The Secrets. While the rock itself can be on the sandier side, the location makes the whole experience rather sublime.
