webSearchForLocation.name: The Citadel
webSearchForLocation.description:
**50% of the revenue from this guide is donated to the Southeastern Climbers Coalition**

Special thanks to the Southeastern Climbers Coalition, Adam Henry, Bob Cormany, Craig Stannard, Jake Slaney, Daron Harris, Christy Wood, Chris Harris, Chris Watford, Rob Robinson, Andrew Traylor, Michael Hanks, Maurice Reed, John Barr, Anne Shields, Brad McLeod, Gus Fontenot, Nathan Steele, and Kanaan Crutchfield for helping make this area what it is and securing permanent access to a very special place.  Meagan Evans, Kate Hanes, and Caleb Timmerman with the Southeastern Climbers Coalition worked tirelessly to make public permanent access to the Citadel a reality, so thank them when you see them.  Thanks to Cal Graffeo for creating the maps and helping with kiosk signage.  The information in this guide is the culmination of many climbers helping to clean, climb, and verify grades of problems. Many more have surely been lost to moss and lichen over the years.  This guide is a living document, so if you have information regarding problem names/grades that are not listed in this guide, please submit them in KAYA and/or send pictures and info to George Evans at ghevans90@gmail.com.

JOIN AND DONATE TO THE SOUTHEASTERN CLIMBERS COALITION! 50% of the revenue from this guide is donated to the SCC.

When visiting this area:

- Park in designated areas, avoiding parking on the side of the road or in the old parking area near the tall low angle slab.

- Pack it out - don’t trash the area - leave it better than you found it.  Show the local community that climbers are a user group that makes places better.

- Don’t be a nuisance - leave the bluetooth speakers at home and be kind to non-climbers/locals visiting the area.  Make a good impression.

- Brush your ticks - if you need ‘rookie stripes’ to climb your mega proj, make sure they’re gone when you leave the boulder.

- Dogs must be leashed and controlled at all times -  If Fido can’t be stopped from digging, barking, and running on the pads, leave him at home.  Don’t leave dog poop for others to drop their pads in…

- No fires or camping - there are primitive options nearby and tons of AirBnB/VRBO options in the area.
Avoid areas that are off property.

- If it is not covered on the map, it is outside of SCC property boundaries and should not be visited.  This currently also includes the Pearl (across the road).

- Climb smart - rock climbing is an inherently dangerous sport.  Use pads and spotters. The grades and lines in this guide are suggestions and are not guaranteed to be correct so use your best judgment and climb within your abilities.

- Keep pads and feet on established trails and durable surfaces - don’t create spider trails by shortcutting to your proj and don’t smash plant life with your pads.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
ACCESS HISTORY

Native Lands: Tsalaguwetiyi (Cherokee, East), S'atsoyaha (Yuchi)
source: Native-Land.ca

The Southeastern Climbers Coalition (SCC) is a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization dedicated to preserving access to outdoor climbing areas in the southeast for present and future generations. The SCC acquired the Citadel Boulders in 2023 to conserve this unique climbing area and open it to the public for climbing access and passive recreation for generations to come.

The iconic Citadel Boulders were secured thanks to hard work from local volunteers and with support from Access Fund, Riverview Foundation, Lyndhurst Foundation, and the Georgia Alabama Land Trust. By all our powers combined, our climbing community was able to gain access and preserve the Citadel Boulders.

Fort Payne locals remember the property as Citadel Rocks, a local attraction owned by the Eberhart family in the 1950s. The land was later owned by the Klatt Family. Ernest F. Klatt "Ernie" diligently worked from a young age as a migrant farmer in exchange for land so that he could build a better life for him and his family. The Citadel held a sentimental and special value for Ernest's daughter, Elsie Winchester and her family, as Earnest loved the incredible rock formations here.

The Citadel also has a long history of climbing dating back to the late 80s and early 90s. Many legendary southeastern names can be found on first ascents throughout The Citadel. SCC welcomes the public to enjoy the rock climbing, hiking trails and natural beauty of this area.

Access is offered in accordance with the Alabama Recreational Use Statute (Alabama Code 35-15-1 et seq.). If you choose to enter this area you are voluntarily choosing to assume all risk of personal injury and/or property loss.

webSearchForLocation.name: Great Falls
webSearchForLocation.description: Great Falls bouldering is characterized by its unique river polished rock, creating powerful slopey movement. While crimpy lines can be found more inland, much of the harder test-pieces are found closer to the Potomac and feature low friction compression. The bouldering history of Great Falls is shrouded in mystery. The old masters from Carderock would venture here as training for routes. While very little was recorded, there is evidence that most of the boulders within this guidebook had been climbed long ago. The approaches can be tricky and the boulders difficult to find, but the beauty of the park makes it truly rewarding. If planning your first trip, I recommend Purple Horse Area as most of the boulders are right off the trail and there are some solid classics like Show of Hands V3, Purple Horse Problem V5 and Emergence V6. For those looking for a challenge choose Spitzbergen for classics like Double Slap V9, Violent Touch V10 and Art of Flight V8.

webSearchForLocation.description_short_bouldering: Adventure crag with low friction, powerful movement on river polished rock. Over 100 boulders up to V12 with potential for more development.
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: On the MD side, parking at Old Angler Inn will be the best approach. The lot is free, but it fills up quickly on weekends so plan accordingly. Entrance fee required to enter the VA portion of the park. An America the Beautiful national park card can be used to cover the entrance fees, otherwise it is $20 per car. Alternative free parking available at the Difficult Run lot off Georgetown Pike (also gets crowded fast). Some areas are significantly off the main trails and have been flagged as "access sensitive." While access is being clarified with the park, prioritize areas that are right off the trails, especially on busy weekends.

webSearchForLocation.name: Hammond Pond
webSearchForLocation.description:
Nestled within the Hammond Pond Reservation in Newton, just southwest of Boston, Hammond Pond is one of the most accessible outdoor bouldering areas in the greater Boston region. The climbing here takes place on Roxbury puddingstone, a distinctive sandstone-conglomerate that’s actually the official state rock of Massachusetts. This rock is made up of pebbles and cobbles set in a finer matrix, giving the surfaces a unique texture - pockets, dimples, and irregular edges that feel very different from the granite or basalt you’ll find at many other New England crags.

LOWER GRADES HERE ARE STIFF! Many of the lower graded climbs here were established decades ago, in an era where the hardest climbs were V3s. Over the years, while climbing grading has adapted, the grades on these problems haven't. On the uber-classic Alcove wall, climbers who've sent V6 or higher indoors may still struggle on the V3s here. Embrace it, and enjoy the humble pie. You're climbing on history.

The season here favors spring and fall, when temperatures are cooler. Summer can be sticky and humid, and winter sees fewer visits due to cold and moisture on the rock, though determined climbers can still find good conditions on drier, sunny days.

As always, please treat this crag and other park visitors with respect. Pack out what you pack in, leave no trace, brush your ticks, wipe your shoes, and lets keep this little outdoor urban gym accessible for generations to come.

Head to Hammond Pond Trail for the Alcove Boulders. The approach from the parking is steep but short.

For the Temple Boulders, a new parking area has just been built. Follow the GPS in this guide to access it. Do NOT park at the Temple itself! Parking for the Pinnacle Boulders is in flux with the newly constructed greenway, but however you access these boulders, make sure you park legally.

webSearchForLocation.name: Sierra Buttes
webSearchForLocation.description:
About an hour northeast of Truckee, In the Lakes Basin at the Sierra Buttes you will find steep, powerful face climbing on rock that is very unique in texture to the Tahoe area. If you're looking to pull down hard this is the spot.

THE GOOD: Outstanding Boulders, Steep Problems, Multiple Areas

THE BAD: Rattlesnakes, Slick Rock, Lots Of Edge Ladder Problems, Gnar Approach

The data in this guide comes from Dave Hatchett's Bouldering Lake Tahoe Outlying Addition.

webSearchForLocation.name: Tieton River
webSearchForLocation.description: Bouldering following along the Tieton River from Rimrock lake down to the end of US 12. Lots of solid rock and plenty of choss. The area is mostly know for its trad and sport climbing but for the boulderers that want to get out there, there is an option.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Coming up from Yakima take a left onto Highway 12 and pull off for road side bouldering. 
Coming from Packwood head East on Highway 12. There will be boulders as soon as Clear Lake and as far as the Elk feeding station.

webSearchForLocation.name: Nut Tree
webSearchForLocation.description:
Overview: Everything we do, and every choice we make, is the result of an uncountable number of causal processes. In order for you to climb at the Nut Tree boulders, you must be first introduced to climbing. For this to happen, you had to be born, and this required the evolution of life on this planet, which wouldn’t have been possible without the Big Bang. It’s easy to get lost in this forest of causation, but for the moment, let’s focus on one tiny slice of causal history. How did a scattering of basalt boulders end up on an unassuming hillside in Vacaville?

Basalt is a volcanic rock that forms when a lava flow rapidly cools down. You’re probably thinking that there are no volcanoes in the Central Valley. There are, however, plenty on the east side of the Sierra Nevada, and the going theory is that Thompson Peak (north of Lake Tahoe near Susanville) erupted about 15 million years ago, depositing basalt across Northern California. Your day of bouldering required a giant explosion that sent lava flying hundreds of miles.

Today this grassy hillside is part of Browns Valley Open Space. While the adjacent land is covered in houses, the climbing is surrounded by oak trees and cattle. The rock forms blocky features, and because of the natural fissures between the basalt chunks, holds are numerous.

The City of Vacaville has a good relationship with climbers overall, but there has recently been tension with local homeowners due to noise. Remember, you’re visiting someone’s backyard, so keep the noise down.

Conditions: The summer is hot, 110 degrees hot, so don't even try. The dry days of winter are the best, although the cooler days in the fall and spring can also make for a pleasant outing. Because the area is subject to the “rain shadow” effect, Nut Tree generally has less precipitation than the boulders on the western side of the Coastal Range.

Rules: Open from sunrise to sunset. Dogs need to be on a leash so that they don’t bother the cattle. Be respectful of the surrounding neighborhoods, keep the noise down, and don’

webSearchForLocation.name: Santee Boulders
webSearchForLocation.description: Comparable to Berkeley's urban crags, Santee is the most accessible bouldering area in San Diego. Made up of a small collection of good quality and well developed granite boulders, Santee offers up a diverse set of climbing styles and difficulties. Although you can pretty much see all the boulders from the trailhead, most blocks have been combed over by locals for several decades and many feature a shocking number of fun routes. Unlike other San Diego crags like Mount Woodson, Santee's extensive trail network means no bushwhacking is required. Due to its age, many of the routes are stiff to sandbagged, but if you can leave the ego at the door the humility is worth the reward.

webSearchForLocation.name: Bellingham
webSearchForLocation.description:
Sandstone in the PNW! It's a thing. Please don't climb on wet rock, and give it a couple days to dry out. 

A note about Lost Ledge: Please stay on trails, and do not develop new boulders on the Rock Trail down to the boulders. The park has explicitly made this request of climbers, and we need to follow it to ensure access remains sustainable at Lost Ledge.

Purchase the paper book by Jason D. Martin at https://shop.alpineinstitute.com/products/rock-climbing-and-bouldering-in-the-chuckanut-mountains

A Discover Pass is required to park at any of the parking spots within Larrabee State Park. This pass can be purchased at many outdoor gear stores throughout Washington, such as REI, Big 5 Sporting Goods, and other local shops. The Discover Pass costs $35 for the year and must be displayed while parked.

Click here for more info: https://www.discoverpass.wa.gov/133/Where-to-Buy
webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering:
!!!NO CLIMBING ON WET SANDSTONE!!!

Please allow 48-72 hours to pass after rainfall for sandstone to adequately dry before climbing. Larrabee sandstone is particularly soft and prone to breaking once it is wet. Have patience to ensure climbs remain intact for years to come!

webSearchForLocation.name: Wadi Rum
webSearchForLocation.description: Wadi Rum, an absolutely breathtaking landscape. It is filled with endless rock, from towering sandstone walls to aesthetic boulders. Climbing there always feels as if you're on an epic adventure, wether you choose to boulder, multi pitch or sport climb. Season: The main season is from October to mid April, Where You're met with mild temperatures during the day and cold temperatures at night with overall a small amount of rainy days.The experience of wadi rum as a whole is truly unique as you will get to know the culture, food and the ways of the local Bedouins who are some of the most hospitable people you will come across.

webSearchForLocation.description_short_bouldering: A climbers absolute dream. From Boulders to Big walls. Wadi Rum will provide an unforgettable experience
webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering:
Getting There: Climbers visiting Wadi Rum should use the Queen alia international airport in amman. Transportation to the desert can be done by renting a car (4x4 recommended), and driving on the desert highway which will be about a three and a half hour drive to wadi rum. There are Busses running from Amman to wadi rum as well.

Arriving in Wadi rum: Upon arrival if in a private vehicle an entrance fee for the vehicle and for visitors must be paid at the wadi rum visitors centre. If you are not driving your own vehicle and hiring a local to drive you around you will be able to organise transportation and meeting points with your guide. 

Jordan pass: A good recommendation is buying the Jordan pass before traveling to Jordan as it covers the cost of the entrance fee to wadi rum as well as multiple touristic sites such as Petra.

Accommodation: There is a large selection of camps to choose from in wadi rum with ranging prices and comfort. Camping on your own is also possible!

Ethics and tips: Please respect the locals and keep the desert clean. Always remember that some climbing areas are remote with no cell signal. A good tip is to make sure someone knows where you will be going before you head off, That be your camp or a friend. For more info visithttps://www.almahabouldering.com

webSearchForLocation.name: Lion’s Den
webSearchForLocation.description:
Overview Description -
Lion’s Den is where the strong reign and the weak become strong. Grading has been made consistent per the OG developer’s wishes. Thus, making this place perfect for projects and training.
Topo Line - 
The line follows where the hips will generally be. Your center of gravity will generally follow this line. If the climb has circles around hold(s), those are the starting hand holds for the climb.  
Crag Season -
This is a Fall/ Winter Crag. Spring brings too many wild plants to life that makes moving around hard. Summer is just hot, but the early morning and evening works. Early Spring is still worth it, I will try to create a sustainable trail system.
Geology - 
The geology of this place is mesozoic granite, quartz monzonite, granodiorite, and quartz diorite and tonalite. All these rock types are igneous rocks that are coarse-grained, resembling granite. 
Local Beta - 
Not much is around Lion’s Den. I recommend bringing water, food and snacks. There’s no public restroom either, so take care of your business before arriving. From the 215 fwy, you have several restaurants and groceries off of Newport Road or Scott Road. From the 79 hwy, there’s not much around so use what you can find.Local Ethic - 
Follow Leave No Trace (LNT) principle. Respect the signs of trespassing. Don’t overcrowd the parking lot, a lot of workers and construction trucks go by.
Additional Info/History - 
Skyler Irish was the first person to document climbing potential for this area. He brought over some friends who helped out a lot like Gavin Bridgeman and Isamer Bilog. Gavin helped establish numerous lines with Skyler in order to fill in Lion’s Den climbing list while Isamer put up some astonishing climbs that will make any one hesitate. Now Adan Morales and Baboon Stewardship will continue this legacy to help expand this climbing area properly.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: The main parking lot is small and a bit secluded. As of 2026, this small space is being blocked by construction workers. You have to park inside the area in a small turnout on the right, but you will need high clearance for that. Driving there is accessible from either the north or south side. From the north, you’ll drive from Domenigoni Pkwy to Leon Rd. Turn into Leon Rd heading south, the road turns into dirt road and bends to the right heading east. At the next bend is the parking spot.  From the south, drive from Scott Rd to Leon Rd. Turn into Leon Rd heading north. It’ll eventually become a dirt road. At the bend is the parking lot.
webSearchForLocation.access_issues_description_bouldering: All bouldering at The Lion's Den is situated on privately owned property. Historically, climbers have accessed the main Lion's Den boulders without push back from land owners. Serengeti, Narwal, and Ramon's Egg Ranch are off limit at this time. However, access to these areas may be subject to restrictions imposed by the current property owner(s) at any given time, so climbers should respect property rights and adhere to any posted signage or regulations.

webSearchForLocation.name: Conejo Mountain
webSearchForLocation.description:
Great sandstone boulder field located underneath the powerlines of the Conejo open space. Often visited by hikers and bikers, the climbing here can make for a great day out with something for everyone. Most of the climbing is in the easy to moderate range making it a great place for beginner to intermediate climbers looking to boulder outside with fewer pads. 

This area's rock is fragile and requires some time to dry after rain. 

It is also within close proximity to private property, so please keep a low profile, don't play music or make a lot of noise, and generally respect the neighborhood around you, otherwise access will be at risk.

A special thanks to Randall Phenning, Stuart Wilson, Alex Ostrovsky, Michael DiFronzo for their time in developing the area.

webSearchForLocation.access_description_bouldering: The only legal access point to these boulders is by following the trail that begins on Calle Alta Vista. Parking GPS can be found in the Approach information, on individual climb pages, or by tapping the P on the map.

webSearchForLocation.name: McKinney Falls
webSearchForLocation.description:
McKinney Falls State Park is the backyard Austin bouldering destination for many central Texas climbers during the winter season. Being about 20 minutes from downtown Austin, it’s relatively easy to access. The park is open daily from 8 am to 10 pm with adult day passes costing $6. McKinney consists of about 50 yards of rock climbing that follows along Onion Creek. McKinney is home to a number of quality lines that will mainly test your incut and pocket strength. The climbing in this area is classically known for being stout and tweaky. Therefore, a proper warmup is essential for longevity in the park. Climbing temps for McKinney fall during the winter months, with the ideal temperatures being sub-60 degrees. Additionally, with the park being open till 10 pm, you can capture even better temps at night.

Climbing is only accessible during operating hours of the park.

There are a few local ethics that are crucial to McKinney Falls and outdoor climbing as a whole. 1. Chalk up before you touch the rock; don’t be a grease monkey.   
2. Don’t spray beta; people don’t care.  
3. Pack in pack out; this isn’t yo mommas house. 
4. Brush your ticks off the wall after climbing.

parent_location.name: Little Cottonwood Canyon
parent_location.description:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s climbing area sits just 20 minutes southeast of downtown Salt Lake City and stands as one of North America’s most concentrated city-side climbing spots. Both local and professional traveling climbers have spent decades developing the canyon, which now boasts over 5,000 boulder problems. 

The canyon’s granite walls have drawn climbers’ attention for more than 40 years, however, the area has experienced rapid growth over the last several years—now hosting two of the hardest problems in the country, “The Grand Illusion” and “Sosa,” both (V16).

Little Cottonwood’s unique quartz monzonite walls give climbers a unique granite experience, with some small pockets of limestone throughout—particularly at the mouth of the canyon. The rock is characterized by crystal-heavy slopers and crimps lower in the canyon, tighter grained rock at higher elevations, friction dependence, and slippery, textureless holds on more popular climbs.

Season:
Little Cottonwood Canyon’s best climbing happens during fall and spring. The canyon’s climbing conditions reach their sweet spot in October/November. Temperatures stay between 66°F highs and 44°F lows. Nearly all areas will be accessible during these months.The spring also offers great conditions, however climber’s will have to navigate the melting snowpack, the degree to which varies year-to-year.

History:
Mike Beck began climbing in the mid 1980s. In 1988, following a bouldering trip to the world-famous Fontainebleau, France, Mike Beck was inspired upon returning back home to Salt Lake City. At the time, there were maybe 50 problems in the canyon, maximum. That visit to France kicked off an explosion of him and his friends seeking out and developing the bouldering in LCC in a concerted effort.

He and his friends collaborated to create The Black Bible, a guidebook to Utah bouldering. Mike lead the charge on the LCC chapters and this was the primary source of recorded bouldering information for many years. In more recent years, Mike teamed up with a newer climber and data geek, Scott Stoddard. Together, using Scott’s technical and organization skills and Mike’s historical knowledge, they authored a new and extremely comprehensive guidebook for Little Cottonwood Canyon on KAYA.

Read the full article for everything you need to know when bouldering at Little Cottonwood Canyon: https://blog.kayaclimb.com/essential-lcc-climbing-guide-when-where-how-to-boulder-in-little-cottonwood/

Take the 6200 South exit from I-215 and follow the ski resort signs. The canyon road (Route 210) guides you straight to the climbing spots, and you'll park along the road to reach most areas. Use KAYA to navigate the approaches directly to your climb of choice.

Due to the city-side nature of the canyon, you are never more than 20 minutes from snacks, gas, food, and water. There are numerous great places to eat in Salt Lake City, but climber favorites include Central 9th Market, Pretty Bird Hot Chicken, and Spitz.
